passages.stem_html: Let \(f:[0,1]\to\mathbb R\) (the set of all real numbers) be a function. Suppose the function \(f\) is twice differentiable, \(f(0)=f(1)=0\) and satisfies \(f''(x)-2f'(x)+f(x)\ge e^x\), \(x\in[0,1]\).
Consider the polynomial \(f(x)=1+2x+3x^2+4x^3\). Let \(s\) be the sum of all distinct real roots of \(f(x)\) and let \(t=|s|\).

Let \(f_1:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\) and \(f_2:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\) be defined by \(f_1(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x\prod_{j=1}^{21}(t-j)^j\,dt\), \(x>0\) and \(f_2(x)=98(x-1)^{50}-600(x-1)^{49}+2450\), \(x>0\), where, for any positive integer \(n\) and real numbers \(a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n\), \(\prod_{i=1}^na_i\) denotes the product of \(a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n\). Let \(m_i\) and \(n_i\), respectively, denote the number of points of local minima and the number of points of local maxima of function \(f_i\), \(i=1,2\), in the interval \((0,\infty)\).
Let \(F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be a thrice differentiable function. Suppose that \(F(1)=0\), \(F(3)=-4\) and \(F'(x)<0\) for all \(x\in(1/2,3)\). Let \(f(x)=xF(x)\) for all \(x\in\mathbb R\).
Consider the function \(f:(-\infty,\infty)\to(-\infty,\infty)\) defined by \(f(x)=\dfrac{x^2-ax+1}{x^2+ax+1}\), \(0<a<2\).
Let \(f(x)=(1-x)^2\sin^2x+x^2\) for all \(x\in\mathbb R\), and let \(g(x)=\displaystyle\int_1^x\left(\frac{2(t-1)}{t+1}-\ln t\right)f(t)\,dt\) for all \(x\in(1,\infty)\).

Answer the following questions by appropriately matching the information given in the three columns of the following table. Let \(f(x)=x+\log_ex-x\log_ex\), \(x\in(0,\infty)\). Column 1 contains information about zeros of \(f(x)\), \(f'(x)\) and \(f''(x)\). Column 2 contains information about the limiting behavior of \(f(x)\), \(f'(x)\) and \(f''(x)\) at infinity. Column 3 contains information about increasing/decreasing nature of \(f(x)\) and \(f'(x)\).
Column 1 Column 2 Column 3
(I) \(f(x)=0\) for some \(x\in(1,e^2)\) (i) \(\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)=0\) (P) \(f\) is increasing in \((0,1)\)
(II) \(f'(x)=0\) for some \(x\in(1,e)\) (ii) \(\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)=-\infty\) (Q) \(f\) is decreasing in \((e,e^2)\)
(III) \(f'(x)=0\) for some \(x\in(0,1)\) (iii) \(\lim_{x\to\infty}f'(x)=-\infty\) (R) \(f'\) is increasing in \((0,1)\)
(IV) \(f''(x)=0\) for some \(x\in(1,e)\) (iv) \(\lim_{x\to\infty}f''(x)=0\) (S) \(f'\) is decreasing in \((e,e^2)\)

Let \(\psi_1:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\), \(\psi_2:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\), \(f:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\) and \(g:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\) be functions such that \(f(0)=g(0)=0\), \(\psi_1(x)=e^{-x}+x\), \(x\ge0\), \(\psi_2(x)=x^2-2x-2e^{-x}+2\), \(x\ge0\), \(f(x)=\displaystyle\int_{-x}^{x}\left(|t|-t^2\right)e^{-t^2}dt\), \(x>0\) and \(g(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^{x^2}\sqrt te^{-t}\,dt\), \(x>0\).

If a continuous function \(f\) defined on the real line \(\mathbb R\) assumes positive and negative values in \(\mathbb R\) then the equation \(f(x)=0\) has a root in \(\mathbb R\). For example, if it is known that a continuous function \(f\) on \(\mathbb R\) is positive at some point and its minimum value is negative then the equation \(f(x)=0\) has a root in \(\mathbb R\). Consider \(f(x)=ke^x-x\) for all real \(x\) where \(k\) is a real constant.

Consider the curve \(C_1\) given by \(y=e^{-x}\) for \(x\in[0,10\pi]\), and the curve \(C_2\) given by \(y=e^{-x}(\sin x+\cos x)\) for \(x\in[0,10\pi]\). Let \(n\) be the total number of points of intersection of the curves \(C_1\) and \(C_2\). Suppose that \(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\dots,\alpha_n\in[0,10\pi]\) are the \(x\)-coordinates of the points of intersection of the curves \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) such that \(\alpha_1<\alpha_2<\cdots<\alpha_n\).
A tangent \(PT\) is drawn to the circle \(x^2+y^2=4\) at the point \(P(\sqrt3,1)\). A straight line \(L\), perpendicular to \(PT\) is a tangent to the circle \((x-3)^2+y^2=1\).

Let the circles \(C_1:x^2+y^2=9\) and \(C_2:(x-3)^2+(y-4)^2=16\), intersect at the points \(X\) and \(Y\). Suppose that another circle \(C_3:(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2\) satisfies the following conditions: (i) centre of \(C_3\) is collinear with the centres of \(C_1\) and \(C_2\), (ii) \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) both lie inside \(C_3\), and (iii) \(C_3\) touches \(C_1\) at \(M\) and \(C_2\) at \(N\). Let the line through \(X\) and \(Y\) intersect \(C_3\) at \(Z\) and \(W\), and let a common tangent of \(C_1\) and \(C_3\) be a tangent to the parabola \(x^2=8\alpha y\). There are some expressions given in the List-I whose values are given in List-II below:
List-I List-II
(I) \(2h+k\) (P) 6
(II) \(\dfrac{\text{Length of }ZW}{\text{Length of }XY}\) (Q) \(\sqrt6\)
(III) \(\dfrac{\text{Area of triangle }MZN}{\text{Area of triangle }ZMW}\) (R) \(\frac54\)
(IV) \(\alpha\) (S) \(\frac{21}5\)
(T) \(2\sqrt6\)
(U) \(\frac{10}3\)
Let \(S\) be the circle in the \(xy\)-plane defined by the equation \(x^2+y^2=4\).

A circle \(C\) of radius 1 is inscribed in an equilateral triangle \(PQR\). The points of contact of \(C\) with the sides \(PQ,QR,RP\) are \(D,E,F\), respectively. The line \(PQ\) is given by the equation \(\sqrt3x+y-6=0\) and the point \(D\) is \(\left(\frac{3\sqrt3}2,\frac32\right)\). Further, it is given that the origin and the centre of \(C\) are on the same side of the line \(PQ\).

Let \(ABCD\) be a square of side length 2 units. \(C_2\) is the circle through vertices \(A,B,C,D\) and \(C_1\) is the circle touching all the sides of the square \(ABCD\). \(L\) is a line through \(A\).

Consider the region \(R=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R:x\ge0\text{ and }y^2\le4-x\}\). Let \(\mathcal F\) be the family of all circles that are contained in \(R\) and have centers on the \(x\)-axis. Let \(C\) be the circle that has largest radius among the circles in \(\mathcal F\). Let \((\alpha,\beta)\) be a point where the circle \(C\) meets the curve \(y^2=4-x\).

Consider the circle \(x^2+y^2=9\) and the parabola \(y^2=8x\). They intersect at \(P\) and \(Q\) in the first and the fourth quadrants, respectively. Tangents to the circle at \(P\) and \(Q\) intersect the \(x\)-axis at \(R\) and tangents to the parabola at \(P\) and \(Q\) intersect the \(x\)-axis at \(S\).

Let \(S=S_1\cap S_2\cap S_3\), where \(S_1=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|<4\}\),
\(S_2=\left\{z\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Im}\left[\dfrac{z-1+\sqrt3i}{1-\sqrt3i}\right]>0\right\}\) and \(S_3=\{z\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Re}z>0\}\).

Let \(A,B,C\) be three sets of complex numbers as defined below:
\(A=\{z:\operatorname{Im}z\ge1\}\), \(B=\{z:|z-2-i|=3\}\), \(C=\{z:\operatorname{Re}((1-i)z)=\sqrt2\}\).

Let \(g_i:\left[\frac\pi8,\frac{3\pi}8\right]\to\mathbb R\), \(i=1,2\), and \(f:\left[\frac\pi8,\frac{3\pi}8\right]\to\mathbb R\) be functions such that \(g_1(x)=1\), \(g_2(x)=|4x-\pi|\) and \(f(x)=\sin^2x\), for all \(x\in\left[\frac\pi8,\frac{3\pi}8\right]\). Define \(S_i=\displaystyle\int_{\pi/8}^{3\pi/8}f(x)\cdot g_i(x)\,dx\), \(i=1,2\).

Let \(f:\left[0,\frac\pi2\right]\to[0,1]\) be the function defined by \(f(x)=\sin^2x\) and let \(g:\left[0,\frac\pi2\right]\to[0,\infty)\) be the function defined by \(g(x)=\sqrt{\frac{\pi x}2-x^2}\).

Given that for each \(a\in(0,1)\), \(\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0^+}\int_h^{1-h}t^{-a}(1-t)^{a-1}\,dt\) exists. Let this limit be \(g(a)\). In addition, it is given that the function \(g(a)\) is differentiable on \((0,1)\).

Suppose we define the definite integral using the following formula \(\displaystyle\int_a^bf(x)\,dx=\frac{b-a}2\big(f(a)+f(b)\big)\); for more accurate result for \(c\in(a,b)\), \(F(c)=\frac{c-a}2\big(f(a)+f(c)\big)+\frac{b-c}2\big(f(b)+f(c)\big)\). When \(c=\frac{a+b}2\), \(\displaystyle\int_a^bf(x)\,dx=\frac{b-a}4\big(f(a)+f(b)+2f(c)\big)\).
Consider the ellipses given by \(x^2+4y^2=1\) and \(4x^2+y^2=1\).

Let \(F_1(x_1,0)\) and \(F_2(x_2,0)\), for \(x_1<0\) and \(x_2>0\), be the foci of the ellipse \(\dfrac{x^2}9+\dfrac{y^2}8=1\). Suppose a parabola having vertex at the origin and focus at \(F_2\) intersects the ellipse at point \(M\) in the first quadrant and at point \(N\) in the fourth quadrant.
Tangents are drawn from the point \(P(3,4)\) to the ellipse \(\dfrac{x^2}9+\dfrac{y^2}4=1\) touching the ellipse at points \(A\) and \(B\).
The circle \(x^2+y^2-8x=0\) and hyperbola \(\dfrac{x^2}9-\dfrac{y^2}4=1\) intersect at the points \(A\) and \(B\).

Consider the lines \(L_1\) and \(L_2\) defined by \(L_1:x\sqrt2+y-1=0\) and \(L_2:x\sqrt2-y+1=0\). For a fixed constant \(\lambda\), let \(C\) be the locus of a point \(P\) such that the product of the distance of \(P\) from \(L_1\) and the distance of \(P\) from \(L_2\) is \(\lambda^2\). The line \(y=2x+1\) meets \(C\) at two points \(R\) and \(S\), where the distance between \(R\) and \(S\) is \(\sqrt{270}\). Let the perpendicular bisector of \(RS\) meet \(C\) at two distinct points \(R'\) and \(S'\). Let \(D\) be the square of the distance between \(R'\) and \(S'\).

Let \(\alpha,\beta\) and \(\gamma\) be real numbers such that the system of linear equations
\(x+2y+3z=\alpha,\ \ 4x+5y+6z=\beta,\ \ 7x+8y+9z=\gamma-1\)
is consistent. Let \(|M|\) represent the determinant of the matrix \(M=\begin{bmatrix}\alpha&2&\gamma\\\beta&1&0\\-1&0&1\end{bmatrix}\).
Let \(P\) be the plane containing all those \((\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\) for which the above system of linear equations is consistent, and \(D\) be the square of the distance of the point \((0,1,0)\) from the plane \(P\).

Let \(p\) be an odd prime number and \(T_p\) be the following set of \(2\times2\) matrices:
\(T_p=\left\{A=\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&a\end{bmatrix}:a,b,c\in\{0,1,2,\dots,p-1\}\right\}\).
Let \(\mathcal A\) be the set of all \(3\times3\) symmetric matrices all of whose entries are either 0 or 1. Five of these entries are 1 and four of them are 0.

Let \(a,b\) and \(c\) be three real numbers satisfying
\(\begin{bmatrix}a&b&c\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1&9&7\\8&2&7\\7&3&7\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0&0&0\end{bmatrix}\qquad\dots(E)\)

\(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\2&1&0\\3&2&1\end{bmatrix}\). If \(U_1,U_2\) and \(U_3\) are column matrices satisfying \(AU_1=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\\0\end{bmatrix}\), \(AU_2=\begin{bmatrix}2\\3\\0\end{bmatrix}\), \(AU_3=\begin{bmatrix}2\\3\\1\end{bmatrix}\) and \(U\) is \(3\times3\) matrix whose columns are \(U_1,U_2,U_3\), then answer the following questions.

Consider the functions defined implicitly by the equation \(y^3-3y+x=0\) on various intervals in the real line. If \(x\in(-\infty,-2)\cup(2,\infty)\), the equation implicitly defines a unique real valued differentiable function \(y=f(x)\). If \(x\in(-2,2)\), the equation implicitly defines a unique real valued differentiable function \(y=g(x)\) satisfying \(g(0)=0\).

Let \(a,r,s,t\) be nonzero real numbers. Let \(P(at^2,2at)\), \(Q\), \(R(ar^2,2ar)\) and \(S(as^2,2as)\) be distinct points on the parabola \(y^2=4ax\). Suppose that \(PQ\) is the focal chord and lines \(QR\) and \(PK\) are parallel, where \(K\) is the point \((2a,0)\).
Let \(PQ\) be a focal chord of the parabola \(y^2=4ax\). The tangents to the parabola at \(P\) and \(Q\) meet at a point lying on the line \(y=2x+a\), \(a>0\).

Answer the following questions by appropriately matching the information given in the three columns of the following table. Columns 1, 2 and 3 contain conics, equations of tangents to the conics and points of contact, respectively.
Column 1 Column 2 Column 3
(I) \(x^2+y^2=a^2\) (i) \(my=m^2x+a\) (P) \(\left(\frac a{m^2},\frac{2a}m\right)\)
(II) \(x^2+a^2y^2=a^2\) (ii) \(y=mx+a\sqrt{m^2+1}\) (Q) \(\left(\frac{-ma}{\sqrt{m^2+1}},\frac a{\sqrt{m^2+1}}\right)\)
(III) \(y^2=4ax\) (iii) \(y=mx+\sqrt{a^2m^2-1}\) (R) \(\left(\frac{-a^2m}{\sqrt{a^2m^2+1}},\frac1{\sqrt{a^2m^2+1}}\right)\)
(IV) \(x^2-a^2y^2=a^2\) (iv) \(y=mx+\sqrt{a^2m^2+1}\) (S) \(\left(\frac{-a^2m}{\sqrt{a^2m^2-1}},\frac{-1}{\sqrt{a^2m^2-1}}\right)\)

Let \(a_n\) denote the number of all \(n\)-digit positive integers formed by the digits 0, 1 or both such that no consecutive digits in them are 0. Let \(b_n=\) the number of such \(n\)-digit integers ending with digit 1 and \(c_n=\) the number of such \(n\)-digit integers ending with digit 0.

There are five students \(S_1,S_2,S_3,S_4\) and \(S_5\) in a music class and for them there are five seats \(R_1,R_2,R_3,R_4\) and \(R_5\) arranged in a row, where initially the seat \(R_i\) is allotted to the student \(S_i\), \(i=1,2,3,4,5\). But, on the examination day, the five students are randomly allotted the five seats.
Let \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) be the number of red and black balls, respectively, in box I. Let \(n_3\) and \(n_4\) be the number of red and black balls, respectively, in box II.

There are \(n\) urns each containing \(n+1\) balls such that the \(i\)th urn contains \(i\) white balls and \((n+1-i)\) red balls. Let \(u_i\) be the event of selecting \(i\)th urn, \(i=1,2,3,\dots,n\) and \(w\) denotes the event of getting a white ball.

Consider a \(6\times6\) square divided into 36 unit squares by lines parallel to its sides. Let \(A_1,A_2,\dots,A_{49}\) be the 49 points of intersection (the lattice points of this grid, including those on the boundary) in some order. We say that \(A_i\) and \(A_j\) are friends if they are adjacent along a row or along a column. Assume that each point \(A_i\) has an equal chance of being chosen.

Let \(U_1\) and \(U_2\) be two urns such that \(U_1\) contains 3 white and 2 red balls, and \(U_2\) contains only 1 white ball. A fair coin is tossed. If head appears then 1 ball is drawn at random from \(U_1\) and put into \(U_2\). However, if tail appears then 2 balls are drawn at random from \(U_1\) and put into \(U_2\). Now 1 ball is drawn at random from \(U_2\).

A box \(B_1\) contains 1 white ball, 3 red balls and 2 black balls. Another box \(B_2\) contains 2 white balls, 3 red balls and 4 black balls. A third box \(B_3\) contains 3 white balls, 4 red balls and 5 black balls.

Box 1 contains three cards bearing numbers 1, 2, 3; box 2 contains five cards bearing numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; and box 3 contains seven cards bearing numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. A card is drawn from each of the boxes. Let \(x_i\) be the number on the card drawn from the \(i^{\text{th}}\) box, \(i=1,2,3\).

Football teams \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) have to play two games against each other. It is assumed that the outcomes of the two games are independent. The probabilities of \(T_1\) winning, drawing and losing a game against \(T_2\) are \(\frac12,\frac16\) and \(\frac13\), respectively. Each team gets 3 points for a win, 1 point for a draw and 0 point for a loss in a game. Let \(X\) and \(Y\) denote the total points scored by teams \(T_1\) and \(T_2\), respectively, after two games.

Three numbers are chosen at random, one after another with replacement, from the set \(S=\{1,2,3,\dots,100\}\). Let \(p_1\) be the probability that the maximum of chosen numbers is at least 81 and \(p_2\) be the probability that the minimum of chosen numbers is at most 40.
A fair die is tossed repeatedly until a six is obtained. Let \(X\) denote the number of tosses required.

Consider an obtuse angled triangle \(ABC\) in which the difference between the largest and the smallest angle is \(\frac\pi2\) and whose sides are in arithmetic progression. Suppose that the vertices of this triangle lie on a circle of radius 1.

The curve \(y=f(x)\) passes through the point \((0,1)\) and the curve \(y=g(x)=\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{x}f(t)\,dt\) passes through the point \(\left(0,\frac12\right)\). The tangents drawn to the two curves at points with equal abscissae always intersect on the \(x\)-axis.

Let \(P(x) = x^n + c_{n-1}x^{n-1} + \dots + c_1 x + c_0\) be a polynomial with complex roots \(\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \dots, \alpha_n\). The power sums \(p_k = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i^k\) satisfy Newton-Girard identities:
	\[
	p_k + c_{n-1}p_{k-1} + c_{n-2}p_{k-2} + \dots + k c_{n-k} = 0 \quad (1 \le k \le n)
	\]
	Consider the polynomial \(f(x) = x^3 - 2x^2 + x - 3 = 0\) with roots \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\).

A purse contains five coins whose probabilities of showing heads are respectively
	\(\dfrac27,\dfrac37,\dfrac47,\dfrac57,\dfrac67\). One coin is selected at random and tossed \(n\) times; let \(n_H\) and \(n_T\) denote the numbers of heads and tails, respectively. Define
	\[
	L=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n_H}{n_T}.
	\]

Let \(f : D_f \to \mathbb{R}\) and \(g : D_g \to \mathbb{R}\) be real-valued functions defined on their maximal domains by:
\[f(x) = \sqrt{\log_{1/3}\left(\frac{2|x| - 1}{|x| + 2}\right)}\]
and
\[g(x) = \frac{\lfloor x \rfloor + 2}{\lceil x \rceil - \lfloor x \rfloor + 1} \cdot \operatorname{sgn}(x^2 - 9)\]
where \(\lfloor \cdot \rfloor\), \(\lceil \cdot \rceil\), \(\operatorname{sgn}(\cdot)\), and \(|\cdot|\) denote the floor, ceiling, signum, and modulus functions, respectively.

A particle starts at \((4,4)\) and moves until it first hits the \(x\)-axis, the \(y\)-axis, or both axes simultaneously. At a lattice point \((a,b)\) with \(a,b\in\mathbb N\), it moves with probability \(\frac13\) to each of \((a-1,b)\), \((a,b-1)\) and \((a-1,b-1)\), independently of its previous moves.

Let \(f(x)\) and \(g(x)\) be two differentiable functions, defined as
	\[
	f(x)=x^2+xg'(1)+g''(2),\qquad g(x)=f(1)x^2+xf'(x)+f''(x).
	\]

Consider the sequence of polynomial identities arising from multiple angles. It is known that for any odd prime \(p = 2m+1\), the roots of the polynomial equation 
\[\sum_{k=0}^{m} (-1)^k \binom{2m+1}{2k+1} x^{m-k} = 0\]
 are given by \(x_r = \cot^2\left(\frac{r\pi}{2m+1}\right)\) for \(r = 1, 2, \dots, m\).

Consider the non-linear coupled trigonometric system for real variables \(x, y \in \left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\):
	\[
	\begin{cases}
		2\sin x \cos y = 1 \\
		16\sin^2 x + 9\sec^2 y = 25
	\end{cases}
	\]
	Constrained extrema and algebraic substitution isolate the permissible locus and coordinates of simultaneous intersection points.
Let \(f(x)=ax^2+bx+c\) and \(g(x)=dx^2+cx+e\) be quadratic polynomials, where \(a,b,c,d,e\in\mathbb R\).

Let \(a=a(t)\) be a function of \(t\) such that \(\dfrac{da}{dt}=2\) for all values of \(t\), and \(a=0\) when \(t=0\). Further, \(y=m(t)x+c(t)\) is the tangent to the curve
	\[
	y=x^2-2ax+a^2+a
	\]
	at the point whose abscissa is \(0\), where \(m(t)\) and \(c(t)\) are functions of \(t\).

Consider the family of quadratic forms in complex variables generated by distance constraints. Let \(A(z_1)\) and \(B(z_2)\) be fixed points in the Argand plane. The Apollonius locus defined by
	\[
	\left|\frac{z - z_1}{z - z_2}\right| = \lambda \quad (\lambda > 0, \; \lambda \neq 1)
	\]
	is a circle whose centre and radius are determined by harmonic division points. Let \(z_1 = 3\) and \(z_2 = -1\) with ratio \(\lambda = 3\).

Let \(f(x) = \cos(\cos x) - \sin(\sin x)\) defined for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\). The analytical and structural behaviour of nested trigonometric functions gives rise to sharp global bounds and localized root-isolation intervals.

Let \(z_1,z_2\) be complex numbers such that
	\[
	z_1^2-4z_2=16+20i.
	\]
	The roots \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) of
	\[
	x^2+z_1x+z_2+m=0
	\]
	for some complex number \(m\) satisfy \(|\alpha-\beta|=2\sqrt7\).

Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be a differentiable function such that \(f(1)=1\), \(f(2)=20\), \(f(-4)=-4\), \(f'(0)=0\) and
	\[
	f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)+3xy(x+y)+bxy+c(x+y)+4\quad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathbb R,
	\]
	where \(b,c\) are constants.

Let \(y=f(x)\) be a curve and \(P(x,y)\) any point on it. The tangent and the normal at \(P\) meet the \(x\)-axis at \(T\) and \(N\); \(PT\) and \(PN\) are the lengths of the tangent and the normal at \(P\). If \(M\) is the foot of the perpendicular from \(P\) on the \(x\)-axis, then \(MT\) and \(MN\) are the lengths of the sub-tangent and the sub-normal at \(P\).

Let \(\vec a\) and \(\vec b\) be position vectors of points \(A\) and \(B\) respectively, and let \(\vec c\) be the position vector of a variable point in the plane of triangle \(OAB\), where \(O\) is the origin.

Let two real-valued functions \(f(x)\) and \(g(x)\) be defined on their maximal domains by:
\[f(x) = \sqrt{\lfloor x \rfloor + \lfloor -x \rfloor + \operatorname{sgn}(|x| - 2) + 2}\]
and
\[g(x) = \log_2\left(\frac{4^x + 1}{2^x}\right) - |x|\]
where \(\lfloor \cdot \rfloor\), \(|\cdot|\), and \(\operatorname{sgn}(\cdot)\) denote the greatest integer, modulus, and signum functions, respectively.

Suppose
	\[
	f(x)=a\sin x-\frac12\cos2x+a-\frac3a+\frac12,\qquad a\in\mathbb R,\ a\ne0.
	\]

Consider the set
	\[
	\mathcal P=\{S=0: S\text{ represents a conic with directrix }x+ky+7=0,\ k\in\mathbb R\}
	\]
	and the circle \(C:x^2+y^2=16\). Suppose every member of \(\mathcal P\) intersects \(C\) in a common chord lying along the \(x\)-axis, and that this chord has maximum possible length. If the members of \(\mathcal P\) are parabolas only, then:

Consider the family
	\[
	L_{a,b}:a(2x+y+4)+b(x-2y-3)=0,\qquad (a,b)\ne(0,0).
	\]
	It is generated by the two fixed lines \(2x+y+4=0\) and \(x-2y-3=0\). Let \(I\) be their point of intersection and let \(M=(2,-3)\).

If \(f(x)\) is a real-valued function, continuous on \([a,b]\) and differentiable on \((a,b)\), then there exists at least one real number \(c\in(a,b)\) such that
	\[
	f'(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}.
	\]

Let \(M\) be a \(4 \times 4\) block upper-triangular matrix defined as \(M = \pmtx{ A & B \\ \mathbf{0} & C }\), where \(A, B\), and \(C\) are \(2 \times 2\) matrices, and \(\mathbf{0}\) is the \(2 \times 2\) zero matrix. The determinant of \(M\) factors multiplicatively over its diagonal blocks as \(|M| = |A| \cdot |C|\), and matrix polynomials evaluate component-wise along the diagonal.
	Let \(A = \pmtx{ 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 }\) and \(C = \pmtx{ 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 }\).
A curve \(y=f(x)\) passes through the point \((1,1)\). For every point \(P\) of the curve, the tangent at \(P\) meets the \(y\)-axis at a point \(T\) above the origin \(O\) such that \(OT=OP\).

Let \(f(x) = \dfrac{x - 1}{x + 1}\) and \(g(x) = \dfrac{2x + 3}{x - 1}\). Consider the composite rational mapping \(h(x) = (f \circ g)(x)\) defined on its maximal real domain \(A \subset \set{R}\) such that \(h: A \to B\) is a bijection, where \(B \subset \set{R}\) is the range of \(h(x)\).

Consider the family of lines
	\[
	L_t:\quad ty=x+2t^2,\qquad t\in\mathbb R.
	\]
	Each member is a tangent to the parabola \(y^2=8x\). The point of contact corresponding to parameter \(t\) is \(P_t=(2t^2,4t)\).

Let \(A(z_1), B(z_2), C(z_3)\) be three points on the circle \(|z| = R\) in the complex plane. A fourth point \(P(z)\) lies on the same circle. By Ptolemy's Theorem, for any cyclic quadrilateral \(ABCP\), the products of the opposite sides satisfy \[|z - z_2||z_1 - z_3| \le |z - z_1||z_2 - z_3| + |z - z_3||z_1 - z_2|.\]
Let \(\triangle ABC\) be an equilateral triangle inscribed in \(|z| = 1\) with \(z_1 = 1\), \(z_2 = e^{i\frac{2\pi}{3}}\), and \(z_3 = e^{i\frac{4\pi}{3}}\).

Let \(f(x)\) be a polynomial function of degree \(2\) satisfying
	\[
	\int\frac{f(x)}{x^3-1}\,dx=\ln\left|\frac{x^2+x+1}{x-1}\right|+\frac{2}{\sqrt3}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2x+1}{\sqrt3}\right)+C,
	\]
	where \(C\) is the constant of integration.

Let \(\triangle ABC\) be an acute-angled triangle with circumradius \(R\), inradius \(r\), and side lengths \(a, b, c\). Let \(H\) be the orthocentre, and let \(H_A, H_B, H_C\) be the reflections of \(H\) across the sidelines \(BC, CA, AB\) respectively. It is known that \(H_A, H_B, H_C\) lie on the circumcircle of \(\triangle ABC\).

Let \(\triangle ABC\) be a triangle with side lengths \(a, b, c\) and semi-perimeter \(s\). Let \(r\) be the inradius and \(r_1, r_2, r_3\) be the exradii. Consider the cubic polynomial whose roots are \(r_1, r_2, r_3\):
	\[
	P(t) = (t - r_1)(t - r_2)(t - r_3) = t^3 - S_1 t^2 + S_2 t - S_3
	\]
	where \(S_1 = r_1 + r_2 + r_3\), \(S_2 = r_1 r_2 + r_2 r_3 + r_3 r_1\), and \(S_3 = r_1 r_2 r_3\).

A process has three states \(A\), \(B\) and \(D\), where \(D\) is an absorbing (disappeared) state. The transition probabilities are
	\[
	\begin{array}{c|ccc}
		\text{Current state}&A&B&D\\ \hline
		A&\frac12&\frac13&\frac16\\
		B&\frac14&\frac12&\frac14\\
		D&0&0&1
	\end{array}
	\]
	At time \(0\), the process is in state \(A\).

Consider the sequence of inverse tangent arguments defined by polynomials. Telescoping techniques in inverse trigonometry typically reduce an infinite sum into a boundary difference via the addition formula:
	\[
	\tan^{-1}(A) - \tan^{-1}(B) = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{A-B}{1+AB}\right) \quad (AB > -1)
	\]
	Let \(f(n) = n^2 + 3n + 3\) and define \(T_n = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{f(n)}\right)\) for each \(n \in \mathbb{N}\).

Consider the sequence of matrices defined by the recurrence relation corresponding to the Fibonacci sequence. Let \(A = \pmtx{ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 }\). For any positive integer \(n\), the \(n\)-th power of \(A\) takes the structural form
	\[
	A^n = \pmtx{ F_{n+1} & F_n \\ F_n & F_{n-1} }
	\]
	where \(F_n\) is the \(n\)-th Fibonacci number (\(F_0 = 0\), \(F_1 = 1\), \(F_2 = 1\), and \(F_n = F_{n-1} + F_{n-2}\) for \(n \ge 2\)).

Let
	\[
	I=\int_0^{10\pi}\frac{\cos6x\cos7x\cos8x\cos9x}{1+e^{2\sin^34x}}\,dx.
	\]
\(Q(a,b,c)\) is a variable point on the plane \(x-y+z=3\), and \(A(0,0,0)\) and \(B(1,1,1)\) are two fixed points.

Let \(f(\theta) = \sin\theta(\sin\theta + \sin 3\theta) + \cos\theta(\cos\theta - \cos 3\theta)\) defined for all \(\theta \in \mathbb{R}\). Through compound angle transformations, nested combinations collapse into compact phase profiles, dictating the locus of extremal tangents.

Let \(f: \set{R} \setminus \curlybrace{0, 1} \to \set{R}\) be a function satisfying the cyclic functional equation
\[2f(x) + 3f\opop{\frac{1}{1-x}} = 3x + 2 - \frac{2}{x} \quad \text{for all } x \in \set{R} \setminus \curlybrace{0, 1}.\]
Define the finite sets \(A = \curlybrace{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}\) and \(B = \curlybrace{1, 2, \dots, n}\), where \(n = 2f(2) + 1\).

At a family get-together, three sisters—Satakshi, Akanshi, and Ditya—invite eight other family members to a party. The eleven people sit around a round table, with the sisters' seats fixed and at least one person seated between any two of the fixed seats. Two members, Pramod and Ajay, do not wish to sit together.

Let \(f: \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0, 1\} \to \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0, 1\}\) be the rational Möbius transformation defined by
	\[
	\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1 - x}
	\]
	Let \(\mathcal{G} = \{\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \sigma_3, \dots, \sigma_k\}\) denote the finite group formed by the iterated compositions of \(\sigma\) under function composition, where \(\sigma_1(x) = \sigma(x)\) and \(\sigma_{n+1}(x) = \sigma(\sigma_n(x))\).
Consider the hyperbola \(xy=4\) and the line \(y+2x=4\). Let \(O\) be the centre of the hyperbola. The tangent at any point \(P\) of the hyperbola meets the coordinate axes at \(A\) and \(B\).

Let \(f : \mathbb{R} \setminus \{1\} \to \mathbb{R} \setminus \{1\}\) be a bijective rational function satisfying the functional equation:
	\[ f\left(\frac{x}{x-1}\right) + 2f(x) = \frac{2x^2 - x + 3}{x-1} \quad \text{for all } x \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0, 1\}. \]
	Define the iterated compositions by \(f_1(x) = f(x)\) and \(f_{n+1}(x) = f(f_n(x))\) for all \(n \ge 1\). Let \(N = 3f(4)\), and define the finite sets:
	\[ X = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7\} \quad \text{and} \quad Y = \{1, 2, \dots, N\}. \]

Let \(X = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7\}\) and \(Y = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\). A function \(g : X \to Y\) is called a balanced-type surjection if \(g\) is onto and there exists at least one element \(y \in Y\) such that \(|g^{-1}(\{y\})| = 2\).

Let \(f(x)\) be a cubic polynomial with leading coefficient \(1\) such that \(f(a)=b\) and \(f'(a)=f''(a)=0\). Let
	\[
	g(x)=f(x)-f(a)+(a-x)f'(x)+3(x-a)^2,
	\]
	and suppose the conclusion of Rolle's theorem for \(g\) on \([a,b]\) holds at \(x=2\), where \(2\in(a,b)\).
Consider the hyperbola \(xy=4\) and the line \(y+2x=4\). Let \(O\) be the centre of the hyperbola. The tangent at any point \(P\) of the hyperbola intersects the coordinate axes at \(A\) and \(B\).

Let \(f(x) = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{2x}{1+x^2}\right) + 2\tan^{-1}x\) and \(g(x) = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1-x^2}{1+x^2}\right) - 2\tan^{-1}x\).
	The analytic behaviour, piecewise representation, and range of these composite functions partition the real line into distinct operational intervals.

Consider a grid in the Cartesian plane where paths consist of single unit steps in the positive \(x\)-direction (Right: \(R(1, 0)\)) or positive \(y\)-direction (Up: \(U(0, 1)\)). The total number of monotonic paths from \((0, 0)\) to \((m, n)\) is given by \(\binom{m+n}{m}\). If paths are restricted such that they never touch or cross the diagonal barrier line \(y = x + 1\), the reflection principle allows exact enumerations via combinatorial subtractions.

Let \(f\) and \(g\) be two real-valued differentiable functions on \(\mathbb R\) satisfying
	\[
	\int_0^xg(t)\,dt=3x+\int_x^0\cos^2t\cdot g(t)\,dt
	\]
	and
	\[
	f(x)=\lim_{\alpha\to0}\frac{1}{\alpha^4}\int_0^{\alpha}\frac{\left(e^{x+t}-e^x\right)\ln^2(1+t)}{2t^3+3}\,dt.
	\]
Consider the hyperbola \(9x^2-16y^2=144\) with centre \(O\). The tangent at a variable point \(P\) of the hyperbola meets its asymptotes at \(L\) and \(M\).
Let \(f\) be a real-valued function defined on \(\mathbb R\) such that \(f(x)=\sin^{-1}(\sin x)+\cos^{-1}(\cos x)\).

Let \(\Pi\) be the plane parallel to the \(y\)-axis that contains the points \((1,0,1)\) and \((3,2,-1)\). Let \(A=(4,0,0)\) and \(B=(6,0,-2)\), and let \(P=(x_0,y_0,z_0)\) be a variable point on \(\Pi\).

Let \(f : I \to \mathbb{R}\) be a twice-differentiable strictly convex function on an interval \(I \subset \mathbb{R}\) (i.e., \(f''(x) > 0\) for all \(x \in I\)). By Jensen's Inequality, for any \(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n \in I\) and positive weights \(w_1, w_2, \dots, w_n\) with \(\sum w_i = 1\):
	\[
	f\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i x_i\right) \le \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i f(x_i)
	\]
	Equality holds if and only if \(x_1 = x_2 = \dots = x_n\).

Let \(X = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7\}\) and \(Y = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\). A function \(g: X \to Y\) is called an equi-partitioned surjection if \(g\) is surjective (onto) and there exists a designated target element whose pre-image contains a prescribed number of elements.

Let \(P(x) = x^n - 1\) have roots \(\omega_k = e^{i\frac{2k\pi}{n}}\) for \(k = 0, 1, \dots, n-1\). Algebraic identities and distance sums across complex nodes can be derived by evaluating \(P(x)\) and its derivatives at geometric boundaries. Consider the specific case \(n = 8\), where \(\zeta_k = e^{i\frac{k\pi}{4}}\) for \(k = 0, 1, \dots, 7\).

Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be a differentiable function such that
	\[
	f(x)=x^2+\int_0^xe^{-t}f(x-t)\,dt.
	\]
Consider the parabola \(y^2=4x\) and the circle \((x+1)^2+y^2=1\).

If \(m>0\), \(n>0\), the definite integral \(\displaystyle I=\int_0^1x^{m-1}(1-x)^{n-1}\,dx\) depends on \(m\) and \(n\); it is denoted by \(\beta(m,n)\) and called the beta function. For example,
	\[
	\int_0^1x^4(1-x)^5\,dx=\beta(5,6),\qquad \int_0^1\frac{x^{5/2}}{\sqrt{1-x}}\,dx=\beta\left(\frac72,\frac12\right).
	\]
	Clearly \(\beta(n,m)=\beta(m,n)\).

Let two real-valued functions \(f(x)\) and \(g(x)\) be defined on their maximal real domains by:
\[f(x) = \sqrt{\lfloor x \rfloor + \lfloor -x \rfloor + \operatorname{sgn}(|x| - 3) + 2}\]
and
\[g(x) = \log_2\left(\frac{4^x + 1}{2^x}\right) - |x|,\]
where \(\lfloor \cdot \rfloor\), \(|\cdot|\), and \(\operatorname{sgn}(\cdot)\) denote the greatest integer, absolute value, and signum functions, respectively.

Let \(H\) be the hyperbola
	\[
	\frac{x^2}{16}-\frac{y^2}{9}=1.
	\]
	Write its semi-transverse axis as \(a\) and semi-conjugate axis as \(b\).

Let \(\omega = e^{i\frac{2\pi}{2n+1}}\) be the primitive \((2n+1)\)-th root of unity. By factorising the polynomial 
\[z^{2n+1} - 1 = (z-1) \displaystyle \prod_{k=1}^{n} (z^2 - 2z\cos\frac{2k\pi}{2n+1} + 1)\]
 and substituting suitable boundary arguments on the unit circle, one derives canonical identities for products and sums of trigonometric multiple angles.

For each integer \(n \ge 1\), define the polynomial \(P_n(x) = (1 + x)^n = \sum_{r=0}^n \binom{n}{r} x^r\). Differentiation, integration, and roots-of-unity filter substitutions yield closed-form evaluations for multivariable binomial lattices and weighted indices.

Let \(n \in \mathbb{N}\) with \(n \ge 3\), and let \(\omega_k = e^{i\frac{2k\pi}{n}}\) for \(k = 0, 1, \dots, n-1\) denote the complete set of \(n\)-th roots of unity. The canonical polynomial decomposition
	\[
	z^n - 1 = \prod_{k=0}^{n-1} (z - \omega_k)
	\]
	allows evaluation of rational trigonometric sums, cyclotomic products, and multi-point potential invariants along circles concentric with the origin.

Let \(A=[a_{ij}]\) be a \(2\times2\) matrix such that \(\operatorname{Tr}(A)=5\). Let
	\[
	f(x)=\det(A-xI),\qquad f(A)=A^2+aA+3I,
	\]
	where \(I\) is the identity matrix of order \(2\).

Let \(f(x)=\left(1+\dfrac1x\right)^x\) \((x>0)\) and
	\[
	g(x)=\begin{cases}x\ln\left(1+\dfrac1x\right), & 0<x,\\[4pt] 0, & x=0.\end{cases}
	\]

Let \(f(x) = \cos(\cos x) - \sin(\sin x)\) defined for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\). The analytical and structural behaviour of nested trigonometric functions gives rise to extreme bounds and localized parity patterns.

Two circles are given by
	\[
	C_1:x^2+y^2-2x-4y+1=0,
	\qquad
	C_2:x^2+y^2+4x-2y-11=0.
	\]
	Their common chord is the radical axis of the pair.

Consider the family of circles
	\[
	C_t:x^2+y^2+2t(x+y)-1-2t=0,\qquad t\in\mathbb R.
	\]
	Every member passes through the fixed points \(A(1,0)\) and \(B(0,1)\).

For \(-1<t<2\), consider the family of lines
	\[
	L_t:(t+1)x+(2-t)y-6=0.
	\]
	Every member cuts the positive coordinate axes. Its \(x\)- and \(y\)-intercepts are denoted by \(a_t\) and \(b_t\), respectively.

Let \(f(x)=e^x(2x-1)-ax+a\), where \(a\) is a parameter and \(a<1\). If there exists one and only one integer \(x_0\) such that \(f(x_0)<0\), then the range of \(a\) is \(\left[\dfrac{p}{qe},r\right)\), where \(p,q\) are co-prime.

Let \(A = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\). A binary relation \(R\) on \(A\) is called a quasi-order (or pre-order) if it is reflexive and transitive. If, in addition, \(R\) is symmetric, it is an equivalence relation; if \(R\) is antisymmetric, it is a partial order.
In a class of 10 students, the probability that exactly \(i\) students pass an examination is directly proportional to \(i^2\), for \(i=1,2,\ldots,10\).

Let \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\) be the roots of the cubic equation \(x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6 = 0\). By Vieta's relations and symmetric Newton-Girard sums, multivariable forms can be reduced to power sums \(p_k = \alpha^k + \beta^k + \gamma^k\).
Let \(C\) be the curve \(y=x^3-3x+2\).

Let \(f(x)\) and \(g(x)\) be two quadratic polynomials
	\[
	f(x)=ax^2+bx+c,\qquad g(x)=dx^2+cx+e,
	\]
	where \(a,b,c,d,e\in\mathbb R\).

Let \(\{a_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}\) be an arithmetic progression with first term \(a_1 > 0\) and common difference \(d > 0\). For any \(k \in \mathbb{N}\), the reciprocal product sum
	\[
	S_n(k) = \sum_{r=1}^{n} \frac{1}{a_r a_{r+1} \cdots a_{r+k}}
	\]
	can be resolved into a telescoping difference by expressing the numerator as \(\dfrac{a_{r+k} - a_r}{k d}\).
	Let \(a_1 = 1\) and \(d = 2\), so that \(a_r = 2r - 1\).
A person repeatedly tosses a fair die, scoring 2 points for a perfect square and 1 point otherwise. Let $P_n$ be the probability that he reaches a score of exactly $n$.
$y=f(x)$ is differentiable for all $x\in\mathbb R$ and satisfies $\frac{dy}{dx}=|y|+1$, $f(0)=0$.

Let $f,f',f''$ be continuous on $[0,\ln2]$ with $f(0)=0$, $f'(0)=3$, $f'(\ln2)=4$, $f(\ln2)=6$ and $\int_0^{\ln2}e^{-2x}f(x)\,dx=3$. Also let $g$ be continuous with $\int_0^1g(x)\left(4x^2-g(x)\right)dx=\frac45$. Answer the following.

Let \(S=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\) and \(X\) be the set of all relations \(R\) from \(S\) to \(S\) that satisfy both the following properties: (i) \(R\) has exactly 6 elements; (ii) for each \((a,b)\in R\), we have \(|a-b|\ge2\). Let \(Y=\{R\in X:\text{The range of }R\text{ has exactly one element}\}\) and \(Z=\{R\in X:R\text{ is a function from }S\text{ to }S\}\). Let \(n(A)\) denote the number of elements in a set \(A\).

Let \(A_1,G_1,H_1\) denote the arithmetic, geometric and harmonic means, respectively, of two distinct positive numbers. For \(n\ge2\), let \(A_{n-1}\) and \(H_{n-1}\) have arithmetic, geometric and harmonic means as \(A_n,G_n,H_n\), respectively.

Let \(p,q\) be integers and let \(\alpha,\beta\) be the roots of the equation \(x^2-x-1=0\), where \(\alpha\ne\beta\). For \(n=0,1,2,\dots\), let \(a_n=p\alpha^n+q\beta^n\).
FACT: If \(a\) and \(b\) are rational numbers and \(a+b\sqrt5=0\), then \(a=0=b\).

Let \(V_r\) denote the sum of the first \(r\) terms of an arithmetic progression (A.P.) whose first term is \(r\) and the common difference is \((2r-1)\). Let \(T_r=V_{r+1}-V_r-2\) and \(Q_r=T_{r+1}-T_r\) for \(r=1,2,\dots\)

Let \(S_0=0\) and, for \(n\ge1\), let \(S_n\) denote the sum of the first \(n\) terms of this progression. For \(n\ge1\), let \(C_n\) denote the circle with center \((S_{n-1},0)\) and radius \(a_n\), and \(D_n\) denote the circle with center \((S_{n-1},S_{n-1})\) and radius \(a_n\).
Consider the lines \(L_1:\dfrac{x+1}3=\dfrac{y+2}1=\dfrac{z+1}2\), \(L_2:\dfrac{x-2}1=\dfrac{y+2}2=\dfrac{z-3}3\).

Area \(=\int_0^1(e-e^x)dx=e-(e-1)=1\).
(B) Put \(u=e+1-y\): it becomes \(\int_1^e\ln u\,du=1\) ✓. (C) \(e-(e-1)=1\) ✓. (D) \(\int_1^e\ln y\,dy=[y\ln y-y]_1^e=1\) ✓. Answer: (B), (C), (D).

wrong_options.A: \(e-1\) is the area under \(y=e^x\), not between it and \(y=e\).

solutions.focus_note: Vertical and horizontal slicing must give the same area: a good self-check.

solutions.key_idea: Direct integration.
solutions.full_html: \(\frac13-\frac23(1-b)^3=\frac14\Rightarrow(1-b)^3=\frac18\Rightarrow b=\frac12\). Answer (B).
solutions.focus_note: Total area is \(\frac13\), so \(R_1=\frac7{24}\), \(R_2=\frac1{24}\).

solutions.key_idea: Add the two forms of \(R_1\).
solutions.full_html: \(2R_1=\int_{-1}^2[x+(1-x)]f(x)dx=\int_{-1}^2f(x)dx=R_2\) (area, since \(f\ge0\)). Answer (C).
solutions.focus_note: \(f\) is symmetric about \(x=\frac12\), so the 'average \(x\)' under it is \(\frac12\): \(R_1=\frac12R_2\).

solutions.key_idea: Bound the integral with step and comparison functions.
hints: Compare \(e^{-x^2}\) with simpler functions on \([0,1]\): \(e^{-1}\le e^{-x^2}\) and \(x^2\le x\).
For (D), split at \(x=\frac1{\sqrt2}\) and bound by a step function.
solutions.full_html:
\(S\approx0.747\).
(A) \(e^{-x^2}\ge e^{-1}\) on \([0,1]\), so \(S\ge\frac1e\) ✓.
(B) \(x^2\le x\Rightarrow e^{-x^2}\ge e^{-x}\), so \(S\ge\int_0^1e^{-x}dx=1-\frac1e\) ✓.
(D) On \([0,\frac1{\sqrt2}]\) use \(e^{-x^2}\le1\); on \([\frac1{\sqrt2},1]\) use \(e^{-x^2}\le e^{-1/2}\). This gives \(S\le\frac1{\sqrt2}+\frac1{\sqrt e}\left(1-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)\) ✓. Answer: (A), (B), (D).

wrong_options.C: \(\frac14(1+e^{-1/2})\approx0.40<0.747\): too small to be an upper bound.

solutions.focus_note: Upper bounds from step functions use the left-end (larger) value on each piece of a decreasing function.

solutions.key_idea: Remove the modulus by splitting the interval.
hints: Split at \(\frac\pi4\), where \(\cos x-\sin x\) changes sign.
On \([0,\frac\pi4]\): difference \(=2\sin x\). On \([\frac\pi4,\frac\pi2]\): difference \(=2\cos x\).
solutions.full_html: \(\int_0^{\pi/4}2\sin x\,dx+\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2}2\cos x\,dx=2\left(1-\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\right)\cdot2=4-2\sqrt2=2\sqrt2(\sqrt2-1)\). Answer (B).
solutions.focus_note: The two pieces are mirror images about \(x=\frac\pi4\).

solutions.key_idea: Leibniz rule, then differentiate once more.
solutions.full_html: \(F''(x)=4\cos^2\!\left(x^2+\frac\pi6\right)+2x\cdot\frac{d}{dx}[\dots]+2\sin2x\). At \(x=0\): \(F''(0)=4\cos^2\frac\pi6=4\cdot\frac34=3\). So \(f(0)=3\). Answer: 3.
solutions.focus_note: Consistency check: at \(a=0\) the area is 0, and indeed \(F'(0)+2=-2+2=0\).

solutions.key_idea: Find where the line is above \(y=\sqrt{|x+3|}\), then subtract areas.
hints: The line \(y=\frac{x+9}5\) meets \(y=\sqrt{x+3}\) at \(x=1,6\) and \(y=\sqrt{-x-3}\) at \(x=-4\) (and \(-39\)).
The line lies above the curve only for \(-4\le x\le1\).
solutions.focus_note: Check the condition \(x+9\le15\) last: it holds on \([-4,1]\), so it cuts nothing.

solutions.key_idea: Half-area condition gives a quartic in \(\alpha\).
solutions.full_html: \(\frac{\alpha^2}2-\frac{\alpha^4}4=\frac18\Rightarrow2\alpha^4-4\alpha^2+1=0\) (C ✓). Then \(\alpha^2=\frac{2-\sqrt2}2\approx0.293\), so \(\alpha\approx0.541\in(\frac12,1)\) (B ✓). Answer: (B), (C).
solutions.focus_note: Pick the root with \(\alpha^2<1\): \(\frac{2+\sqrt2}2>1\) is rejected.

solutions.key_idea: Set the area equal to 0.3.
hints: Region between \(y=x\) and \(y=x^n\) on \([0,1]\) has area \(\frac12-\frac1{n+1}\).
solutions.full_html: \(\frac12-\frac1{n+1}=\frac3{10}\Rightarrow\frac1{n+1}=\frac15\Rightarrow n=4\). Answer: 4.
solutions.focus_note: \(x^n\le x\) on \([0,1]\) for \(n>1\), so the curve is below \(PQ\).

solutions.key_idea: Split at the intersection.
hints: Need \(x^2\ge1\); take \(x\ge1\). Curves \(y=x^2\) and \(y=\frac8x\) meet at \(x=2\); \(\frac8x=1\) at \(x=8\).
solutions.full_html: \(\int_1^2(x^2-1)dx+\int_2^8\left(\frac8x-1\right)dx=\frac43+8\ln4-6=16\ln2-\frac{14}3\). Answer (A).
solutions.focus_note: Intended region is \(x>0\): for \(x\le-1\), \(xy\le8\) is automatic and the set would be unbounded.

solutions.key_idea: Area between \(g\) (top) and \(f\) (bottom), from \(x=0\) to the intersection.
solutions.full_html:
On \([0,1]\): \(\int_0^1g\,dx=\frac12\left[e^{x-1}-e^{1-x}\right]_0^1=\frac12(e-e^{-1})\).
On \([1,1+\frac12\ln3]\), with \(u=x-1\): \(\int_0^{\ln\sqrt3}\left(\frac32e^{-u}-\frac12e^u\right)du=\left[-\frac32e^{-u}-\frac12e^u\right]_0^{\ln\sqrt3}=2-\sqrt3\).
Total \((2-\sqrt3)+\frac12(e-e^{-1})\). Answer (A).
solutions.focus_note: \(g\) is a shifted \(\cosh\) and \(f\) a shifted \(2\sinh\) for \(x\ge1\).

solutions.key_idea: The region is a quadrilateral; use the shoelace formula or split it.
solutions.full_html: Big triangle \(O,(\frac94,0),(\frac94,\frac34)\) minus triangle \(O,(2,0),(\frac32,\frac12)\): \(\frac12\cdot\frac94\cdot\frac34-\frac12\cdot2\cdot\frac12=\frac{27}{32}-\frac12=\frac{11}{32}\). Answer (A).
solutions.focus_note: \(y\le1\) is automatic here since \(y\le\frac x3\le\frac34\).

solutions.key_idea: Below the crossing take \(f\), beyond it take \(g\).
hints: Both functions are even: work on \([0,\frac34]\) and double.
solutions.full_html: \(\int_0^{1/2}\left(x^2+\frac5{12}\right)dx=\frac1{24}+\frac5{24}=\frac14\). \(\int_{1/2}^{3/4}g\,dx\) is a triangle with base \(\frac14\), height \(g(\frac12)=\frac23\): \(\frac1{12}\). Half-area \(\frac13\), so \(\alpha=\frac23\) and \(9\alpha=6\). Answer: 6.
solutions.focus_note: Check which function is smaller on each side of \(x=\frac12\): at 0, \(f=\frac5{12}<2=g\).

solutions.key_idea: Sum triangle areas.
hints: The graph is four straight pieces: each piece and the \(x\)-axis form a triangle.
solutions.full_html: Areas: \(\frac12\cdot\frac1{2n}\cdot n=\frac14\); \(\frac12\cdot\frac1{2n}\cdot n=\frac14\) (the middle 'tent'); \(\frac12\cdot\frac{n-1}n\cdot n=\frac{n-1}2\). Total \(\frac n2=4\Rightarrow n=8\). Maximum of \(f\) is \(n=8\). Answer: 8.
solutions.focus_note: All three peaks have the same height \(n\).

solutions.key_idea: Use the area bookkeeping \(G_\uparrow+R_\uparrow=1-h\), \(G_\downarrow+R_\downarrow=h\), \(R_\uparrow+R_\downarrow=\frac12\).
hints: \(\int_0^1f=\frac12\): red and green each have area \(\frac12\). Above \(L_h\) the total area is \(1-h\); below it is \(h\).
solutions.full_html:
(C) \(G_\uparrow-R_\downarrow=(1-h-R_\uparrow)-R_\downarrow=\frac12-h\). Zero at \(h=\frac12\in[\frac14,\frac23]\) ✓.
(D) \(R_\uparrow-G_\downarrow=R_\uparrow-(h-R_\downarrow)=\frac12-h\). Zero at \(h=\frac12\) ✓.
(B) Need \(R_\downarrow=\frac14\). At \(h=\frac14\) the line is below \(f\) everywhere, so \(R_\downarrow=\frac14\) ✓.
Answer: (B), (C), (D).
solutions.focus_note: Bookkeeping identities beat computing any integral here.

solutions.key_idea: Top boundary: \(2\sqrt x\) on \([0,2]\), the line on \([2,5]\).
hints: \(y^2=4x\) and \(y^2=12-2x\) meet at \((2,2\sqrt2)\). The line \(y=\frac{2\sqrt2}3(5-x)\) passes through the same point.
For \(x\in[2,5]\) the line is below \(y=\sqrt{12-2x}\) (they meet again only at \(x=5.75\)).
solutions.full_html: \(\int_0^22\sqrt x\,dx=\frac{8\sqrt2}3\). Triangle under the line: \(\frac12\cdot3\cdot2\sqrt2=3\sqrt2\). Total \(\frac{17\sqrt2}3\), so \(\alpha=\frac{17}3\). Answer (B).
solutions.focus_note: The second parabola never becomes the active boundary: the line cuts it off.

solutions.key_idea: Area under the 'roof' minus area under the hyperbola.
hints: Intersections: \(y=\frac1x\) with \(5x-4y=1\) at \(x=1\); with \(4x+4y=17\) at \(x=\frac14,4\). The lines meet at \((2,\frac94)\).
Region: \(1\le x\le4\), between \(y=\frac1x\) and the lower of the two lines.
solutions.full_html: \(\int_1^2\frac{5x-1}4dx+\int_2^4\frac{17-4x}4dx-\int_1^4\frac{dx}x=\frac{13}8+\frac52-\ln4=\frac{33}8-\ln4\). Answer (B).
solutions.focus_note: Check a point: \((2,1)\) satisfies all three inequalities.

solutions.key_idea: Cancel the positive factor \(e^{-x}\).
solutions.full_html: In \([0,10\pi]\): \(x=0,2\pi,\dots,10\pi\) (6 values) and \(\frac\pi2,\frac{5\pi}2,\dots,\frac{17\pi}2\) (5 values). \(n=11\). Answer: 11.
solutions.focus_note: Both endpoints \(0\) and \(10\pi\) count.

solutions.key_idea: Split at the crossings and take absolute values.
hints: An antiderivative of \(e^{-x}(\sin x+\cos x-1)\) is \(F(x)=e^{-x}(1-\cos x)\).
solutions.focus_note: \(\frac{d}{dx}(-e^{-x}\cos x)=e^{-x}(\sin x+\cos x)\): a useful pair.

solutions.key_idea: Vandermonde's identity for both sums, after adjusting for starting at \(r=1\).
hints: Vandermonde: \(\sum_{r}\binom{10}r\binom{20}r=\binom{30}{10}\) and \(\sum\binom{10}r^2=\binom{20}{10}\). Watch the missing \(r=0\) term.

wrong_options.C: The \(r=0\) terms are missing, so the two parts don't cancel completely.

solutions.focus_note: \(\sum\binom mr\binom nr=\binom{m+n}{m}\) (Vandermonde). Always check where the sum starts.

solutions.key_idea: Ratios of consecutive binomial coefficients give two linear equations.
hints: Let the coefficients be \(\binom N{r},\binom N{r+1},\binom N{r+2}\) with \(N=n+5\).
solutions.focus_note: \(\frac{\binom n{r+1}}{\binom nr}=\frac{n-r}{r+1}\). This is the fastest tool for ratio questions.

solutions.key_idea: List the non-negative solutions of \(2a+3b+4c=11\) and add the products of binomial coefficients.
hints: You need \(2a+3b+4c=11\) with \(0\le a\le4,\ 0\le b\le7,\ 0\le c\le12\). The coefficient is \(\sum\binom4a\binom7b\binom{12}c\).
\(b\) must be odd (since \(11-3b\) must be even): \(b=1\) or \(3\).

wrong_options.A: Misses the term \(a=1,b=3\) and part of another.

solutions.focus_note: For products of binomials in different powers of \(x\), set up the exponent equation and use parity to cut the cases.

solutions.key_idea: \(\prod(1+x^k)\) generates partitions into distinct parts.
hints: The coefficient of \(x^9\) counts ways of writing 9 as a sum of distinct positive integers.
solutions.focus_note: \(\prod(1+x^k)\) means distinct parts. \(\prod\frac1{1-x^k}\) means unrestricted partitions.

solutions.key_idea: Hockey-stick identity, then reduce to \(m^2=51n+1\).
hints: \(\sum_{k=2}^{49}\binom k2=\binom{50}3\) (hockey stick). The last term contributes \(\binom{50}2m^2\).
solutions.full_html:
Coefficient \(=\binom{50}3+\binom{50}2m^2=1225(16+m^2)\). This must equal \((3n+1)\cdot17\cdot1225\).
\(16+m^2=51n+17\), so \(m^2=51n+1\). For \(n\ge1\), the smallest \(m\) with \(m^2\equiv1\pmod{51}\) and \(m>1\) is \(m=16\): \(256=51\cdot5+1\).
So \(n=5\). Answer: 5.
solutions.focus_note: \(\binom22+\binom32+\dots+\binom k2=\binom{k+1}3\). The hockey stick appears again and again.

solutions.key_idea: Absorb \(r\) into the coefficient, then apply Vandermonde.
solutions.focus_note: \(r\binom nr=n\binom{n-1}{r-1}\) removes the factor \(r\). Then the sum is Vandermonde.

solutions.key_idea: Standard binomial sums give \(n\). Then integrate \((1+x)^n\) from 0 to 1.
hints: The determinant equals 0 gives \(n=4\). Then \(\sum\frac{\binom nk}{k+1}=\frac{2^{n+1}-1}{n+1}\).
solutions.focus_note: \(\sum\frac{\binom nk}{k+1}\) is always \(\int_0^1(1+x)^n\,dx\).

solutions.key_idea: The awkward ratio collapses to \(\binom n{p-i}\), so each inner sum is \(2^n\) and \(g(m,n)=2^{m+n}\).
solutions.full_html:
\(\dfrac{\binom{n+i}{p}\binom{n+p}{p-i}}{\binom{n+p}{p}}=\dfrac{(n+i)!}{p!\,(n+i-p)!}\cdot\dfrac{(n+p)!}{(p-i)!\,(n+i)!}\cdot\dfrac{p!\,n!}{(n+p)!}=\dfrac{n!}{(p-i)!\,(n+i-p)!}=\binom n{p-i}\).
So \(g(m,n)=\sum_{i}\binom mi\sum_{p}\binom n{p-i}=\sum_i\binom mi\,2^n=2^{m+n}\). (Check: \(g(1,1)=4\).)
(A) \(2^{m+n}\) is symmetric ✓. (B) both sides are \(2^{m+n+1}\) ✓. (C) \(2^{2(m+n)}\ne2\cdot2^{m+n}\) in general ✗. (D) \(2^{2(m+n)}=(2^{m+n})^2\) ✓.
Answer: (A), (B), (D).
solutions.focus_note: Behind a frightening sum there is usually a factorial cancellation. Also compute one small case, here \(g(1,1)=4\), to confirm the pattern.

solutions.key_idea: Find the matching general term in each expansion and equate the coefficients.
hints: In \(\left(ax^2+\frac{70}{27bx}\right)^4\), the general term has power \(x^{8-3r}\). Set \(8-3r=5\).
solutions.full_html:
First: \(r=1\): \(\binom41a^3\cdot\frac{70}{27b}=\frac{280a^3}{27b}\).
Second: \(r=4\): \(\binom74a^3\cdot\frac{1}{b^4}=\frac{35a^3}{b^4}\).
\(\frac{280}{27b}=\frac{35}{b^4}\Rightarrow b^3=\frac{27}8\Rightarrow b=\frac32\), so \(2b=3\). Answer: 3.
solutions.focus_note: In the second expansion the sign is \((-1)^4=+1\). Check the sign of the term you pick.

solutions.key_idea: Closure of \(\mathbb Z[\sqrt2]\) under multiplication, plus the size of \(\sqrt2\pm1\).
hints: \((\pm1+\sqrt2)^n\) expands to an integer plus an integer times \(\sqrt2\).
\(0<\sqrt2-1<1\), so its powers tend to 0. For (D), \(e^{i\pi t}\in\mathbb Z\) iff \(t\) is an integer.
solutions.full_html:
(A) Integers are in \(S\), and powers of \(\pm1+\sqrt2\) stay in \(S\) (by the binomial expansion). True.
(B) \((\sqrt2-1)^n\to0\), so some power lies in \(\left(0,\frac1{2024}\right)\). The intersection is non-empty. False.
(C) \((1+\sqrt2)^n\to\infty\). True.
(D) \(e^{i\pi(a+b\sqrt2)}\in\mathbb Z\) iff it is \(\pm1\) iff \(a+b\sqrt2\in\mathbb Z\) iff \(b=0\) (\(\sqrt2\) is irrational). True.
Answer: (A), (C), (D).
solutions.focus_note: \((\sqrt2+1)(\sqrt2-1)=1\). One grows exactly as fast as the other shrinks.

solutions.key_idea: Find the greatest coefficient using the ratio of consecutive terms.
hints: The coefficients increase while this ratio is \(>1\): \(2(23-r)>5(r+1)\).
solutions.full_html:
\(\frac{a_{r+1}}{a_r}>1\iff46-2r>5r+5\iff r<\frac{41}7\approx5.86\).
So the coefficients increase up to \(a_6\), then decrease. \(r=6\). Answer: 6.
solutions.focus_note: For \((1+kx)^n\), the greatest coefficient is at \(r=\left\lfloor\frac{k(n+1)}{1+k}\right\rfloor\) when this is not an integer. Here \(\left\lfloor\frac{48}{7}\right\rfloor=6\).

solutions.key_idea: Use the focus–directrix definition to find the three points directly.
hints: Take \(A=(0,0),B=(2,0),C=(2,2),D=(0,2)\). \(BD\): \(x+y=2\). The locus of \(S\) is the parabola with focus \(A\) and directrix \(BD\).
\(M\): \(x+y=0\). Points on it are \(\sqrt2\) from \(BD\), so they are \(\sqrt2\) from \(A\).
solutions.full_html:
\(T_2,T_3=(1,-1),(-1,1)\). On \(AC\) (\(y=x\)): \(\sqrt2t=\frac{2-2t}{\sqrt2}\) gives \(t=\frac12\), so \(T_1=\left(\frac12,\frac12\right)\).
Area \(=\frac12\cdot2\sqrt2\cdot\frac1{\sqrt2}=1\). Answer (C).
solutions.focus_note: \(T_1\) is the vertex of the parabola: the midpoint of \(A\) and the foot of the perpendicular on \(BD\).

solutions.key_idea: Equal distances to a point and a line define a parabola.
hints: If the moving circle has radius \(\rho\), its centre is at distance \(\rho\) from \(L\) and \(1+\rho\) from the centre of \(C_1\).
Distance to the centre of \(C_1\) = distance to a line parallel to \(L\), shifted by 1.
solutions.full_html: Distance to centre \(=\rho+1=\) distance to the line \(L'\) parallel to \(L\) at distance 1 beyond it. So the locus is a parabola. Answer (C).

wrong_options.A: Constant sum of distances would give an ellipse.
wrong_options.B: Constant difference would give a hyperbola.

solutions.focus_note: Absorb the constant radius by shifting the line. A focus–directrix property appears.

solutions.key_idea: Sum of squared distances to the vertices depends only on the distance to the centre.
hints: For any point \(X\) at distance \(d\) from the centre \(O\): \(\sum XA^2=4d^2+\sum OA^2\).

wrong_options.C: The two circles have different radii.

solutions.focus_note: \(\sum|X-A_i|^2=n|X-G|^2+\sum|A_i-G|^2\), where \(G\) is the centroid of the points.

solutions.key_idea: The line of centres (or axis) is always a common normal. Tangents depend on the position.
hints: Two circles always have a common normal: the line of centres.
A circle strictly inside another has no common tangent. The two branches of a hyperbola have no common tangent either.
solutions.full_html:
(A) Intersecting: 2 common tangents and a normal: (p), (q). (B) External: 4 tangents, normal: (p), (q).
(C) One inside: no tangent, normal: (q), (r). (D) The transverse axis is a common normal, and no line touches both branches: (q), (r).
solutions.focus_note: The asymptotes are not tangents. They touch the hyperbola only at infinity.

solutions.key_idea: Director circle.
hints: Perpendicular tangents come from points on the director circle \(x^2+y^2=2r^2\).
solutions.full_html: The director circle of \(x^2+y^2=169\) is \(x^2+y^2=338\), and \((17,7)\) lies on it. Both statements are true, and Statement-2 explains Statement-1. Answer (A).
solutions.focus_note: Director circle of \(x^2+y^2=a^2\): \(x^2+y^2=2a^2\).

solutions.key_idea: Pitot's theorem plus the area.
hints: The height \(AD=2r\). A tangential quadrilateral has \(AB+CD=AD+BC\).
solutions.focus_note: Pitot's theorem: opposite sides of a tangential quadrilateral have equal sums.

solutions.key_idea: Sine rule with the known side \(RS\).
solutions.full_html:
\(\vec{PR}=(8,-2\sqrt2),\ \vec{PS}=(-2,-2\sqrt2)\). \(\cos P=\frac{-8}{\sqrt{72}\sqrt{12}}\), so \(\sin P=\frac{5}{3\sqrt3}\).
\(R_{circ}=\frac{10}{2\cdot\frac5{3\sqrt3}}=3\sqrt3\). Answer (B).
solutions.focus_note: Alternatively \(R=\frac{abc}{4\Delta}\).

solutions.key_idea: \(r=\frac{\Delta}{s}\).
solutions.full_html: \(s=\frac{4\sqrt2+12\sqrt2}2=8\sqrt2\). \(r=\frac{16\sqrt2}{8\sqrt2}=2\). Answer (D).
solutions.focus_note: In an isosceles triangle, compute the area with base × height.

solutions.key_idea: Both triangles share the base \(PQ\). Compare their heights.
hints: Tangent to the circle at \(P\): \(x+2\sqrt2y=9\), so \(R=(9,0)\). Tangent to the parabola at \(P\): \(2\sqrt2y=4(x+1)\), so \(S=(-1,0)\).
solutions.full_html: \(PQ\) lies on \(x=1\). The heights are \(|1-(-1)|=2\) and \(|9-1|=8\). Ratio \(=1:4\). Answer (C).
solutions.focus_note: Tangent to \(y^2=4ax\) at \((x_1,y_1)\) meets the \(x\)-axis at \((-x_1,0)\).

solutions.key_idea: Centre = point of contact − radius × unit normal.
hints: The centre is 1 unit from \(D\) along the normal to \(PQ\), towards the origin.
solutions.full_html: Centre \(=\left(\frac{3\sqrt3}2,\frac32\right)-\frac12(\sqrt3,1)=(\sqrt3,1)\). Circle: \((x-\sqrt3)^2+(y-1)^2=1\). Answer (D).
solutions.focus_note: 'Origin and centre on the same side' fixes the direction of the normal.

solutions.key_idea: Rotate the known contact point about the incentre.
hints: In an equilateral triangle, the contact points are at \(120^\circ\) intervals around the incentre.
solutions.full_html:
\(\vec{OD}=\left(\frac{\sqrt3}2,\frac12\right)\) (from the centre). Rotations give \(\left(-\frac{\sqrt3}2,\frac12\right)\) and \((0,-1)\).
Points: \(E=\left(\frac{\sqrt3}2,\frac32\right)\), \(F=(\sqrt3,0)\). Answer (A).

wrong_options.C: Second point is not on the circle.

solutions.focus_note: Check every candidate point against the circle equation. It is the quickest elimination.

solutions.key_idea: A repeated root in the elimination means the curves touch.
hints: A double root means tangency, and each \(x\) gives two values of \(y\).
solutions.full_html: \((x-1)^2=0\) gives \(x=1\), \(y=\pm2\). The curves touch at \((1,2)\) and \((1,-2)\). Answer (B).

wrong_options.A: Symmetry about the \(x\)-axis gives two points.
wrong_options.C: The root is repeated, so they touch rather than cross.

solutions.focus_note: For curves symmetric about an axis, one value of \(x\) can give two contact points.

solutions.key_idea: Distance from the centre decides chord versus non-chord.
hints: With \(p=-6\), \(L_2:\ 2x+3y-3=0\) is at distance \(\frac6{\sqrt{13}}<2\) from the centre: a chord.
solutions.full_html:
Statement-2: when \(L_1\) is a diameter, \(L_2\) is a chord. So Statement-2 is false.
Statement-1: \(L_1\) and \(L_2\) are parallel and \(\frac6{\sqrt{13}}\) apart, so both can't pass through the centre in general. \(L_2\) is not always a diameter. True. Answer (C).
solutions.focus_note: Parallel lines at distance \(<2r\) can both be chords.

solutions.key_idea: Intersecting chords plus AM–GM, twice.
hints: Power of a point: \(PS\cdot ST=QS\cdot SR\).
solutions.full_html:
\(\frac1{PS}+\frac1{ST}\ge\frac2{\sqrt{QS\cdot SR}}\ge\frac4{QR}\). Equality would need \(PS=ST\) and \(QS=SR\), i.e. \(S\) the midpoint of both chords, i.e. the centre, which is excluded. So both are strict.
Answer: (B), (D).
solutions.focus_note: Two chords bisecting each other must both be diameters. That is the equality case.

solutions.key_idea: Tangent lines at the contact points.
hints: The side through \(F=(\sqrt3,0)\) is tangent there. The radius to \(F\) is vertical, so the side is horizontal.
The side through \(E\) is perpendicular to the radius \(\left(-\frac{\sqrt3}2,\frac12\right)\).
solutions.full_html: At \(F\): \(y=0\). At \(E\): normal direction \((-\sqrt3,1)\), line \(-\sqrt3x+y=0\), i.e. \(y=\sqrt3x\). Answer (D).

wrong_options.A: These lines are not tangent to the circle.
wrong_options.B: \(y=\frac{x}{\sqrt3}\) is at distance \(\ne1\) from the centre.

solutions.focus_note: Tangent at a point ⊥ radius at that point.

solutions.key_idea: The tangent points and the centre lie on the circle with diameter \(PC\).
hints: \(\angle PAC=\angle PBC=90^\circ\), where \(C=(3,2)\) is the centre.
So the circumcircle of \(PAB\) has diameter \(PC\).

wrong_options.D: Same centre as the given circle.

solutions.focus_note: Circle on diameter \(AB\): \((x-x_1)(x-x_2)+(y-y_1)(y-y_2)=0\).

solutions.key_idea: Two conditions: external tangency with \(C_1\) and tangency of the common line with \(C\).
hints: Put \(C_1,C_2\) at \((\pm3,0)\), \(P\) at the origin. By symmetry, the centre of \(C\) is \((0,k)\).
Tangent from \(P\) to \(C_1\) makes angle \(\varphi\) with \(\sin\varphi=\frac13\). It must also be at distance \(\rho\) from \((0,k)\).
solutions.full_html:
Distance from \((0,k)\) to the line: \(k\cos\varphi=\rho\), so \(k=\frac{3\rho}{2\sqrt2}\). External tangency: \(9+k^2=(1+\rho)^2\).
\(9+\frac{9\rho^2}8=1+2\rho+\rho^2\), so \(\rho^2-16\rho+64=0\) and \(\rho=8\). Answer: 8.
solutions.focus_note: Use symmetry to place the centre on the perpendicular bisector.

solutions.key_idea: Distances from the centre add up to the gap between the chords.
hints: A chord subtending \(2\theta\) at the centre is at distance \(2\cos\theta\) from it.
The chords are on opposite sides: \(2\cos\frac\pi{2k}+2\cos\frac\pi k=\sqrt3+1\).
solutions.full_html: Try \(\frac\pi{2k}=\frac\pi6\), \(\frac\pi k=\frac\pi3\): \(\sqrt3+1\). ✓ So \(k=3\) (the left side decreases in \(\frac1k\), so the solution is unique). Answer: 3.
solutions.focus_note: The numbers \(\sqrt3\) and 1 are \(2\cos30^\circ\) and \(2\cos60^\circ\). Spot the standard angles.

solutions.key_idea: Identify the smaller segment, then test the points.
hints: The line is close to the origin, so the smaller part is the side not containing the origin: \(2x-3y-1>0\).
Check each point: inside the disc (\(x^2+y^2<6\)) and on that side.
solutions.focus_note: The smaller segment is the one away from the centre.

solutions.key_idea: The tangent point fixes the centre's \(y\)-coordinate and the radius.
solutions.focus_note: Substitute each option. It is quicker than re-deriving.

solutions.key_idea: Test the distance conditions for each candidate.
hints: The circles \(x^2+y^2=4\) and \((x-3)^2+y^2=1\) touch externally at \((2,0)\).
Check each option: distance to \((0,0)\) must be 2 and to \((3,0)\) must be 1.
solutions.full_html: \(x+2\sqrt2y=6\): distance from the origin \(\frac63=2\) ✓, from \((3,0)\): \(\frac{3}{3}=1\) ✓. Answer (D).

wrong_options.A: \(x=4\) is at distance 4 from the origin.

solutions.focus_note: The common tangent at the contact point is \(x=2\). The others are found by testing distances.

solutions.key_idea: Pole–polar inversion: the midpoint and the pole lie on the same ray from \(O\).
hints: For an external point \((h,k)\), the chord of contact \(hx+ky=9\) has midpoint \(M=\frac{9(h,k)}{h^2+k^2}\).
solutions.focus_note: Midpoint of the chord of contact from \(P\): \(\frac{r^2}{|OP|^2}P\).

solutions.key_idea: Perpendicular slope plus the tangency condition.
solutions.full_html: \(c=1\) or \(5\). \(x-\sqrt3y=1\) is an option. Answer (A).
solutions.focus_note: Distance from the centre = radius is the tangency test.

solutions.key_idea: Tangency and intercept conditions.
solutions.full_html: Centres \((3,\pm4)\) (and \((-3,\pm4)\)). Equations \(x^2+y^2-6x\mp8y+9=0\). Options (A), (C).
solutions.focus_note: \(y\)-intercept \(=2\sqrt{f^2-c}\) for \(x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy+c=0\).

solutions.key_idea: Orthogonality condition \(2g_1g_2+2f_1f_2=c_1+c_2\).
solutions.focus_note: Orthogonality: \(d^2=r_1^2+r_2^2\).

solutions.key_idea: Distances from points on the \(y\)-axis to the tangent.
solutions.full_html:
(A) \(Q_2Q_3=12\) ✓. (B) \(R_2R_3\) = projection of \(Q_2Q_3\) on the tangent \(=12\cdot\frac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt3}=4\sqrt6\) ✓.
(C) Height from \(O\) \(=\sqrt3\): \(\frac12\cdot4\sqrt6\cdot\sqrt3=6\sqrt2\) ✓. (D) \(\frac12\cdot12\cdot\sqrt2=6\sqrt2\ne4\sqrt2\) ✗.
Answer: (A), (B), (C).

wrong_options.D: The height from \(P\) to the \(y\)-axis is \(\sqrt2\), so the area is \(6\sqrt2\).

solutions.focus_note: Foot-to-foot distance = projection of the segment joining the points onto the line.

solutions.key_idea: Parametrise, then eliminate \(t\).
hints: \(E\) is on the normal \(y=x\tan\theta\) with \(y=\tan\frac\theta2\). Let \(t=\tan\frac\theta2\).
solutions.focus_note: Tangents at \(\theta\) and \(\varphi\) on the unit circle meet at a point with \(\tan\frac{\theta-\varphi}{2}\) structure.

solutions.key_idea: Casework on how the circle meets the axes.
hints: Three common points with the axes: either through the origin, or tangent to one axis and cutting the other twice.
solutions.full_html:
Through the origin: \(p=0\). Points \((0,0),(-2,0),(0,-4)\) ✓.
Tangent to the \(x\)-axis: \(r=2\), \(p=-1\); the \(y\)-axis gives \(y^2+4y+1=0\), two points ✓.
Tangent to the \(y\)-axis: \(r=1\), \(p=-4\); the \(x\)-axis gives \(x^2+2x+4=0\), no points ✗.
Answer: 2.
solutions.focus_note: 'Exactly three points' usually means through the origin or tangent to one axis.

solutions.key_idea: Parametrise, then eliminate \(t\) using \(\cos^2t+\sin^2t=1\).
hints: Tangent at \((2\cos t,2\sin t)\): \(x\cos t+y\sin t=2\).

wrong_options.A: Not satisfied by the midpoint, e.g. \(t=\frac\pi4\): \((\sqrt2,\sqrt2)\).
wrong_options.B: That is the envelope of a different family.

solutions.focus_note: Intercept form of a tangent makes intercepts easy to read.

solutions.key_idea: Equal tangent lengths give \(E_1\). The midpoints of chords through a fixed point give \(E_2\).
hints: The common tangent at \(M\) meets \(T\) at \(K\) with \(KP=KM=KQ\). So \(K\) is the midpoint of \(PQ\) and \(M\) is on the circle with diameter \(PQ\).
\(E_1\): circle centre \((0,1)\), radius \(2\sqrt{10}\), without \(P\) and \(Q\). \(E_2\): midpoints of chords through \(R(1,1)\), the circle with diameter \(CR\).
solutions.full_html:
(A) \(P\) itself is excluded from \(E_1\) ✗. (D) \(\left(0,\frac32\right)\) is \(\frac12\) from \((0,1)\), not on \(E_1\) ✓.
\(E_2\): circle centre \(\left(\frac12,1\right)\), radius \(\frac12\). (C) \(\left(\frac12,1\right)\) is its centre, not on it ✗.
(B) \(\left(\frac45,\frac75\right)\) is on that circle, but its chord through \(R\) has direction \((-1,2)\) and passes through \(P(-2,7)\), which is not in \(E_1\). So it is not in \(E_2\) ✓.
Answer: (B), (D).

wrong_options.C: \(\left(\frac12,1\right)\) is the centre of the \(E_2\) circle.

solutions.focus_note: Remember the excluded points. They change the answer to (B).

solutions.key_idea: Poles of chords through \(P_0\) lie on the polar of \(P_0\).
hints: The tangents at the ends of a chord meet at the pole of that chord.
solutions.full_html: Chords \(y=1\), \(x=1\), \(x+y=2\) have poles \((0,4),(4,0),(2,2)\). All lie on \(x+y=4\), the polar of \((1,1)\). Answer (A).
solutions.focus_note: La Hire: if \(P\) lies on the polar of \(Q\), then \(Q\) lies on the polar of \(P\).

solutions.key_idea: A direct common tangent meets the line of centres at the external homothety centre.
hints: Distance from \(A\) to the line is \(\frac52\), so \(AB=5\).
\(C\) is the external centre of similitude: \(\frac{CA}{CB}=\frac21\).
solutions.full_html: \(CA:CB=2:1\) externally, so \(CA=2AB=10\). Answer: 10.
solutions.focus_note: External centre divides \(AB\) externally in the ratio of the radii.

solutions.key_idea: Midpoint of a chord = foot of the perpendicular from the centre.
hints: The midpoint of the chord is the foot of the perpendicular from the centre \((3,-2)\).
solutions.focus_note: \(CM\perp PQ\) for a chord \(PQ\) with midpoint \(M\).

solutions.key_idea: Compute each entry, then find the wrong pairing.
hints: (III): both triangles have base \(ZM\)-related heights; compute with coordinates. The ratio is \(\frac54\).
(IV): the common tangent at \(M\) is \(3x+4y=-15\). Tangency with \(x^2=8\alpha y\) gives \(\alpha=\frac{10}3\).
solutions.full_html:
(I) \(2h+k=6\) → P. (III) The area ratio is \(\frac54\) → R. (IV) \(x^2+6\alpha x+30\alpha=0\) has a double root: \(36\alpha^2=120\alpha\), so \(\alpha=\frac{10}3\) → U.
(IV), (S) is incorrect. Answer (D).
solutions.focus_note: The question asks for the only INCORRECT combination.

solutions.key_idea: Find \(C_3\), then chord lengths on the radical axis.
hints: \(C_3\) contains both circles and touches them: its diameter is along the line of centres, from \(M=(-\frac95,-\frac{12}5)\) to \(N=(\frac{27}5,\frac{36}5)\). Radius 6, centre \((\frac95,\frac{12}5)\).
solutions.full_html:
\(2h+k=6\). Distance from \(O\) to the radical axis \(=\frac95\), so \(XY=2\sqrt{9-\frac{81}{25}}=\frac{24}5\). Distance from the centre of \(C_3\) to it \(=\frac65\), so \(ZW=2\sqrt{36-\frac{36}{25}}=\frac{12\sqrt{24}}5\).
\(\frac{ZW}{XY}=\sqrt6\). So (II)→(Q). Answer (C).
solutions.focus_note: The common chord lies on the radical axis \(S_1-S_2=0\).

solutions.key_idea: Circumcentre = intersection of perpendicular bisectors.
hints: The circumcentre of \(OPQ\) lies on the perpendicular bisector of \(PQ\), which passes through \(O\) (the line \(y=2x\)).
It is on \(x+2y=4\) too: \(\left(\frac45,\frac85\right)\). Its distance to \(O\) equals its distance to \(P\).
solutions.full_html:
Circumcentre \(K=\left(\frac45,\frac85\right)\), \(|KO|^2=\frac{16}5\). The foot of the perpendicular from \(O\) to \(PQ\) is \(F=\left(\frac12,1\right)\), and \(|KF|=\frac{3\sqrt5}{10}\).
\(|KP|^2=|KF|^2+\text{(half-chord)}^2=\frac{9}{20}+\left(r^2-\frac54\right)=\frac{16}5\), so \(r^2=4\) and \(r=2\). Answer: 2.
solutions.focus_note: For a chord \(PQ\) of a circle centred at \(O\), the perpendicular bisector of \(PQ\) passes through \(O\).

solutions.key_idea: Contact point from the minimisation.
solutions.full_html: \(\alpha=\frac32+\frac12=2\). Answer: 2.
solutions.focus_note: At tangency, the minimising \(x\) is the contact point.

solutions.key_idea: Find the vertices from the orthocentre, then fit the circle.
hints: Vertex \(A=(-1,0)\) where the two sides meet. \(B=(b,0)\), \(C=(c,-1-c)\).
Altitude from \(C\) is vertical (\(\perp\) the \(x\)-axis): \(c=1\). Altitude from \(B\) is \(\perp AC\) (slope 1) through \(H\): \(b=0\).
solutions.full_html: Vertices \((-1,0),(0,0),(1,-2)\). The circle \(x^2+y^2+x+3y=0\) passes through all three. Answer (B).
solutions.focus_note: Use the altitudes: one vertex at a time.

solutions.key_idea: The largest circle touches both the \(y\)-axis and the parabola.
hints: The minimum is at \(x=a+\frac12\): \(\frac{15}4-a\). Balance \(a\) with \(\sqrt{\frac{15}4-a}\).
solutions.full_html: \(a^2=\frac{15}4-a\), so \(a=\frac32\) and \(r=\frac32\). Answer: 1.50.
solutions.focus_note: Minimise the squared distance from the centre to the curve.

solutions.key_idea: A mixtilinear-type incircle: tangency gives a quadratic in \(r\).
hints: The small circle has centre \((r,r)\). Internal tangency: distance between centres \(=R-r\).
solutions.full_html: \(\left(r-\frac12\right)^2+\left(r-\frac32\right)^2=\left(\frac{\sqrt{10}}2-r\right)^2\), so \(r^2-(4-\sqrt{10})r=0\) and \(r=4-\sqrt{10}\approx0.84\). Answer: 0.84.
solutions.focus_note: For a right angle at \(A\), this circle has radius \(b+c-2R=1+3-\sqrt{10}\). A neat check.

solutions.key_idea: \(\sin\frac\pi n=\frac r{R+r}\).
hints: The centres of the small circles form a regular \(n\)-gon at distance \(R+r\) from the centre of \(G\).
solutions.full_html:
\(R=r\left(\frac1{\sin(\pi/n)}-1\right)\).
\(n=4\): \(R=(\sqrt2-1)r\), equality, so (A) ✗. \(n=5\): \(R\approx0.70r<r\), so (B) ✗.
\(n=8\): \(R\approx1.61r>(\sqrt2-1)r\) ✓. \(n=12\): \(R=r\left(\frac{1}{\sin15^\circ}-1\right)\approx2.86r<\sqrt2(\sqrt3+1)r\approx3.86r\) ✓.
Answer: (C), (D).
solutions.focus_note: \(\frac{1}{\sin15^\circ}=\sqrt2(\sqrt3+1)\). That is why (D) is phrased that way.

solutions.key_idea: The line through the midpoints is the radical axis.
hints: The midpoint of a common tangent has equal tangent lengths to both circles, so it lies on the radical axis.
Radical axis: \(8x+2y=18-r^2\). It meets the \(x\)-axis at \(B=\left(\frac{18-r^2}8,0\right)\).
solutions.focus_note: Midpoints of common tangents always lie on the radical axis.

solutions.key_idea: Tangency fixes \(r\) in terms of \(\alpha\). The foot of the perpendicular gives \(A_1\).
solutions.focus_note: The other end of a diameter is the reflection of one end through the centre.

solutions.key_idea: Four quick constructions; test the listed points.
The three points form a right triangle, so \(PQ\) is a diameter.
hints: \(P\) and \(R\) share \(x=2\); \(Q\) and \(R\) share \(y=1\). Angle at \(R\) is \(90^\circ\).
solutions.full_html: \(\angle PRQ=90^\circ\), so the circumradius is \(\frac{PQ}2=\frac{\sqrt{1+9}}2=\sqrt{\frac52}\). Answer (C).
solutions.focus_note: Always check for a right angle before computing a circumcircle.

solutions.key_idea: Use the condition \(u=\bar u\) for real \(u\), then factor out \(w-\bar w=2i\beta\ne0\).
hints: A complex number \(u\) is real exactly when \(u=\bar u\).
Cross-multiply \(\dfrac{w-\bar wz}{1-z}=\dfrac{\bar w-w\bar z}{1-\bar z}\) and collect the terms. Most of them cancel.
solutions.full_html:
Since the quantity is real, \(\dfrac{w-\bar wz}{1-z}=\dfrac{\bar w-w\bar z}{1-\bar z}\). Cross-multiplying:
\((w-\bar wz)(1-\bar z)=(\bar w-w\bar z)(1-z)\)
\(w-w\bar z-\bar wz+\bar w|z|^2=\bar w-\bar wz-w\bar z+w|z|^2\).
The terms \(w\bar z\) and \(\bar wz\) cancel, which leaves \((w-\bar w)-(w-\bar w)|z|^2=0\), that is \((w-\bar w)(1-|z|^2)=0\).
Since \(w-\bar w=2i\beta\ne0\), we get \(|z|=1\). The question already excludes \(z=1\). Answer (D).

wrong_options.A: This includes \(z=1\), where the expression is undefined.
wrong_options.B: \(z=\bar z\) means \(z\) is real, which is not what the algebra gives.
wrong_options.C: Most \(z\ne1\) fail. For example, \(z=2\) gives \(\dfrac{w-2\bar w}{-1}\), and its imaginary part is \(3\beta\ne0\).

solutions.focus_note: When the condition is 'real' or 'purely imaginary', equate the quantity with its conjugate (or with minus its conjugate). It is quicker than splitting into \(x+iy\).

solutions.key_idea: On the unit circle, \(1/z=\bar z\), so the expression becomes \(1/(\bar z-z)\), the reciprocal of a purely imaginary number.
hints: With \(|z|=1\), you have \(\bar z=1/z\). Divide the numerator and the denominator by \(z\).
\(\dfrac{z}{1-z^2}=\dfrac{1}{\frac1z-z}=\dfrac{1}{\bar z-z}\). What kind of number is \(\bar z-z\)?
solutions.full_html:
\(\dfrac{z}{1-z^2}=\dfrac1{z^{-1}-z}=\dfrac1{\bar z-z}=\dfrac{1}{-2i\sin\theta}=\dfrac{i}{2\sin\theta}\), where \(z=e^{i\theta}\) and \(\sin\theta\ne0\) because \(z\ne\pm1\).
This is purely imaginary, so every value lies on the \(y\)-axis. Answer (D).

wrong_options.A: The \(y\)-axis does pass through the origin.
wrong_options.B: The modulus is \(\dfrac1{2|\sin\theta|}\), which varies, so the values are not on one circle.
wrong_options.C: The real part is 0, not the imaginary part.

solutions.focus_note: On \(|z|=1\), always try the substitution \(\bar z=1/z\) first.

solutions.key_idea: Write each displacement as (length) × (unit vector \(e^{i\theta}\)) and add.
hints: North-east is the direction \(e^{i\pi/4}\), and north-west is \(e^{i3\pi/4}\).
solutions.full_html:
First leg: \(3e^{i\pi/4}\). Second leg: \(4e^{i3\pi/4}=4i\,e^{i\pi/4}\).
\(P=3e^{i\pi/4}+4ie^{i\pi/4}=(3+4i)e^{i\pi/4}\). Answer (D).

wrong_options.A: The second leg is not in the \(i\) (north) direction. It is at \(135^\circ\).
wrong_options.B: \(-4i\) would be a turn of \(90^\circ\) clockwise, which is south-east.
wrong_options.C: This swaps the lengths: the walk would be 4 units north-east, then 3 units north-west.

solutions.focus_note: Multiplying by \(i\) is a \(90^\circ\) anticlockwise turn. A walk that turns left by \(90^\circ\) is a factor of \(i\).

solutions.key_idea: \(-1+i\) and \(5+i\) are diametrically opposite on \(B\), so \(PA^2+PB^2\) is fixed for every \(P\) on \(B\).
hints: The points \(-1+i\) and \(5+i\) are the ends of a diameter of circle \(B\). Check that their midpoint is \(2+i\).
For a point \(P\) on a circle with diameter \(AB\), \(PA^2+PB^2=AB^2\), because the angle at \(P\) is a right angle.
solutions.full_html:
The midpoint of \((-1,1)\) and \((5,1)\) is \((2,1)\), the centre of \(B\), and they are 6 apart, which is the diameter.
Any \(z\in A\cap B\cap C\) lies on \(B\), so the angle at \(z\) is \(90^\circ\) and \(|z+1-i|^2+|z-5-i|^2=6^2=36\).
36 lies between 35 and 39. Answer (C).
solutions.focus_note: Before computing \(z\), check whether the fixed points have a special position relative to the locus, such as a diameter, the foci or the centre.

solutions.key_idea: Translations add complex numbers, and a rotation about the origin multiplies by \(e^{i\theta}\).
hints: Track the point step by step: \(1+2i\to6+2i\to6+5i\).
Moving \(\sqrt2\) along \(\hat i+\hat j\) adds \(1+i\). A rotation by \(\frac\pi2\) about the origin is multiplication by \(i\).
solutions.full_html:
Horizontal move away from the origin by 5: \(6+2i\). Vertical move by 3: \(z_1=6+5i\).
\(\sqrt2\) units along \(\hat i+\hat j\) means \(+\sqrt2\cdot\frac{1+i}{\sqrt2}=1+i\), giving \(7+6i\).
Rotating by \(\frac\pi2\) anticlockwise about \(O\): \(z_2=i(7+6i)=-6+7i\). Answer (D).

wrong_options.A: This swaps the coordinates but keeps both signs positive. In fact \(i(7+6i)=7i+6i^2=-6+7i\).
wrong_options.C: This is the point before the rotation.

solutions.focus_note: Rotation about the origin: multiply by \(i\) for \(90^\circ\) anticlockwise, and by \(-i\) for clockwise.

solutions.key_idea: \(A\) is a half-plane, \(B\) is a circle and \(C\) is a line. Count the circle–line intersection points that lie in the half-plane.
hints: Translate each set into geometry: \(\operatorname{Re}((1-i)(x+iy))=x+y\), so \(C\) is the line \(x+y=\sqrt2\).
\(B\) is the circle with centre \((2,1)\) and radius 3. The line cuts it at two points. How many of them have \(y\ge1\)?
solutions.full_html:
\((1-i)(x+iy)=(x+y)+i(y-x)\), so \(C:\ x+y=\sqrt2\).
The distance from the centre \((2,1)\) to the line is \(\dfrac{3-\sqrt2}{\sqrt2}\approx1.12<3\), so the line meets the circle at two points.
Foot of the perpendicular from the centre: \(\left(\frac{1+\sqrt2}{2},\frac{\sqrt2-1}{2}\right)\), with \(y\approx0.21\). Half-chord \(=\sqrt{9-\frac{(3-\sqrt2)^2}{2}}\approx2.78\).
Along the line, \(y\) changes by \(\pm2.78/\sqrt2\approx\pm1.97\). The two points have \(y\approx2.18\) and \(y\approx-1.76\). Only the first satisfies \(y\ge1\).
So \(A\cap B\cap C\) has exactly 1 element. Answer (B).

wrong_options.A: The upper intersection point has \(y\approx2.18\ge1\), so the set is not empty.
wrong_options.C: The lower intersection point has \(y<1\) and lies outside \(A\).
wrong_options.D: A line meets a circle in at most 2 points.

solutions.focus_note: For a half-plane condition, decide which side each intersection point lies on. A rough numerical value of \(y\) is enough.

solutions.key_idea: Use the reverse triangle inequality \(-|z-w|\le|z|-|w|\le|z-w|\) together with \(|z-w|<6\).
hints: You do not need the exact point. Bound \(|z|-|w|\) with the triangle inequality: \(\big||z|-|w|\big|\le|z-w|\).
\(z\) is on the circle and \(w\) is strictly inside it, so \(|z-w|<\) diameter \(=6\).
solutions.full_html:
\(z\) is on circle \(B\) and \(w\) is strictly inside it, so \(|z-w|<6\). Then
\(-6<-|z-w|\le|z|-|w|\le|z-w|<6\), and so \(-3<|z|-|w|+3<9\). This is the answer intended by the official key: (D).
A sharper look: from the previous part, \(z\approx-0.76+2.18i\), so \(|z|\approx2.30\). The origin is inside the circle, so \(|w|\) ranges over \(\big[0,\,3+\sqrt5\big)\). That gives \(|z|-|w|+3\in(0.07,\,5.30]\). This interval also sits inside (B) and (C), but the official key accepts only (D), which is the bound the triangle inequality gives.

wrong_options.A: The expression can exceed 3, for example when \(w\) is near the origin, where it is about 5.3.
wrong_options.B: The true range \((0.07,5.30]\) does fit inside \((-3,6)\), but the official answer for this question is (D), the triangle-inequality bound.
wrong_options.C: Also true numerically, but it was not the official answer. The paper wanted \(-6<|z|-|w|<6\) shifted by 3.

solutions.focus_note: In 'lies between' questions, the examiner usually has one standard inequality in mind. Here it is \(\big||z|-|w|\big|\le|z-w|\).

solutions.key_idea: Sum of sines in arithmetic progression: \(\sum_{m=1}^n\sin(2m-1)\theta=\dfrac{\sin^2n\theta}{\sin\theta}\).
hints: Multiply the sum by \(2\sin\theta\) and use \(2\sin\theta\sin k\theta=\cos(k-1)\theta-\cos(k+1)\theta\). The sum telescopes.
solutions.full_html:
\(2\sin\theta\sum_{m=1}^{15}\sin(2m-1)\theta=\sum(\cos(2m-2)\theta-\cos2m\theta)=1-\cos30\theta=2\sin^215\theta\).
So the sum is \(\dfrac{\sin^215\theta}{\sin\theta}\). At \(\theta=2^\circ\): \(\dfrac{\sin^230^\circ}{\sin2^\circ}=\dfrac{1}{4\sin2^\circ}\). Answer (D).
solutions.alt_html: Take the imaginary part of the geometric series \(z+z^3+\dots+z^{29}=\dfrac{z(1-z^{30})}{1-z^2}\) and simplify using \(z^{30}=e^{i60^\circ}\).

wrong_options.B: There is no factor of 3 in the closed form.

solutions.focus_note: Odd multiples \(\theta,3\theta,5\theta,\dots\) telescope neatly after multiplying by \(2\sin\theta\).

solutions.key_idea: Reduce the equation to \((x^2+y^2)(x^2-y^2)=175\) and search the factor pairs of 175.
hints: So \((x^2+y^2)(x^2-y^2)=175\). Factor 175 into two factors that suit integer \(x,y\).
solutions.full_html:
\(z\bar z(\bar z^2+z^2)=(x^2+y^2)\cdot2(x^2-y^2)=350\), so \((x^2+y^2)(x^2-y^2)=175\).
Both factors are positive, with \(x^2+y^2>x^2-y^2\). The pairs are \((175,1),(35,5),(25,7)\).
