White is only in Box-IV, reached only when \(b\) is green.
solutions.full_html: \(P(\ge1\text{ green})=\frac5{16}+\frac8{16}\cdot\frac{15}{48}+\frac3{16}\cdot\frac{12}{16}=\frac{39}{64}\). \(P(\text{white}\cap\text{green})=\frac5{16}\cdot\frac6{32}=\frac{15}{256}\). Ratio \(\frac5{52}\). Answer (C).

wrong_options.A: That is the joint probability, not conditional.

solutions.focus_note: If \(b\) is green the 'green' event already holds.

solutions.key_idea: Inclusion–exclusion.
solutions.full_html: At least two symptoms: 180. At most one: \(900-180=720\). \(\frac{720}{900}=0.8\). Answer: 0.80.
solutions.focus_note: \(|A\cap B|=|A|+|B|-|A\cup B|\).

solutions.key_idea: Random walk of the score difference.
solutions.focus_note: Symmetry: \(P(X>Y)=P(X<Y)\).

solutions.key_idea: First-step analysis.
hints: Let \(h\) (resp. \(t\)) be the probability of ending with H when the last toss was H (resp. T).
solutions.full_html: \(h=\frac p{1-pq}=\frac37\), \(t=\frac17\). Answer \(=ph+qt=\frac17+\frac2{21}=\frac5{21}\). Answer (B).
solutions.focus_note: Same idea as a Markov chain with two states.

solutions.key_idea: Average degree.
hints: Corners: 2 friends (4 points); edge points: 3 friends (20); interior: 4 friends (25).
solutions.focus_note: \(\sum\deg=2\times\) number of friend pairs.

solutions.key_idea: Two columns, so every triangle has two vertices in one column.
hints: Triangle area \(=\frac d2\), where \(d\) is the gap between the two points in one column.
solutions.full_html: Integer area ⇔ \(d\) even. Column \(x=1\): 4 even-gap pairs × 7 = 28. Column \(x=2\): 9 even-gap pairs × 5 = 45. Total 73 of \(\binom{12}3=220\). Answer (B).
solutions.focus_note: Three points in one column are collinear and are excluded automatically.

solutions.key_idea: Ratio.
solutions.focus_note: Edges of a \(7\times7\) grid: \(2\cdot7\cdot6=84\).

solutions.key_idea: Multiset arrangements.
hints: Multiple of 5 ⇔ last digit 0. Multiple of 20 ⇔ ends in 20 or 40.
solutions.focus_note: Organise by how many 1s, 2s, 4s are used.

solutions.key_idea: Conditional probability after removing two balls.
solutions.full_html: \(9N-81=2N-4\Rightarrow N=11\). Check: \(\frac3{11}\cdot\frac6{10}\cdot\frac29=\frac2{55}=\frac2{5N}\) ✓. Answer: 11.
solutions.focus_note: Both conditions agree; one is enough.

solutions.key_idea: Bayes.
solutions.full_html: \(3(1-k)=k+\frac{1-k}2\Rightarrow k=\frac57\). Answer (C).
solutions.focus_note: Set up \(P(\text{guess}\mid\text{correct})\) carefully.

solutions.key_idea: Bayes, then total probability.
solutions.focus_note: Solve for the unknown rate last.

solutions.key_idea: Independence turns each event into a product.
hints: Take the students independent with probabilities \(s_1,s_2,s_3\). Then \(P(V)=s_1=\frac1{10}\).

solutions.key_idea: Hypergeometric distribution.
solutions.focus_note: Check: weights sum to \(\binom{11}6=462\).

solutions.key_idea: Same composition ⇒ independence.
solutions.focus_note: Box identity carries no information about colour here.

solutions.key_idea: Express \(r\) in terms of the equal side, find it, then compute the area.
hints: Equal sides \(x\), apex angle \(120^\circ\): base \(=x\sqrt3\), area \(=\frac{\sqrt3}4x^2\).
solutions.full_html:
\(r=\dfrac{\frac{\sqrt3}4x^2}{\frac{x(2+\sqrt3)}2}=\dfrac{\sqrt3x}{2(2+\sqrt3)}=\sqrt3\), so \(x=2(2+\sqrt3)\).
\(\Delta=\frac{\sqrt3}4\cdot4(2+\sqrt3)^2=\sqrt3(7+4\sqrt3)=12+7\sqrt3\). Answer (C).

wrong_options.D: No \(\pi\) appears in a triangle's area.

solutions.focus_note: \(\Delta=rs\). With one free length, this pins down the triangle.

solutions.key_idea: Find the angle-bisector length from areas, then use the right triangles at \(D\).
hints: Area split: \(\frac12bc\sin A=\frac12AD\cdot c\sin\frac A2+\frac12AD\cdot b\sin\frac A2\).
solutions.full_html:
(B) \(AD=\frac{2bc}{b+c}\cos\frac A2\) ✓.
(A) \(AE=\frac{AD}{\cos(A/2)}=\frac{2bc}{b+c}\), the H.M. of \(b\) and \(c\) ✓.
(C) \(EF=2AD\tan\frac A2=\frac{4bc}{b+c}\sin\frac A2\) ✓.
(D) \(AD\) bisects \(\angle A\) and is perpendicular to \(EF\), so \(AE=AF\) ✓.
Answer: all four.
solutions.focus_note: A bisector that is also perpendicular to a segment makes the triangle isosceles.

solutions.key_idea: Two triangles from SSA data: compare their areas.
solutions.full_html:
\(C=45^\circ\): \(A=105^\circ\). \(C=135^\circ\): \(A=15^\circ\).
Areas \(=\frac12\cdot2\sqrt2\cdot4\sin A=4\sqrt2\sin A\). Difference \(=4\sqrt2(\sin105^\circ-\sin15^\circ)=4\sqrt2\cdot2\cos60^\circ\sin45^\circ=4\).
Answer: 4.
solutions.focus_note: SSA with \(b<c\) and \(b>c\sin B\) gives two triangles: the ambiguous case.

solutions.key_idea: Find the angle from the area, the third side from the cosine rule, then \(r=\Delta/s\).
hints: \(\frac12ab\sin C=15\sqrt3\) gives \(\sin C=\frac{\sqrt3}2\). Since \(C\) is obtuse, \(C=120^\circ\).
solutions.focus_note: 'Obtuse' is the clue that picks \(120^\circ\) over \(60^\circ\).

solutions.key_idea: The sine rule turns the expression into \(2\sin(A+C)=2\sin B\).
hints: \(\frac ac\sin2C=2\sin A\cos C\) (sine rule). Add the two terms.
solutions.full_html: \(\frac{\sin A}{\sin C}\cdot2\sin C\cos C+\frac{\sin C}{\sin A}\cdot2\sin A\cos A=2(\sin A\cos C+\cos A\sin C)=2\sin B=\sqrt3\). Answer (D).
solutions.focus_note: Angles in A.P. in a triangle always give the middle angle as \(60^\circ\).

solutions.key_idea: Cosine rule plus the positivity of the sides.
hints: Substitute, simplify, and remember that all sides must be positive.

wrong_options.A: It satisfies the algebra, but then \(c=2x+1<0\).
wrong_options.C: Does not satisfy the cosine rule.
wrong_options.D: Does not satisfy the cosine rule.

solutions.focus_note: Always check that every side is positive at the end.

solutions.key_idea: Reduce to \(\tan^2\frac P2\) and use the half-angle formula in terms of \(\Delta\).
solutions.full_html:
\(\tan\frac P2=\frac{\Delta}{s(s-a)}=\frac{\Delta}{8}\). Also \(\Delta^2=4\cdot2\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac32=6\), so \(\frac\Delta8=\frac{6}{8\Delta}=\frac3{4\Delta}\).
Value \(=\left(\frac3{4\Delta}\right)^2\). Answer (C).

wrong_options.A: This is \(\tan\frac P2\), not its square.

solutions.focus_note: \(\tan\frac P2=\frac{r}{s-a}=\frac{\Delta}{s(s-a)}\).

solutions.key_idea: Tangent lengths from the vertices give the sides. The cosine condition gives \(n\).
hints: The tangent lengths are \(s-p,\ s-q,\ s-r\). Call them \(n,n+2,n+4\). The largest side \(p\) is opposite the smallest tangent length, \(s-p=n\).
solutions.focus_note: \(s-a\) is the tangent length from \(A\). The largest side is opposite the smallest tangent length.

solutions.key_idea: The given relation forces \(C=120^\circ\). Then express \(r\) and \(R\).
solutions.full_html:
\(r=\frac{\sqrt3y/4}{(x+c)/2}=\frac{\sqrt3y}{2(x+c)}\). \(R=\frac{c}{2\sin120^\circ}=\frac c{\sqrt3}\).
\(\frac rR=\frac{3y}{2c(x+c)}\). Answer (B).

wrong_options.A: Has \(x\) instead of \(c\) in the denominator.

solutions.focus_note: \(c^2=a^2+b^2+ab\iff C=120^\circ\). Recognise it at once.

solutions.key_idea: Four separate computations: a projection identity, a factorisation, a distance to a line and two areas.
hints: (A) \(\frac{\sin(X-Y)}{\sin Z}=\frac{a^2-b^2}{c^2}=\frac12\). (B) Rewrite as \((\sin X+2\sin Y)(\sin X-\sin Y)=0\).
(C) The acute bisector of \(30^\circ\) and \(60^\circ\) is \(y=x\). (D) Compute two areas with \(y=2\sqrt x\).
solutions.focus_note: \(\frac{\sin(X-Y)}{\sin(X+Y)}=\frac{a^2-b^2}{c^2}\). A useful identity from the projection formula.

solutions.key_idea: The ratios of \(s-x,s-y,s-z\) fix the shape. The inradius fixes the size.
hints: Let \(s-x=4k,\ s-y=3k,\ s-z=2k\). Then \(s=9k\), and the sides are \(5k,6k,7k\).
solutions.full_html:
\(r=\frac{6\sqrt6k^2}{9k}=\frac{2\sqrt6k}3\), \(r^2=\frac{8k^2}3=\frac83\), so \(k=1\). Sides 5, 6, 7.
(A) \(\Delta=6\sqrt6\) ✓. (B) \(R=\frac{abc}{4\Delta}=\frac{210}{24\sqrt6}=\frac{35}{4\sqrt6}\ne\frac{35\sqrt6}6\) ✗.
(C) \(\prod\sin\frac X2=\frac r{4R}=\frac{2\sqrt6/3}{35/\sqrt6}=\frac4{35}\) ✓. (D) \(\sin^2\frac{X+Y}2=\cos^2\frac Z2=\frac{s(s-z)}{xy}=\frac{9\cdot2}{30}=\frac35\) ✓.
Answer: (A), (C), (D).
solutions.focus_note: \(r=4R\sin\frac A2\sin\frac B2\sin\frac C2\). It links (C) directly to \(r\) and \(R\).

solutions.key_idea: A right triangle with sides in A.P. is always similar to 3-4-5.
hints: Sides \(a-d,\ a,\ a+d\), with \(a+d\) the hypotenuse.
solutions.full_html: \((a+d)^2=a^2+(a-d)^2\) gives \(a=4d\). Sides \(3d,4d,5d\), area \(6d^2=24\), so \(d=2\). The smallest side is 6. Answer: 6.
solutions.focus_note: Sides in A.P. and right-angled means \(3:4:5\). Worth remembering.

solutions.key_idea: The third side equals one of the given sides, so the triangle is isosceles.
hints: \(PR=QR=10\), so the triangle is isosceles with \(\angle P=\angle Q=30^\circ\).
solutions.full_html:
\(\angle P=30^\circ\) (A ✗), \(\angle R=120^\circ\). Area \(=\frac12\cdot10\sqrt3\cdot10\cdot\frac12=25\sqrt3\) (B ✓).
\(s=10+5\sqrt3\), \(r=\frac{25\sqrt3}{10+5\sqrt3}=10\sqrt3-15\) (C ✓). \(R=\frac{10}{2\sin30^\circ}=10\), so the area of the circumcircle is \(100\pi\) (D ✓).
Answer: (B), (C), (D).
solutions.focus_note: After finding the third side, check for equal sides. It often simplifies everything.

solutions.key_idea: Fix the triangle, then use coordinates for the median and the altitude.
hints: Sine rule with \(R=1\): \(\sin P=\frac{\sqrt3}2,\ \sin Q=\frac12\). Not right-angled means \(P=120^\circ,\ Q=R=30^\circ\).
Place \(R\) at the origin, \(Q=(\sqrt3,0)\), \(P=\left(\frac{\sqrt3}2,\frac12\right)\). Find \(S\), \(E\) and \(O\) by coordinates.
solutions.full_html:
\(S=\left(\frac{3\sqrt3}4,\frac14\right)\), \(E=\left(\frac{\sqrt3}2,0\right)\). \(O\) is on \(x=\frac{\sqrt3}2\) along \(RS\): \(O=\left(\frac{\sqrt3}2,\frac16\right)\).
(A) \(RS=\sqrt{\frac{27}{16}+\frac1{16}}=\frac{\sqrt7}2\) ✓. (C) \(OE=\frac16\) ✓.
(B) Area \(SOE=\frac12\cdot\frac16\cdot\left(\frac{3\sqrt3}4-\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)=\frac{\sqrt3}{48}\ne\frac{\sqrt3}{12}\) ✗.
(D) \(r=\frac\Delta s=\frac{\sqrt3/4}{(2+\sqrt3)/2}=\frac{\sqrt3}2(2-\sqrt3)\) ✓.
Answer: (A), (C), (D).
solutions.focus_note: 'Non-right-angled' rules out \(P=60^\circ\) (which would give \(R=90^\circ\)).

solutions.key_idea: The condition forces \(\tan\frac Y2=1\): a right angle at \(Y\).
hints: \(\tan\frac X2=\frac{r}{s-x}\). The left side becomes \(\frac{ry}{(s-x)(s-z)}\), and the right side is \(\frac ys\).
solutions.full_html:
\(\Delta^2=s(s-x)(s-y)(s-z)=(s-x)^2(s-z)^2\) gives \(s(s-y)=(s-x)(s-z)\), so \(\tan\frac Y2=1\) and \(Y=90^\circ=X+Z\) (B ✓).
(C) In a right triangle with hypotenuse \(y\): \(\tan\frac X2=\frac{\sin X}{1+\cos X}=\frac{x/y}{1+z/y}=\frac x{y+z}\) ✓.
(A) would mean \(Y=60^\circ\) ✗. (D) \(x^2+z^2-y^2=0\ne xz\) ✗.
Answer: (B), (C).
solutions.focus_note: \(\tan\frac A2=\frac{r}{s-a}\). Sums of half-angle tangents simplify neatly this way.

solutions.key_idea: AM–GM and the projection formulas.
hints: (A) \(q^2+r^2\ge2qr\). (B) Use the projection formulas \(p=q\cos R+r\cos Q\) etc.
solutions.full_html:
(A) \(\cos P=\frac{q^2+r^2-p^2}{2qr}\ge\frac{2qr-p^2}{2qr}\) ✓.
(B) Multiply by \(p+q\): the inequality becomes \((p\cos R+r\cos P)+(q\cos R+r\cos Q)\ge q\cos P+p\cos Q\), i.e. \(q+p\ge r\) ✓.
(C) \(\frac{q+r}p\ge\frac{2\sqrt{qr}}p=\frac{2\sqrt{\sin Q\sin R}}{\sin P}\). The stated strict \(<\) is false ✗.
(D) \(p=0.99,\ q=r=1\): \(\cos Q\approx0.495<0.99\) ✗.
Answer: (A), (B).

wrong_options.D: A near-equilateral triangle is a counterexample.

solutions.focus_note: \(a=b\cos C+c\cos B\): the projection formula turns trigonometric inequalities into side inequalities.

solutions.key_idea: Cotangents in terms of the sides: the \(4\Delta\) cancels.
hints: \(\cot A=\frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{4\Delta}\), and similarly for the others.
solutions.focus_note: \(\cot A=\frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{4\Delta}\) avoids computing any angle.

solutions.key_idea: Angle chasing plus the sine rule. The product \(\beta\sin\theta\) comes straight from the sine rule.
hints: In \(\triangle PQR\): \(\angle PRQ=70^\circ-40^\circ=30^\circ\), so \(\angle QPR=80^\circ\). In \(\triangle QRS\): \(\angle SQR=55^\circ=\angle QSR\), so \(RS=QR=1\).
In \(\triangle PRS\), the sine rule gives \(\beta\sin\theta=RS\sin40^\circ=\sin40^\circ\).
solutions.full_html:
\(\alpha=PQ=\frac{\sin30^\circ}{\sin80^\circ}\) (sine rule in \(\triangle PQR\)).
\(\triangle QRS\) is isosceles, so \(RS=1\). In \(\triangle PRS\): \(\frac{RS}{\sin\theta}=\frac{PS}{\sin40^\circ}\), so \(\beta\sin\theta=\sin40^\circ\).
\(4\alpha\beta\sin\theta=\frac{4\sin30^\circ\sin40^\circ}{\sin80^\circ}=\frac{2\sin40^\circ}{2\sin40^\circ\cos40^\circ}=\sec40^\circ\approx1.305\).
This lies in \((0,\sqrt2)\) and in \((1,2)\). Answer: (A), (B).
solutions.focus_note: You never need \(\beta\) or \(\theta\) separately. The sine rule gives their combination directly.

solutions.key_idea: Turn the A.P. condition into \(\cos C-\sin C=\frac12\). Then compute the area with \(R=1\).
hints: Let \(C\) be the smallest angle and \(A=C+\frac\pi2\). Then \(B=\frac\pi2-2C\).
Sides in A.P.: \(\sin A+\sin C=2\sin B\), i.e. \(\cos C+\sin C=2\cos2C\). Divide by \(\cos C+\sin C\).
solutions.full_html:
\(\cos C+\sin C=2(\cos C-\sin C)(\cos C+\sin C)\), so \(\cos C-\sin C=\frac12\). Squaring: \(\sin2C=\frac34\).
\(\cos2C=\sqrt{1-\frac9{16}}=\frac{\sqrt7}4\) (\(2C\) is acute). The area \(a=2R^2\sin A\sin B\sin C=2\cos C\sin C\cos2C=\sin2C\cos2C=\frac{3\sqrt7}{16}\).
\((64a)^2=(12\sqrt7)^2=1008\). Answer: 1008.
solutions.focus_note: \(\Delta=2R^2\sin A\sin B\sin C\). With \(R=1\) there are no lengths to find.

solutions.key_idea: Use \(r=\frac{\Delta}{s}\) with the A.P. condition \(a+c=2b\).
hints: With \(R=1\): \(s=\sin A+\sin B+\sin C=3\sin B\) (A.P.), and \(\sin B=\cos2C=\frac{\sqrt7}4\).
solutions.full_html:
\(s=\frac{a+b+c}2=\frac{3b}2=3\sin B=\frac{3\sqrt7}4\).
\(r=\frac{3\sqrt7/16}{3\sqrt7/4}=\frac14=0.25\). Answer: 0.25.
solutions.focus_note: Sides in A.P. means \(s=\frac{3b}{2}\). That makes \(r=\frac{\Delta}{s}\) quick.

solutions.key_idea: Turn the discriminant condition into an upper bound on \(\lambda\), then bound that using \(a^2<a(b+c)\), which holds because \(a<b+c\).
hints: Write \((a+b+c)^2=\sum a^2+2\sum ab\). Use the triangle inequality to bound \(\dfrac{\sum a^2}{\sum ab}\) above by 2.
solutions.full_html:
\(D\ge0\): \(4(a+b+c)^2\ge12\lambda(ab+bc+ca)\), so \(\lambda\le\dfrac{\sum a^2+2\sum ab}{3\sum ab}=\dfrac13\left(\dfrac{\sum a^2}{\sum ab}+2\right)\).
Triangle: \(a<b+c\) gives \(a^2<ab+ac\). Adding the three such inequalities: \(\sum a^2<2\sum ab\).
So \(\lambda<\frac13(2+2)=\frac43\). Answer (A).

wrong_options.B: \(\lambda\) is bounded above by something less than \(\frac43\), so \(\lambda>\frac53\) is impossible.
wrong_options.C: Values in \(\left[\frac43,\frac53\right)\) never give real roots.

solutions.focus_note: 'Sides of a triangle' plus a symmetric expression: use \(\sum a^2<2\sum ab\). The lower bound, \(\sum a^2\ge\sum ab\), comes from AM–GM.

solutions.key_idea: Subtracting the 'root' equations for \(a\) and \(c\) cancels the \(10ac\) term and gives \(a+c\) directly.
hints: Write the four Vieta relations: \(a+b=10c,\ ab=-11d,\ c+d=10a,\ cd=-11b\).
\(a\) is a root of the first equation and \(c\) is a root of the second. Subtract \(a^2-10ca-11d=0\) and \(c^2-10ac-11b=0\).
solutions.focus_note: In 'roots of one are coefficients of the other' problems, substitute a root into its own equation. That gives an extra relation for free.

solutions.key_idea: Two linear equations from the sums give \(\alpha,\beta\) in terms of \(p,q\). Then \(r=\alpha\beta\).
hints: Both products equal \(r\): \(\alpha\beta=\frac\alpha2\cdot2\beta\) automatically. So use the sums.
solutions.full_html:
From \(\alpha=p-\beta\): \(\frac{p-\beta}2+2\beta=q\), so \(\beta=\frac{2q-p}3\) and \(\alpha=\frac{2(2p-q)}3\).
\(r=\alpha\beta=\frac29(2p-q)(2q-p)\). Answer (D).

wrong_options.A: The factor \(p-q\) does not appear. Check \(\alpha=\frac{2(2p-q)}3\).
wrong_options.B: Same mistake, with the signs reversed.
wrong_options.C: \((q-2p)\) has the wrong sign, which flips the sign of \(r\).

solutions.focus_note: When the products are automatically equal, all the information is in the sums.

solutions.key_idea: Non-real roots come in conjugate pairs. That, together with \(\beta^2\ne\pm1\), forces real roots for both equations.
hints: If \(\alpha,\beta\) were non-real, then \(\beta=\bar\alpha\), and \(\bar\alpha\) would have to be the other root \(\frac1\beta\) of the second equation.
That forces \(\beta^2=1\), which is excluded. So all the roots are real. For Statement-2: if the equations were proportional, they would have the same roots.
solutions.full_html:
Statement-1. Suppose \(\alpha\) is non-real. Then \(\beta=\bar\alpha\) (first equation). The second equation has real coefficients and root \(\alpha\), so its other root \(\frac1\beta\) equals \(\bar\alpha=\beta\), which gives \(\beta^2=1\), a contradiction. So \(\alpha,\beta\) are real, both discriminants are \(\ge0\), and \((p^2-q)(b^2-ac)\ge0\). True.
Statement-2. If \(b=pa\) and \(c=qa\), the second equation would be \(a\) × the first, with roots \(\alpha,\beta\). Then \(\frac1\beta=\beta\), so \(\beta^2=1\), which is excluded. So \(b\ne pa\) or \(c\ne qa\). True.
Statement-2 only says the equations are different. It does not explain why the roots are real. Answer (B).

wrong_options.A: Statement-1 follows from the conjugate-root argument, not from the equations being different.
wrong_options.C: Statement-2 is true: proportional equations would force \(\beta^2=1\).

solutions.focus_note: In Assertion–Reason, ask whether Statement-2 is the actual reason Statement-1 holds, not just whether it is true.

solutions.key_idea: Location of roots: for both roots to be \(\ge t\), you need \(D>0\), \(-\frac b{2a}>t\) and \(f(t)\ge0\).
hints: Both roots \(\ge4\) and distinct: \(D>0\), vertex \(\ge4\), and \(f(4)\ge0\).
solutions.focus_note: 'At least 4' allows a root equal to 4, so the condition is \(f(4)\ge0\), not \(>0\).

solutions.key_idea: Find \(\alpha\beta\) from the cube-sum identity, then build the equation from the sum and product of the new roots.
hints: The roots \(\frac\alpha\beta,\frac\beta\alpha\) have product 1 and sum \(\frac{s^2-2P}P\).
solutions.full_html:
\(q=-p^3+3pP\), so \(P=\dfrac{p^3+q}{3p}\).
Sum \(=\dfrac{s^2}P-2=\dfrac{3p^3}{p^3+q}-2=\dfrac{p^3-2q}{p^3+q}\). Product \(=1\).
Equation: \((p^3+q)x^2-(p^3-2q)x+(p^3+q)=0\). Answer (B).

wrong_options.A: Sign slip: the sum is \(\frac{p^3-2q}{p^3+q}\), not \(\frac{p^3+2q}{p^3+q}\).
wrong_options.C: This uses \(P=\frac{p^3-q}{3p}\), which comes from a sign error in \(s^3=-p^3\).

solutions.focus_note: With \(s=-p\), \(s^3=-p^3\). Most wrong options in this question come from losing that minus sign.

solutions.key_idea: Common root: subtract to get the root linearly in \(b\), then substitute back.
hints: Subtract the equations to find the common root: \((b-1)x-(1+b)=0\).
solutions.full_html:
\(x=\dfrac{b+1}{b-1}\). Substituting: \((b+1)^2+(b+1)(b-1)+b(b-1)^2=0\), so \(b^3+3b=0\).
\(b=0\) or \(b=\pm i\sqrt3\). Among the options: \(-i\sqrt3\). Answer (B).
solutions.focus_note: Don't assume \(b\) is real. 'A value of \(b\)' with complex options means you must solve completely.

solutions.key_idea: Logarithms turn both equations into linear equations in \(\ln x,\ln y\).
hints: Take logs. Let \(u=\ln x,\ v=\ln y\), \(a=\ln2,\ b=\ln3\).
solutions.full_html:
\(a(a+u)=b(b+v)\) and \(v=\frac{b}{a}u\). Multiplying the first by \(a\): \(a^3+a^2u=ab^2+b^2u\), so \(u(a^2-b^2)=-a(a^2-b^2)\).
Since \(a\ne b\), \(u=-a=-\ln2\), so \(x_0=\frac12\). Answer (C).
solutions.focus_note: Exponents like \(\ln2\) and \(\ln3\) are a strong hint to take natural logs.

solutions.key_idea: Sequences \(\alpha^n\pm\beta^n\) obey the recurrence given by the quadratic.

wrong_options.A: The recurrence gives exactly \(6a_9\) on top.

solutions.focus_note: \(a_n-pa_{n-1}-qa_{n-2}=0\) for roots of \(x^2-px-q\). Recognise it at once.

solutions.key_idea: Find one closed form, then convert each option with the change-of-base rule.
hints: Rewrite each option in natural logs and compare.

wrong_options.D: This would solve \(9^{x}=\dots\) with the bases swapped. It equals \(\frac{\ln9}{\ln9-\ln2}\).

solutions.focus_note: Express everything in \(\ln\) to compare options with different bases.

solutions.key_idea: Real or purely imaginary \(x\) both make \(x^2\) real, but here \(x^2\) must be non-real.
hints: Purely imaginary roots \(\pm ik\) mean \(p(x)=a(x^2+c)\) with \(c>0\).
\(p(p(x))=0\) means \(p(x)=\pm i\sqrt c\), i.e. \(x^2=-c\pm\dfrac{i\sqrt c}a\). Can \(x\) be real or purely imaginary?
solutions.full_html:
\(p(x)=a(x^2+c)\) with \(a\ne0\) and \(c>0\). The roots of \(p\) are \(\pm i\sqrt c\).
\(p(p(x))=0\) means \(a(x^2+c)=\pm i\sqrt c\), so \(x^2=-c\pm\frac{i\sqrt c}{a}\), which is non-real.
If \(x\) were real or purely imaginary, \(x^2\) would be real. So none of the 4 roots is real or purely imaginary. Answer (D).

wrong_options.A: Purely imaginary \(x\) has \(x^2\le0\) real, but the required \(x^2\) is non-real.
wrong_options.C: Neither type is possible, for the same reason.

solutions.focus_note: Test 'real / purely imaginary' through \(x^2\): it must be \(\ge0\) or \(\le0\) respectively, and in both cases it is real.

solutions.key_idea: Use the gap between the roots, \(\frac{\sqrt D}{|a|}\), together with \(D>0\).
solutions.full_html:
\(D>0\): \(|\alpha|<\frac12\). Gap condition: \(1-4\alpha^2<\alpha^2\), so \(\alpha^2>\frac15\).
So \(S=\left(-\frac12,-\frac1{\sqrt5}\right)\cup\left(\frac1{\sqrt5},\frac12\right)\). Answer: (A), (D).

wrong_options.B: For small \(|\alpha|\), the roots are far apart (the gap \(\to\infty\)).
wrong_options.C: Same as (B): \(|\alpha|<\frac1{\sqrt5}\) makes the gap greater than 1.

solutions.focus_note: \(|x_1-x_2|=\sqrt D/|a|\). Use it directly instead of computing the roots.

solutions.key_idea: Write the roots explicitly, paying attention to the sign of \(\tan\theta\), then pick the larger and smaller roots.
hints: In this range, \(\sec\theta>0\) and \(\tan\theta<0\). Solve each quadratic with the formula.
solutions.full_html:
Equation 1: \(x=\sec\theta\pm\sqrt{\sec^2\theta-1}=\sec\theta\pm|\tan\theta|\). The larger root is \(\alpha_1=\sec\theta-\tan\theta\) (because \(\tan\theta<0\)).
Equation 2: \(x=-\tan\theta\pm\sec\theta\). The smaller root is \(\beta_2=-\tan\theta-\sec\theta\).
\(\alpha_1+\beta_2=-2\tan\theta\). Answer (C).

wrong_options.A: This adds the two larger roots.
wrong_options.B: \(2\sec\theta\) is \(\alpha_1+\beta_1\), the sum of the roots of the first equation.
wrong_options.D: 0 needs \(\beta_2=-\alpha_1\). That happens if you take \(\sqrt{\tan^2\theta}=\tan\theta\) and ignore its sign.

solutions.focus_note: \(\sqrt{t^2}=|t|\). Whenever an interval is given, check the sign before taking a square root.

solutions.key_idea: Factor into symmetric functions of each pair and use Vieta's formulas.

wrong_options.A: There is no symmetry that cancels the two groups.
wrong_options.B: Half the true value. Check both groups.
wrong_options.C: \(8080=4\cdot2020\). This is a guess that ignores the \(c^2+d^2\) group. Work out both groups.

solutions.focus_note: Mixed sums over two root pairs separate into a product of single-pair symmetric sums.

solutions.key_idea: Remove the modulus by cases, then check each root against its case.
hints: In each case, solve the quadratic and keep only the roots in the right range.
solutions.full_html:
\(|x|\ge1\): \(3x^2-4x^2+4+x-1=0\), so \(x^2-x-3=0\) and \(x=\frac{1\pm\sqrt{13}}2\approx2.30,\,-1.30\). Both are valid.
\(|x|<1\): \(7x^2+x-5=0\), so \(x=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{141}}{14}\approx0.78,\,-0.92\). Both are valid.
Total: 4 real roots. Answer: 4.
solutions.focus_note: Always check each case's roots against that case's condition before counting.

solutions.key_idea: Take logs to get a biquadratic in \(t\). Its roots come in pairs \(\pm t\), so they sum to 0.
hints: You get \(16t^4-68t^2+16=0\). The product of the \(x\)'s is \(5^{\sum t}\).
solutions.full_html:
\(t(16t^3-68t)=-16\), so \(4t^4-17t^2+4=0\), \(t^2=4\) or \(\frac14\), and \(t=\pm2,\pm\frac12\).
Each \(t\) gives a positive \(x=5^t\). The product is \(5^{2-2+\frac12-\frac12}=5^0=1\). Answer: 1.
solutions.focus_note: Product of \(x\)'s = base\(^{\text{sum of logs}}\). A biquadratic in \(t\) has roots summing to 0.

solutions.key_idea: Positive definite quadratic form: \(a>0\) and \(ac>b^2\). Both systems then have non-zero determinants.
hints: For (C) and (D), check the determinant of each system's coefficient matrix.
solutions.full_html:
\(S=\{a>0,\ ac-b^2>0\}\).
(A) \(2\cdot6-\frac{49}4=-\frac14<0\). Not in \(S\). False.
(B) \(3\cdot\frac1{12}-b^2>0\), so \(b^2<\frac14\) and \(|2b|<1\). True.
(C) The determinant is \(ac-b^2>0\), so the solution is unique. True.
(D) The determinant is \((a+1)(c+1)-b^2=(ac-b^2)+a+c+1>0\), since \(c>0\) too. True.
Answer: (B), (C), (D).

wrong_options.A: \(b^2=\frac{49}4>ac=12\), so the form takes negative values.

solutions.focus_note: \(ax^2+2bxy+cy^2\) is the discriminant test in disguise: divide by \(y^2\) and require \(at^2+2bt+c>0\) for all \(t\).

solutions.key_idea: Reduce powers of \(\omega\) mod 3, keeping track of the sign. For (S), transform the equation instead of finding the roots.
hints: For (S), let \(y=\frac1{x+1}\). It satisfies a new quadratic, so use \(\sum y^3=s^3-3Ps\).
solutions.full_html:
(P) \((1+\omega)^{2026}=\omega^{4052}=\omega^2\), reciprocal \(\omega\). \((1+\omega^2)^{2026}=\omega^{2026}=\omega\), reciprocal \(\omega^2\). Roots \(\omega,\omega^2\): \(x^2+x+1=0\) → (1).
(Q) Odd power: \((-\omega^2)^{2027}=-\omega\), reciprocal \(-\omega^2\). Similarly the other gives \(-\omega\). Roots \(-\omega,-\omega^2\): sum 1, product 1, so \(x^2-x+1=0\) → (2).
(R) \(\gamma=-\omega\), so \(\gamma-1=\omega^2\) and \((\omega^2)^{2026}=\omega^2\), reciprocal \(\omega\). Likewise \(\delta\) gives \(\omega^2\). Sum \(=-1\) → (4).
(S) With \(x=\frac1y-1\): \((1-y)^2+y(1-y)-y^2=0\), so \(y^2+y-1=0\). \(\sum y^3=(-1)^3-3(-1)(-1)=-4\) → (5).
Answer (C).

wrong_options.A: (R) is \(-1\) and (S) is \(-4\). This option swaps them.
wrong_options.D: Both the equations and the values are mismatched.

solutions.focus_note: The parity of the exponent decides the sign: \((-\omega^2)^{n}=(-1)^n\omega^{2n}\).

solutions.key_idea: Turn the AP condition into a factorisation in the roots. Only \(\{m,n\}=\{3,5\}\) works.
hints: All coefficients are positive, so integer roots are \(-m,-n\) with \(m,n\ge1\): \(m+n=\frac ba\), \(mn=\frac ca\).
solutions.full_html:
\(2(m+n)=1+mn\) ⇒ \((m-2)(n-2)=3\). With \(m,n\ge1\): \(\{m,n\}=\{3,5\}\) (the pair \((1,-1)\) fails). Roots \(-3,-5\); \(b=8a,\ c=15a\).
(A) \(c-b=7a\). True. (B) \(-3,-5\) are odd. True.
(C) \(c=15\) ⇒ \(a=1,b=8\), so \(ab=8\). True. (D) The roots are negative; 3 is not a root. False.
Answer: (A), (B), (C).
solutions.focus_note: Integer roots plus a linear condition: rewrite it as \((m-k)(n-k)=\text{constant}\) (Simon's factoring trick).

solutions.key_idea: Angle-bisector theorem for Statement-1. Statement-2 is false in general.
hints: \(P=(-2,-2)\), \(Q=(1,-2)\), and the lines meet at \(O\). The bisector from \(O\) divides \(PQ\) in the ratio \(OP:OQ\).
\(OP=2\sqrt2\), \(OQ=\sqrt5\). Is Statement-2 true for a general triangle?
solutions.full_html:
\(PR:RQ=OP:OQ=2\sqrt2:\sqrt5\). The angle \(POQ\) is acute (\(\vec{OP}\cdot\vec{OQ}=-2+4>0\)), so the acute bisector is the one inside the triangle. Statement-1 is true.
Statement-2: the two triangles formed by a bisector are generally not similar (their angles differ). False. Answer (C).
solutions.focus_note: The angle-bisector theorem follows from equal heights, not from similarity.

solutions.key_idea: Equal areas \(OPR=PQR=OQR\) characterise the centroid.
hints: The point that splits a triangle into three equal areas is a famous centre.
solutions.full_html: \(R=\left(\frac{0+3+6}3,\frac{0+4+0}3\right)=\left(3,\frac43\right)\). Answer (C).

wrong_options.D: Not the average of the vertices.

solutions.focus_note: Each medial triangle has area \(\frac13\) of the whole exactly at the centroid.

solutions.key_idea: The product is zero when either factor is. Classify each factor.
hints: \(ax^2+by^2+c=0\) with \(a=b\) and \(c\) of opposite sign is a real circle.
solutions.full_html: The second factor gives the lines \(x=2y\) and \(x=3y\). With \(a=b\), \(ac<0\): \(x^2+y^2=-\frac ca>0\), a circle. Answer (B).

wrong_options.A: With \(c=0\) and \(a,b\) the same sign, \(ax^2+by^2=0\) is only the origin.
wrong_options.C: Same signs give an ellipse, not a hyperbola.
wrong_options.D: The second factor gives lines, not a circle.

solutions.focus_note: A homogeneous quadratic in \(x,y\) factors into lines through the origin.

solutions.key_idea: Check the area of \(PQR\). It is non-zero in general.
hints: Test collinearity with the cross product \((Q-P)\times(R-P)\).
solutions.full_html: With \(\alpha=0.3,\ \beta=0.5,\ \theta=0.2\): \((Q-P)\times(R-P)\approx-0.137\ne0\). So the points are not collinear in general, and (A), (B), (C) all fail. Answer (D).

wrong_options.A: Not collinear, so no point lies on a segment through the others.

solutions.focus_note: For 'which lies between' questions, test collinearity first.

solutions.key_idea: Three lines fail to form a triangle iff two are parallel or all three are concurrent.
hints: \(L_1\cap L_3=(2,1)\). Concurrency needs \(L_2\) to pass through it.
\(L_2\) has slope \(\frac3k\). It is parallel to \(L_1\) (slope \(-\frac13\)) or \(L_3\) (slope \(-\frac52\)) for special \(k\).
solutions.focus_note: No triangle ⇔ parallel pair or concurrency. Check both.

solutions.key_idea: Compute the orthocentre explicitly. It always lies on \(x+y=0\).
hints: The first two lines meet the \(x\)-axis at \((-p,0)\) and \((-q,0)\). Find their intersection point.
The altitude from that vertex is vertical. Intersect it with the altitude from \((-p,0)\).
solutions.full_html:
The lines meet at \((pq,\ (1+p)(1+q))\). The altitude from this vertex is \(x=pq\).
The altitude from \((-p,0)\) is perpendicular to the second line (slope \(\frac{1+q}q\)): \(y=-\frac q{1+q}(x+p)\). At \(x=pq\): \(y=-\frac{q\cdot p(1+q)}{1+q}=-pq\).
Orthocentre \((pq,-pq)\): the line \(x+y=0\). Answer (D).
solutions.focus_note: With the base on the \(x\)-axis, one altitude is vertical, which makes the orthocentre quick to find.

solutions.key_idea: Two candidate directions. The 'meets the \(x\)-axis' condition rules one out.
hints: \(\sqrt3x+y=1\) makes an angle of \(120^\circ\) with the \(x\)-axis. Lines at \(60^\circ\) to it are at \(60^\circ\) or \(180^\circ\).
A horizontal line through \((3,-2)\) never meets the \(x\)-axis.
solutions.full_html:
The slope is \(\tan60^\circ=\sqrt3\) (the other choice, slope 0, is \(y=-2\), parallel to the \(x\)-axis).
\(y+2=\sqrt3(x-3)\), i.e. \(y-\sqrt3x+2+3\sqrt3=0\). Answer (B).

wrong_options.A: Slope \(-\sqrt3\) is parallel to the given line.
wrong_options.C: Slope \(\frac1{\sqrt3}\) makes \(90^\circ\) with the given line.

solutions.focus_note: 'Inclined at \(\theta\) to a line' gives two directions. Read the extra condition.

solutions.key_idea: Symmetry puts the intersection on \(y=x\), which reduces the condition to one inequality.
hints: The lines are reflections of each other in \(y=x\), so they meet on \(y=x\): \(x=y=-\frac c{a+b}\).
solutions.full_html:
\(1+\frac c{a+b}<2\Rightarrow c<a+b\): (A) ✓. Also \(a>b\) gives \(a-b+c>0\): (C) ✓.
Answer: (A), (C).
solutions.focus_note: Swapping the coefficients of \(x\) and \(y\) reflects a line in \(y=x\).

solutions.key_idea: The region is between two squares \(\max(x,y)=\text{const}\).
solutions.full_html:
\(2\le\sqrt2\max(x,y)\le4\iff\sqrt2\le\max(x,y)\le2\sqrt2\).
Area \(=(2\sqrt2)^2-(\sqrt2)^2=8-2=6\). Answer: 6.
solutions.focus_note: \(|a-b|+|a+b|=2\max(|a|,|b|)\). Level sets of \(\max\) are squares.

solutions.key_idea: Sign charts: write both \(f(x)\) and \(f(x)-1\) as products of linear factors and read their signs on each interval.
hints: Factorise: \(f(x)=\dfrac{(x-1)(x-5)}{(x-2)(x-3)}\). The sign of \(f\) is decided by four linear factors.
For the comparison with 1, simplify \(f(x)-1\) into a single fraction first.
solutions.focus_note: In matrix-match, one row usually has several answers. (p) automatically implies (r) and (s), so tick all three whenever (p) holds.

solutions.key_idea: Four independent mini-problems: AM–GM after substitution, transpose rules for symmetric/skew matrices, log simplification, and general solutions of a trig equation.
hints: (A) Put \(t=x+2\). (B) Expand the given commutation condition. (C) Simplify \(3^{-a}\) first.
solutions.full_html:
(A) With \(t=x+2\): \(\dfrac{x^2+2x+4}{x+2}=\dfrac{t^2-2t+4}{t}=t+\dfrac4t-2\). For \(t>0\) this is \(\ge 4-2=2\) (equality at \(t=2\)), the local minimum value. Answer (r).
(B) \((A+B)(A-B)=(A-B)(A+B)\) gives \(-AB+BA=AB-BA\), i.e. \(AB=BA\). Then \((AB)^t=B^tA^t=(-B)A=-BA=-AB\), so \((-1)^k=-1\): \(k\) odd, giving 1 and 3. Answer (q), (s).
(C) \(3^{-a}=\dfrac{1}{\log_32}=\log_23\approx1.585\). The condition \(1<2^{-k+\log_23}<2\) means \(0<\log_23-k<1\), so \(0.585<k<1.585\), i.e. \(k=1\). Then \(k\) is less than 2 and less than 3: (r), (s).
(D) \(\sin\theta=\sin\left(\frac\pi2-\varphi\right)\) gives \(\theta=2n\pi+\frac\pi2-\varphi\) or \(\theta=2n\pi+\frac\pi2+\varphi\). So \(\theta+\varphi-\frac\pi2=2n\pi\) or \(\theta-\varphi-\frac\pi2=2n\pi\), and \(\frac1\pi\left(\theta\pm\varphi-\frac\pi2\right)\) is an even integer: 0, 2 from the list. Answer (p), (r).
solutions.focus_note: In (A) the function has no global minimum (it goes to \(-\infty\) for \(x<-2\)); the intended answer is the local minimum on \(x>-2\). Read 'minimum value' in such old questions as the local minimum.

solutions.key_idea: Use \(\tan^{-1}(e^{-u})=\frac\pi2-\tan^{-1}(e^u)\) to test parity, and the sign of \(g'\) for monotonicity.
solutions.full_html:
\(g(-u)=2\tan^{-1}(e^{-u})-\frac\pi2=2\left(\frac\pi2-\tan^{-1}e^u\right)-\frac\pi2=\frac\pi2-2\tan^{-1}e^u=-g(u)\), so \(g\) is odd.
\(g'(u)=\dfrac{2e^u}{1+e^{2u}}>0\) for every \(u\), so \(g\) is strictly increasing on \((-\infty,\infty)\). Answer (C).

wrong_options.B: \(g'>0\) everywhere, so it increases, not decreases.

solutions.focus_note: The identity \(\tan^{-1}x+\tan^{-1}\frac1x=\frac\pi2\) (for \(x>0\)) is the standard tool for parity checks with inverse tangents.

solutions.key_idea: Intermediate value theorem + monotonicity, determinant = 0 for a homogeneous system, piecewise-linear evaluation, and a first-order ODE.
hints: (A) Check signs at the ends and monotonicity. (B) Three planes through the origin meet in a line exactly when the coefficient determinant is 0 (rank 2).
(C) The sum of distances is a piecewise-linear function; list its values at integers. (D) Solve the linear ODE.
solutions.full_html:
(A) \(h(x)=xe^{\sin x}-\cos x\): \(h(0)=-1<0\), \(h\left(\frac\pi2\right)=\frac\pi2e>0\), and \(h'(x)=e^{\sin x}(1+x\cos x)+\sin x>0\) on \(\left(0,\frac\pi2\right)\). Exactly one root: (p).
(B) \(\begin{vmatrix}k&4&1\\4&k&2\\2&2&1\end{vmatrix}=k(k-4)-4(4-4)+(8-2k)=k^2-6k+8=(k-2)(k-4)\). For \(k=2\) and \(k=4\) the rank is 2 (the planes are distinct), so they meet in a line: (q), (s).
(C) \(S(x)=|x-1|+|x-2|+|x+1|+|x+2|\) equals 6 for \(x\in\{-1,0,1\}\) and \(4|x|\) for integers \(|x|\ge2\): values 6, 8, 12, 16, 20, … So \(4k\in\{6,8,12,16,20,\dots\}\) gives \(k=\frac32,2,3,4,5,\dots\). From the list: (q), (r), (s), (t).
(D) \(\dfrac{dy}{y+1}=dx\Rightarrow y+1=Ce^x\); \(y(0)=1\Rightarrow C=2\). \(y(\ln2)=2\cdot2-1=3\): (r).
solutions.focus_note: For (B), remember: a homogeneous system has a line of solutions when the determinant is 0 and the rank is exactly 2. Always check the rank is not 1 (coincident planes).

solutions.key_idea: Invertibility needs a bijection onto the stated codomain. \(f\) is decreasing from \(b\) to \(-1\), so its range \((-1,b)\) is not \(\mathbb R\).
hints: Find the range of \(f\) on \((0,1)\): compute \(f(0^+)\) and \(f(1^-)\) and check monotonicity.
The codomain is \(\mathbb R\). Is \(f:(0,1)\to\mathbb R\) onto?
solutions.full_html:
\(f'(x)=\dfrac{-(1-bx)+b(b-x)}{(1-bx)^2}=\dfrac{b^2-1}{(1-bx)^2}<0\), so \(f\) is strictly decreasing on \((0,1)\), from \(f(0^+)=b\) to \(f(1^-)=\dfrac{b-1}{1-b}=-1\).
Range \(=(-1,b)\ne\mathbb R\), so \(f:(0,1)\to\mathbb R\) is one-one but not onto, hence not invertible. Answer (A).

wrong_options.B: \(f\) is not invertible as a map \((0,1)\to\mathbb R\), so \(f^{-1}\) on \((0,1)\) is not defined.
wrong_options.C: Algebraically \(f(f(x))=x\) and \(f'(b)=\frac1{f'(0)}\) hold, but \(f\) maps \((0,1)\) onto \((-1,b)\), not onto \((0,1)\), so '\(f=f^{-1}\) on \((0,1)\)' is not meaningful. This is the trap option.
wrong_options.D: \(f^{-1}\) would only be defined on the range \((-1,b)\), which does not contain all of \((0,1)\).

solutions.focus_note: Always check the codomain in 'invertible' questions. One-one alone is not enough; the function must be onto the stated codomain.

solutions.key_idea: Reduce the composite equation to \(s^2=s\) and use the bound \(|\sin x^2|\le1<\frac\pi2\).
hints: Write both sides in terms of \(s=\sin(\sin x^2)\).
The equation becomes \(s^2=s\). Can \(\sin(\sin x^2)\) ever be 1?
solutions.full_html:
\((g\circ g\circ f)(x)=\sin(\sin x^2)=s\) and \((f\circ g\circ g\circ f)(x)=s^2\). So \(s^2=s\Rightarrow s=0\) or \(s=1\).
Since \(|\sin x^2|\le1<\frac\pi2\), \(\sin(\sin x^2)=1\) is impossible. And \(\sin(\sin x^2)=0\) needs \(\sin x^2=0\) (because \(|\sin x^2|<\pi\)), i.e. \(x^2=n\pi\), \(n=0,1,2,\dots\)
So \(x=\pm\sqrt{n\pi}\), \(n\in\{0,1,2,\dots\}\). Answer (A).

wrong_options.B: Misses \(n=0\): \(x=0\) does satisfy the equation (both sides are 0).
wrong_options.C: These come from solving \(\sin x=1\), not from the composite equation.
wrong_options.D: These are zeros of \(\sin x\), not of \(\sin x^2\).

solutions.focus_note: Read the order of composition carefully: \(f\circ g\circ g\circ f\) means apply \(f\) first, then \(g\), \(g\), \(f\).

solutions.key_idea: Each row is a range/domain computation: polar form of a unit complex number, the \(\sin^{-1}\) domain condition, a determinant identity, and the sign of a derivative.
hints: (A) Put \(z=e^{i\theta}\) and simplify \(1-z^2\) by dividing numerator and denominator by \(z\).
(B) Put \(u=3^{x-1}>0\) and impose \(-1\le\frac{8u/3}{1-u^2}\le1\). (C) Expand the determinant. (D) Differentiate.
solutions.full_html:
(A) \(z=e^{i\theta}\): \(\dfrac{2iz}{1-z^2}=\dfrac{2i}{\bar z-z}=\dfrac{2i}{-2i\sin\theta}=-\dfrac1{\sin\theta}\), real with \(|{\cdot}|\ge1\). Set \(=(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)\): (s).
(B) With \(u=3^{x-1}\), the argument is \(\dfrac{8u}{3(1-u^2)}\). For \(0<u<1\): \(8u\le3-3u^2\iff(3u-1)(u+3)\le0\iff u\le\frac13\iff x\le0\). For \(u>1\): \(8u\le3u^2-3\iff(3u+1)(u-3)\ge0\iff u\ge3\iff x\ge2\). Domain \((-\infty,0]\cup[2,\infty)\): (t).
(C) Expanding along row 1: \(1(1+\tan^2\theta)-\tan\theta(-\tan\theta+\tan\theta)+1(\tan^2\theta+1)=2\sec^2\theta\). For \(0\le\theta<\frac\pi2\) this takes every value in \([2,\infty)\): (r).
(D) \(f'(x)=\frac{15}2x^{3/2}-15x^{1/2}=\frac{15}2\sqrt x\,(x-2)\ge0\) for \(x\ge2\). Increasing on \([2,\infty)\): (r).
solutions.focus_note: In (B) treat the two cases \(u<1\) and \(u>1\) separately; the sign of \(1-u^2\) flips the inequality.

solutions.key_idea: A function that rises then falls on the interval is not one-one; check the extreme values to decide onto.
hints: Factorise \(f'(x)\) and find where \(f\) increases and decreases on \([0,3]\).
Compare the range with the codomain \([1,29]\).
solutions.full_html:
\(f'(x)=6x^2-30x+36=6(x-2)(x-3)\): increasing on \([0,2]\), decreasing on \([2,3]\).
\(f(0)=1\), \(f(2)=29\), \(f(3)=28\). Range \(=[1,29]\), equal to the codomain, so \(f\) is onto. Values in \([28,29)\) are taken twice (once on each side of \(x=2\)), so \(f\) is not one-one. Answer (B).

wrong_options.A: Not one-one: e.g. \(f(3)=28\) and some \(x\in(1,2)\) also gives 28.
wrong_options.C: The range covers \([1,29]\) fully, so it is onto.

solutions.focus_note: Onto depends on the codomain: compute the minimum and maximum on the closed interval, including endpoints.

solutions.key_idea: \(u(x)=\log(\sec x+\tan x)\) is odd, strictly increasing (derivative \(\sec x>0\)) and runs from \(-\infty\) to \(\infty\); cubing keeps all three properties.
hints: Let \(u(x)=\log(\sec x+\tan x)\). Note \((\sec x+\tan x)(\sec x-\tan x)=1\).
\(u'(x)=\sec x\). What are the limits of \(u\) at \(\pm\frac\pi2\)?
solutions.full_html:
\(u(-x)=\log(\sec x-\tan x)=\log\dfrac1{\sec x+\tan x}=-u(x)\), so \(u\) and \(f=u^3\) are odd: (A).
\(u'(x)=\sec x>0\) on \(\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)\), so \(u\), and hence \(f\), is strictly increasing: one-one (B).
As \(x\to\frac\pi2^-\), \(\sec x+\tan x\to\infty\), so \(u\to\infty\); as \(x\to-\frac\pi2^+\), \(u\to-\infty\). By continuity \(f\) takes every real value: onto (C).

wrong_options.D: A non-zero odd function cannot be even.

solutions.focus_note: Remember \(\frac{d}{dx}\log(\sec x+\tan x)=\sec x\). It turns many 'one-one' checks into one line.

solutions.key_idea: Build each function piecewise, then test continuity/differentiability at \(x=0\) and look for two inputs with the same output.
hints: Write \(f_4\) and \(f_2\circ f_1\) explicitly on \(x<0\) and \(x\ge0\).
Check continuity at 0 by comparing one-sided limits, and one-one by looking for repeated values.
solutions.full_html:
\(f_2\circ f_1(x)=x^2\) for \(x<0\) and \(e^{2x}\) for \(x\ge0\); \(f_4(x)=x^2\) for \(x<0\) and \(e^{2x}-1\) for \(x\ge0\).
P: \(f_4\) takes values \((0,\infty)\) on \(x<0\) and \([0,\infty)\) on \(x\ge0\): onto \([0,\infty)\), but e.g. \(f_4(-1)=1=f_4\left(\frac{\ln2}2\right)\): not one-one. (1)
Q: \(f_3\): left derivative at 0 is \(\cos0=1\), right derivative 1, so differentiable; \(\sin x\) repeats on \(x<0\), so not one-one. (3)
R: \(f_2\circ f_1(0^-)=0\ne1=f_2\circ f_1(0)\): not continuous; \(x^2\) on \(x<0\) repeats values of \(e^{2x}\), so not one-one. (2)
S: \(f_2(x)=x^2\) on \([0,\infty)\) is continuous and one-one. (4)
Code P–1, Q–3, R–2, S–4: answer (D).

wrong_options.A: P→3 is wrong: \(f_4\) has left derivative 0 and right derivative 2 at \(x=0\), so it is not differentiable. S→2 is also wrong: \(f_2\) is continuous.
wrong_options.B: R→4 is wrong: \(f_2\circ f_1\) is discontinuous at 0 (it jumps from 0 to 1).
wrong_options.C: P→3 is wrong (\(f_4\) is not differentiable at 0), and Q→1 is wrong: \(f_3\) has range \((-1,\infty)\), so it is not onto \(\mathbb R\).

solutions.focus_note: For piecewise functions, always test the joining point first: one-sided limits for continuity, one-sided derivatives for differentiability.

solutions.key_idea: Nested ranges: track the interval at every layer. Near 0 every sine behaves like its argument.
hints: Work from the inside out: what interval does \(\frac\pi2\sin x\) lie in, then \(\sin(\cdot)\) of it, and so on?
For (C) use \(\sin t\approx t\) near 0. For (D) find the largest possible value of \(g(f(x))\).
solutions.full_html:
(A) \(\frac\pi2\sin x\in\left[-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right]\), so \(\sin\left(\frac\pi2\sin x\right)\in[-1,1]\) (all of it), so \(\frac\pi6\sin(\cdot)\in\left[-\frac\pi6,\frac\pi6\right]\) and \(f\in\left[-\frac12,\frac12\right]\). True.
(B) \(f\circ g(x)=f(t)\) with \(t=\frac\pi2\sin x\in\left[-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right]\). \(f(t)\) depends on \(\sin t\), and \(\sin t\) still covers \([-1,1]\), so the range is again \(\left[-\frac12,\frac12\right]\). True.
(C) Near 0: \(f(x)\approx\frac\pi6\cdot\frac\pi2x\) and \(g(x)\approx\frac\pi2x\), so \(\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}\to\frac\pi6\). True.
(D) \(g(f(x))=\frac\pi2\sin(f(x))\le\frac\pi2\sin\frac12\approx0.75<1\). Never 1. False.
Answer (A), (B), (C).
solutions.focus_note: For composite ranges, write the interval after each layer; the sine of an interval containing \(\left[-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right]\) is all of \([-1,1]\).

solutions.key_idea: Rewrite each factor as \(a^{\log_a b}\): \(x^{1/\log_2x}=2\) and \(7^{\log_74}=4\).
hints: Let \(L=\log_29\). Write \((L^2)^{1/\log_2L}\) as a power of 2.
For the second factor use \(a^{\log_ab}=b\) with \(\frac1{\log_47}=\log_74\).
solutions.focus_note: The identity \(x^{1/\log_b x}=b\) (for \(x>0,x\ne1\)) appears often; spot it by the exponent \(\frac1{\log}\).

solutions.key_idea: Onto functions from a 7-set to a 5-set \(=5!\times\)(number of ways to split 7 elements into 5 non-empty groups).
hints: \(\alpha={}^7P_5\). For \(\beta\), partition the 7 elements of \(Y\) into 5 non-empty blocks, then assign the blocks to \(X\).
Partition types of 7 into 5 parts: \(3+1+1+1+1\) and \(2+2+1+1+1\).
solutions.full_html:
\(\alpha=7\cdot6\cdot5\cdot4\cdot3=2520\).
Splitting 7 elements into 5 non-empty groups: type \(3,1,1,1,1\): \(\binom73=35\); type \(2,2,1,1,1\): \(\frac{\binom72\binom52}{2!}=105\). Total 140.
\(\beta=5!\times140=16800\). So \(\frac1{5!}(\beta-\alpha)=140-21=119\).
solutions.focus_note: Onto counting: either partition-and-assign or inclusion–exclusion. Partitioning is faster when the numbers are small.

solutions.key_idea: Follow the inner quantity \(t=\frac{x}{x-1}\): on \(E_1\) it covers \((0,\infty)\setminus\{1\}\). Ranges and domains then follow from \(\log\) and \(\sin^{-1}\).
hints: Solve \(\frac{x}{x-1}>0\) for \(E_1\), and track which values \(\frac{x}{x-1}\) can take there.
solutions.full_html:
\(E_1=(-\infty,0)\cup(1,\infty)\). There \(t=\frac{x}{x-1}\) takes all values in \((0,1)\) (for \(x<0\)) and \((1,\infty)\) (for \(x>1\)).
P: range of \(f=\log t\) is \((-\infty,0)\cup(0,\infty)\): (4).
Q: \(\log t\) covers \([-1,1]\setminus\{0\}\) on \(E_2\), so \(g\) covers \(\left[-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right]\setminus\{0\}\), which contains \((0,1)\): (2).
S: \(\frac1e\le t\le e\). For \(x<0\): \(t=\frac{|x|}{|x|+1}\ge\frac1e\iff x\le\frac1{1-e}\). For \(x>1\): \(t\le e\iff x\ge\frac e{e-1}\). Domain of \(g\) \(=\left(-\infty,\frac1{1-e}\right]\cup\left[\frac e{e-1},\infty\right)\): (1).
R: this set lies inside \(E_1\) (since \(\frac1{1-e}<0\) and \(\frac e{e-1}>1\)), so the domain of \(f\) contains it: (1).
Answer (A).

wrong_options.B: P→3 is wrong: \(\log t\) is unbounded, not confined to \(\left[-\frac12,\frac12\right]\).
wrong_options.C: S→6 is wrong: the domain of \(g\) is exactly the set in (1).
wrong_options.D: Q→3 is wrong: 0 is not in the range of \(g\), so it cannot contain \(\left[-\frac12,\frac12\right]\).

solutions.focus_note: Note 0 is missing from the range of \(f\) because \(t=1\) is never attained. Excluded points like this decide matching options.

solutions.key_idea: Symmetry \(f(x)+f(1-x)=1\) turns the sum into a count of pairs.
solutions.full_html:
\(f(1-x)=\dfrac{4^{1-x}}{4^{1-x}+2}=\dfrac{4}{4+2\cdot4^x}=\dfrac{2}{4^x+2}\), so \(f(x)+f(1-x)=1\).
Among \(k=1,\dots,39\), the pairs \((k,40-k)\) for \(k=1,\dots,19\) give 19, and the middle term \(k=20\) is \(f\left(\frac12\right)\), which is subtracted.
Value \(=19\).
solutions.focus_note: Whenever a sum runs symmetrically over \(\frac k n\), test \(f(x)+f(1-x)\) first.

solutions.key_idea: \(f\) is odd, and strictly increasing on \((0,\infty)\) with \(f\to\infty\); oddness transfers both properties to the whole line.
hints: For \(x>0\), check the sign of \(f'(x)\) using \(x>\sin x\) and \(\cos x\le1\).
solutions.full_html:
\(|x|\) is even and \(x-\sin x\) is odd, so \(f\) is odd.
For \(x>0\): \(f(x)=x^2-x\sin x\), \(f'(x)=2x-\sin x-x\cos x=x(1-\cos x)+(x-\sin x)>0\). So \(f\) is strictly increasing on \([0,\infty)\) with \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(x)\to\infty\).
By oddness \(f\) is strictly increasing on \(\mathbb R\) with range \(\mathbb R\): one-one and onto. Answer (C).

wrong_options.A: \(f(x)\ge x^2-x\to\infty\), so every real value is reached: onto.

solutions.focus_note: For odd functions, studying \(x>0\) is enough: monotone on \((0,\infty)\) plus oddness gives monotone on \(\mathbb R\).

solutions.key_idea: \(S\) has three interval pieces and \(T\) is finite: continuity forces constancy on each piece.
hints: A continuous function on an interval into a finite set must be constant on that interval.
A strictly increasing function on an infinite set takes infinitely many distinct values.
solutions.full_html:
(A) \(S\) is infinite, so there are infinitely many functions \(S\to T\) (e.g. change the value at one point). True.
(B) A strictly increasing function is one-one, so on the infinite set \(S\) it would need infinitely many values, but \(T\) has 4. None exist. False.
(C) A continuous function is constant on each of the three intervals (intermediate value property in a finite set), so there are \(4^3=64\le120\) of them. True.
(D) Such a function is locally constant, so its derivative exists and equals 0 everywhere on \(S\). True.
Answer (A), (C), (D).

wrong_options.B: Strict increase means one-one; an infinite set cannot map one-one into a 4-element set.

solutions.focus_note: 'Continuous into a finite set' is a classic signal: the function is constant on each connected piece.

solutions.key_idea: \(Y\) is empty because no column has 6 allowed entries; \(Z\) is a product of choices per element.
hints: For \(Y\): fix the single range element \(b\); how many \(a\) satisfy \(|a-b|\ge2\)? Can it be 6?
For \(Z\): a function uses exactly one pair for each \(a\in S\); count choices for each \(a\).
solutions.full_html:
\(n(Y)\): for \(b=1,\dots,6\) the number of \(a\) with \(|a-b|\ge2\) is \(4,3,3,3,3,4\). A relation in \(Y\) needs 6 pairs with the same \(b\), impossible. \(n(Y)=0\).
\(n(Z)\): a function from \(S\) has exactly 6 pairs \((a,f(a))\), one per \(a\), with \(|a-f(a)|\ge2\). Choices: \(4\cdot3\cdot3\cdot3\cdot3\cdot4=1296\).
\(n(Y)+n(Z)=1296=36^2\), so \(|k|=36\).
solutions.focus_note: 'Range has one element' means every pair shares the same second coordinate; check the column counts.

solutions.key_idea: Spot \(a^2=18\) and \(b^{-6}=1080\), solve the linear system for \(x,y\).
solutions.focus_note: Before using change of base, look for a hidden power relation between the base and the argument.

solutions.key_idea: \(X\) is the set of 6-element subsets of the allowed pairs, so \(n(X)=\binom{N}{6}\) with \(N\) the number of allowed pairs.
hints: Count the ordered pairs \((a,b)\in S\times S\) with \(|a-b|\ge2\).
Of the 36 pairs, remove those with \(|a-b|=0\) and \(|a-b|=1\).
solutions.full_html:
Total pairs \(36\). \(|a-b|=0\): 6 pairs. \(|a-b|=1\): 10 pairs. Allowed: \(36-16=20\).
Any 6 of them form a valid relation: \(n(X)=\binom{20}6\), so \(m=20\).
solutions.focus_note: A relation is just a subset of \(S\times S\); count the allowed pairs first.

solutions.key_idea: Cauchy's equations: on rationals, \(f(x)=cx\) and \(g(x)=a^x\), with no continuity needed.
hints: Additivity gives \(f(r)=cr\) for every rational \(r\); find \(c\) from \(f\left(-\frac35\right)=12\).
Multiplicativity with \(g>0\) gives \(g(r)=a^r\) for rational \(r\); find \(a\) from \(g\left(-\frac13\right)=2\).
solutions.full_html:
\(f\left(-\frac35\right)=-\frac35c=12\Rightarrow c=-20\), so \(f\left(\frac14\right)=-5\).
\(g\left(-\frac13\right)=a^{-1/3}=2\Rightarrow a=\frac18\), so \(g(-2)=a^{-2}=64\) and \(g(0)=1\).
\((-5+64-8)\times1=51\).
solutions.focus_note: For rational inputs, Cauchy-type equations give linear/exponential forms directly.

solutions.key_idea: Strip away factors that never vanish, and use monotonicity of \(p(x)=x^{2023}+2024x+2025\).
hints: Which factors can never be zero? Then count real roots of \(p(x)=x^{2023}+2024x+2025\).
solutions.full_html:
\(\sin x+2>0\), \(e^{\pi x}>0\), and \(x^2-x+3>0\) (discriminant \(-11\)). So \(f(x)=0\iff p(x)=0\).
\(p'(x)=2023x^{2022}+2024>0\): \(p\) is strictly increasing, and an odd-degree polynomial runs from \(-\infty\) to \(\infty\). Exactly one real root.
Answer 1.
solutions.focus_note: Large-degree polynomials in JEE usually yield to monotonicity, not to factorisation.

solutions.key_idea: The zeros are \(x=\pm\frac1{\sqrt n}\); each interval becomes a range of \(n\), finite or infinite.
hints: Translate each interval condition into a condition on \(n\).
solutions.full_html:
Positive zeros: \(x=\frac1{\sqrt n}\), \(n=1,2,3,\dots\)
(A) \(x\ge10^{-10}\iff n\le10^{20}\): finitely many. False.
(B) \(x\ge\frac1\pi\iff n\le\pi^2\approx9.87\): \(n=1,\dots,9\) give zeros. False.
(C) \(x<10^{-10}\iff n>10^{20}\): infinitely many. False.
(D) \(\frac1{\pi^2}<x<\frac1\pi\iff\pi^2<n<\pi^4\approx97.4\): \(n=10,\dots,97\), that is 88 zeros, more than 25. True.
Answer (D).

wrong_options.A: Only \(n\le10^{20}\) qualify: a huge but finite number.
wrong_options.C: Zeros accumulate at 0, so there are infinitely many near 0.

solutions.focus_note: Zeros of \(\sin(\text{something})\) are easiest to count after converting to the integer parameter \(n\).

solutions.key_idea: A real cubic always has a real root, so \(f-g\) cannot be cubic: \(a_3=b_3\). The \(x^3\) coefficient of \(h\) then comes only from the \(x^4\) terms.
hints: \(f-g\) never vanishes. What does that force about the \(x^3\) coefficients \(a_3,b_3\)?
solutions.full_html:
\(f(x)-g(x)=(a_1-b_1)+7x+(a_2-b_2)x^2+(a_3-b_3)x^3\). If \(a_3\ne b_3\) this cubic has a real root, contradicting \(f\ne g\) everywhere. So \(a_3=b_3\).
\(x^3\) coefficient of \(h(x)=f(x+1)-g(x+2)\): from \((x+1)^4-(x+2)^4\): \(4-8=-4\); from \(a_3(x+1)^3-b_3(x+2)^3\): \(a_3-b_3=0\). Total \(-4\).
Answer (C).

wrong_options.A: 8 is the coefficient from \((x+2)^4\) alone, forgetting the subtraction.
wrong_options.B: Ignores that \(a_3=b_3\) cancels and miscounts the binomial coefficients.

solutions.focus_note: 'Never equal' or 'never zero' conditions on polynomials usually mean: no odd-degree difference.

solutions.key_idea: 10 elements = 6 forced diagonal pairs + 2 symmetric off-diagonal pairs.
hints: Reflexive forces the 6 diagonal pairs. How many more pairs are needed?
Symmetric off-diagonal pairs come in twos \((x,y),(y,x)\).
solutions.full_html:
The 6 pairs \((x,x)\) must be present. The remaining 4 elements form 2 symmetric pairs \(\{(x,y),(y,x)\}\), i.e. 2 unordered pairs \(\{x,y\}\) chosen from \(\binom62=15\).
Number \(=\binom{15}2=105\).
solutions.focus_note: Count symmetric relations by unordered pairs \(\{x,y\}\); each contributes 2 ordered pairs.

solutions.key_idea: \(f\) hits 1 twice (\(n=1,2\)) and is otherwise a bijection onto \(\mathbb Z\); \(g\) is one-one but misses 1.
hints: Which value does \(f\) repeat? Which natural number does \(g\) miss?
solutions.full_html:
\(f\): odd \(n\mapsto1,2,3,\dots\); even \(n\mapsto1,0,-1,-2,\dots\). So \(f(1)=f(2)=1\): not one-one; every integer is hit: onto. (D) true.
\(g\): \(n\ge0\mapsto3,5,7,\dots\); \(n<0\mapsto2,4,6,\dots\). One-one, but 1 is never hit: not onto. (C) false.
\(g\circ f\): \(g(f(1))=g(f(2))\): not one-one; its values lie in the range of \(g\), which misses 1: not onto. (A) true.
\(f\circ g\): \(g\) is one-one onto \(\mathbb N\setminus\{1\}\), and \(f\) restricted to \(\mathbb N\setminus\{1\}\) is a bijection onto \(\mathbb Z\) (the only clash was \(n=1\)). So \(f\circ g\) is one-one and onto. (B) false.
Answer (A), (D).

wrong_options.B: \(f\circ g\) is one-one: the only repeated value of \(f\) came from \(n=1\), which is not in the range of \(g\).
wrong_options.C: \(g(n)=1\) has no solution, so \(g\) is not onto.

solutions.focus_note: For composites, track exactly which inputs the inner function feeds to the outer one.

solutions.key_idea: Such a \(g\) exists exactly when \(f\) is one-one; then count injections avoiding two fixed values.
hints: If \(g(f(x))=2^x\) for all \(x\), what does \(f(x)=f(y)\) imply?
So \(T\) is the set of one-one \(f\) with \(f(2)\ne2,\ f(4)\ne4\). Use inclusion–exclusion.
solutions.full_html:
If \(f(x)=f(y)\) then \(2^x=g(f(x))=g(f(y))=2^y\), so \(x=y\): \(f\) must be one-one. Conversely, if \(f\) is one-one, define \(g(f(x))=2^x\) and \(g=1\) elsewhere. So \(T\) = one-one \(f\in S\).
One-one maps \(A\to B\): \(7\cdot6\cdot5\cdot4\cdot3=2520\). With \(f(2)=2\): \(6\cdot5\cdot4\cdot3=360\); with \(f(4)=4\): 360; with both: \(5\cdot4\cdot3=60\).
\(n(T)=2520-360-360+60=1860\).
solutions.focus_note: 'There exists \(g\) with \(g\circ f=\) one-one function' is equivalent to \(f\) being one-one.

solutions.key_idea: Count partitions of \(S\) whose class sizes satisfy \(\sum k_i=10\) and \(\sum k_i^2=42\).
hints: An equivalence relation is a partition; a class of size \(k\) contributes \(k^2\) ordered pairs.
Find all partitions of 10 with \(\sum k_i^2=42\).
solutions.focus_note: Remember to divide by the factorial of the number of equal-sized classes when counting partitions.

solutions.key_idea: Sum the G.P. in closed form, then reduce the condition to \(\left(\frac34\right)^n<\frac16\) for odd \(n\).
hints: \(a_n\) is a finite G.P. with ratio \(-\frac34\): \(a_n=\frac37\left(1-\left(-\frac34\right)^n\right)\).
\(b_n>a_n\iff a_n<\frac12\iff\left(-\frac34\right)^n>-\frac16\). This is automatic for even \(n\). Check odd \(n\).
solutions.full_html:
\(a_n=\dfrac{\frac34\left(1-(-\frac34)^n\right)}{1+\frac34}=\frac37\left(1-(-\tfrac34)^n\right)\). \(b_n>a_n\iff a_n<\frac12\iff(-\tfrac34)^n>-\tfrac16\).
Even \(n\): the left side is positive, so the condition always holds. Odd \(n\): you need \(\left(\frac34\right)^n<\frac16\).
\(\left(\frac34\right)^5=\frac{243}{1024}\approx0.237>\frac16\) fails, and \(\left(\frac34\right)^7\approx0.133<\frac16\) holds.
So the condition fails at \(n=5\) and holds for every \(n\ge6\). Hence \(n_0=6\). Answer: 6.
solutions.focus_note: For alternating G.P.s, split into even and odd \(n\). Only one parity is ever a problem.

solutions.key_idea: The product \(AH\) is invariant under the AM–HM iteration, so every \(G_n\) is the same.
solutions.full_html:
For any two positive numbers \(x,y\): \(\frac{x+y}2\cdot\frac{2xy}{x+y}=xy=G^2\).
So \(G_n^2=A_{n-1}H_{n-1}=G_{n-1}^2\), and \(G_1=G_2=G_3=\cdots\). Answer (C).

wrong_options.D: There is no oscillation; \(G\) is constant.

solutions.focus_note: \(AM\times HM=GM^2\) for two numbers. This is the key fact for this whole passage.

solutions.key_idea: Find \(V_r\) as a cubic in \(r\), then use the standard power sums.
solutions.full_html:
\(V_r=\frac r2(2r^2-r+1)\). So \(\sum V_r=\sum r^3-\frac12\sum r^2+\frac12\sum r\)
\(=\frac{n^2(n+1)^2}4-\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{12}+\frac{n(n+1)}4=\frac{n(n+1)}{12}\left[3n(n+1)-(2n+1)+3\right]=\frac1{12}n(n+1)(3n^2+n+2)\).
Answer (B).

wrong_options.C: It matches for \(n=1,2\), but at \(n=3\) it gives 24, while the true value is \(1+6+21=28\).

solutions.focus_note: Test the options with \(n=1,2,3\). It is often the fastest check for a closed-form sum.

solutions.key_idea: A quadratic \(T_r\) has linear first differences, so the \(Q_r\) form an A.P.
solutions.full_html: \(Q_r=3(2r+1)+2=6r+5\). So the \(Q_r\) form an A.P. with common difference 6. Answer (B).

wrong_options.A: 5 is the constant term of \(Q_r\), not its common difference.
wrong_options.C: \(Q_1=11\) is the first term, not the common difference.
wrong_options.D: \(Q_r\) depends on \(r\), so the terms are not all equal.

solutions.focus_note: Second differences of a quadratic \(ar^2+\dots\) are constant and equal to \(2a\).

solutions.key_idea: Each new A.M. is the average of the old A.M. and a smaller number, so it decreases.
hints: An average of two numbers is less than the larger one.
solutions.full_html: \(A_{n-1}>H_{n-1}\) (the numbers stay distinct), so \(A_n=\frac{A_{n-1}+H_{n-1}}2<A_{n-1}\). Answer (A).
solutions.focus_note: The AM–HM iteration squeezes both sequences towards the fixed G.M.: the A.M.s from above and the H.M.s from below.

solutions.key_idea: \(H_n=G^2/A_n\) with \(G\) fixed and \(A_n\) decreasing.
solutions.full_html: \(H_n=\dfrac{G_1^2}{A_n}\), and \(A_n\) strictly decreases, so \(H_n\) strictly increases. Answer (B).
solutions.focus_note: Use the invariant: once you know one sequence, the other follows from \(AH=G^2\).

solutions.key_idea: \(T_r\) factors into two integers that are both at least 2.
solutions.full_html:
\(V_{r+1}-V_r=\frac12\left[2(3r^2+3r+1)-(2r+1)+1\right]=3r^2+2r+1\). So \(T_r=3r^2+2r-1=(r+1)(3r-1)\).
For \(r\ge1\), both factors are \(\ge2\), so \(T_r\) is always composite. Answer (D).
solutions.focus_note: 'Always prime/composite' questions are usually settled by factorising the expression.

solutions.key_idea: Check A.P., G.P. and H.P. directly. A numerical example quickly disproves Statement-2.
solutions.full_html:
A.P.? The differences are \(ar,ar^2\), equal only if \(r=1\), which is excluded. G.P.? \(b_2^2=b_1b_3\) gives \((1+r)^2=1+r+r^2\), so \(r=0\), which is excluded. So Statement-1 is true.
H.P.? With \(a=1,r=2\): \(1,3,7,15\). The reciprocals \(1,\frac13,\frac17,\frac1{15}\) have differences \(-\frac23,-\frac4{21}\), which are not equal. So Statement-2 is false.
Answer (C).

wrong_options.A: Statement-2 is false, as the example shows.

solutions.focus_note: One concrete counterexample settles a 'for all' claim.

solutions.key_idea: Find the general term from \(S_n\), then use the sum of squares of the first \(n\) odd numbers.

wrong_options.B: \(4n^2+1\) is wrong. Check \(n=1\): the answer must be \(c^2\), and \(\frac{5c^2}{3}\ne c^2\).

solutions.focus_note: Always check \(n=1\): the sum must equal \(a_1^2=c^2\).

solutions.key_idea: Telescoping: \(\dfrac{k^2-3k+1}{(k-1)!}=\dfrac{k-1}{(k-2)!}-\dfrac{k}{(k-1)!}\) for \(k\ge2\).
hints: Write \(\dfrac{k^2-3k+1}{(k-1)!}\) as a telescoping difference, such as \(\frac{k-1}{(k-2)!}-\frac{k}{(k-1)!}\).
solutions.focus_note: The extra term \(\frac{100^2}{100!}\) is a signal: it cancels the leftover from a telescoping sum.

solutions.key_idea: Recognise the A.P., use the sum of squares to find \(d\), and use the inequality to pick it.
hints: Use \(\sum a_k^2=990\) to get a quadratic in \(d\), and \(a_2<13.5\) to choose the root.
solutions.focus_note: The mean of an A.P. with an odd number of terms is its middle term.

solutions.key_idea: A ratio \(\frac{\alpha+\beta n}{\gamma+\delta n}\) is constant iff \(\alpha\delta=\beta\gamma\).
hints: This is independent of \(n\) only if \(d=0\) or the constant parts vanish, i.e. \(6-d=0\).
solutions.full_html:
Ratio \(=5\cdot\dfrac{(6-d)+5nd}{(6-d)+nd}\). It is constant iff \(d=0\) (ratio 5) or \(d=6\) (ratio 25).
So \(a_2=3\) or \(9\). Answer: 3 or 9 (both accepted).
solutions.focus_note: Don't miss the trivial case \(d=0\). The official key accepted both values.

solutions.key_idea: Split terms so that the exponents sum to zero, then use AM ≥ GM.
hints: Split \(3a^{-3}\) into three copies of \(a^{-3}\), giving 8 terms.
Check that the product of the 8 terms is 1, then apply AM–GM.
solutions.full_html:
The 8 terms are \(a^{-5},a^{-4},a^{-3},a^{-3},a^{-3},1,a^8,a^{10}\). The exponents sum to \(-5-4-9+0+8+10=0\), so the product is 1.
AM–GM: sum \(\ge8\sqrt[8]{1}=8\), with equality at \(a=1\). Answer: 8.
solutions.focus_note: A coefficient like \(3a^{-3}\) is a hint to split it into three equal terms.

solutions.key_idea: Work with the reciprocal A.P. and find when it first becomes negative.
hints: The reciprocals form an A.P.: \(\frac15\) and \(\frac1{25}=\frac15+19d\).
solutions.focus_note: H.P. questions: always convert to the reciprocal A.P.

solutions.key_idea: An infinite nested radical satisfies a self-referential equation.
solutions.focus_note: Nested radicals and continued fractions: set the whole expression equal to \(y\) and solve.

solutions.key_idea: Estimate \(n\) from \(\frac{n(n+1)}2\approx1224\), then check the parity and range of \(2k+1\).
solutions.full_html:
\(n=49\): \(1225-1224=1\) gives \(k=0\), which is invalid. \(n=50\): \(1275-1224=51=2k+1\) gives \(k=25\). ✓
\(n=51,52\) give even differences, and \(n\ge53\) gives \(k>n\).
So \(k=25\) and \(k-20=5\). Answer: 5.
solutions.focus_note: Integer equations: bound the variable, then check the few candidates.

solutions.key_idea: Group by the period of the sign pattern. Each block is linear in \(j\), so the total is a quadratic.
hints: The signs \((-1)^{k(k+1)/2}\) for \(k=1,2,3,4\) are \(-,-,+,+\), repeating every 4.
solutions.focus_note: Find the period of the sign pattern first. Here \(k(k+1)/2\) is odd, odd, even, even.

solutions.key_idea: Turn the condition into \(a(r-1)^2=6\) and use that 6 is square-free.
hints: Let \(b=ar,\ c=ar^2\) with \(r\) a positive integer.
solutions.focus_note: '\(\frac ba\) is an integer' means the common ratio is an integer. Use it.

solutions.key_idea: The ratio condition fixes \(a/d\). The range of the 7th term then fixes \(d\).
solutions.focus_note: \(S_n=n\times\) (middle term). So \(S_7=7a_4\) and \(S_{11}=11a_6\), a faster route to the same equation.

solutions.key_idea: A G.P. (convex in the index) lies below the A.P. through the same endpoints, and beyond the endpoints it overtakes it.
hints: The \(b_i\) form a G.P. with ratio 2. The \(a_i\) form an A.P. with the same 1st and 51st terms.
Between equal endpoints, a convex G.P. lies below the straight-line A.P.
solutions.full_html:
\(b_i=b_12^{i-1}\). Pair the terms symmetrically: \(b_ib_{52-i}=b_1b_{51}\), and with a fixed product the sum is largest when the two numbers are furthest apart. So \(b_i+b_{52-i}<b_1+b_{51}=a_i+a_{52-i}\) for \(1<i<51\), and therefore \(t<s\).
\(a_{101}=2a_{51}-a_1=b_1(2^{51}-1)\), while \(b_{101}=b_12^{100}\). So \(a_{101}<b_{101}\).
Answer (B).

wrong_options.A: Beyond the 51st term the G.P. grows much faster: \(b_{101}=2^{100}b_1\gg a_{101}\).
wrong_options.C: \(s>t\): the A.P. terms are larger in between.

solutions.focus_note: \(a_i+a_{52-i}=a_1+a_{51}=b_1+b_{51}\ge b_i+b_{52-i}\) pairs the terms neatly.

solutions.key_idea: Sequences built from the roots of \(x^2-x-1\) satisfy the Fibonacci recurrence.
solutions.full_html: \(\alpha^{12}=\alpha^{11}+\alpha^{10}\), and the same for \(\beta\). Multiply by \(p,q\) and add: \(a_{12}=a_{11}+a_{10}\). Answer (B).
solutions.focus_note: Read the recurrence straight off the quadratic: \(x^2=px+q\Rightarrow a_{n+2}=pa_{n+1}+qa_n\).

solutions.key_idea: Write \(a_4\) as rational \(+\) rational\(\cdot\sqrt5\). The FACT forces \(p=q\).
hints: Substitute \(\alpha,\beta=\frac{1\pm\sqrt5}2\) and use the FACT: the coefficient of \(\sqrt5\) must vanish.
solutions.full_html:
\(a_4=3(p\alpha+q\beta)+2(p+q)=\frac72(p+q)+\frac{3\sqrt5}2(p-q)=28\).
By the FACT, \(p=q\) and \(7p=28\), so \(p=q=4\). Then \(p+2q=12\). Answer (D).
solutions.focus_note: The FACT is a hint to separate the rational and irrational parts.

solutions.key_idea: Inclusion–exclusion. The common terms form an A.P. with difference \(\operatorname{lcm}(5,7)=35\).
hints: Common terms: \(x\equiv1\pmod5\) and \(x\equiv2\pmod7\), so \(x\equiv16\pmod{35}\). They must also be \(\le\) the last term of \(X\).
solutions.full_html:
The last term of \(X\) is \(1+5\cdot2017=10086\). The last term of \(Y\) is \(9+7\cdot2017=14128\).
Common terms: \(16,51,86,\dots\) up to \(10086\). \(16+35j\le10086\) gives \(j\le287\), so there are 288 terms.
\(|X\cup Y|=4036-288=3748\). Answer: 3748.
solutions.focus_note: The common terms are limited by the shorter range, here \(X\)'s last term.

solutions.key_idea: Chinese Remainder Theorem: the common terms recur with period 105.
hints: The intersection is an A.P. with \(d=\operatorname{lcm}(3,5,7)=105\).
solutions.focus_note: For CRT by hand, list terms of the largest modulus and filter.

solutions.key_idea: Fibonacci identities and generating functions evaluated at \(x=\frac1{10}\).
hints: \(a_n\) is the Fibonacci sequence \(1,1,2,3,5,\dots\). \(b_n=a_{n-1}+a_{n+1}\) is the Lucas sequence.
solutions.full_html:
(A) \(\sum_{k=1}^n a_k=a_{n+2}-1\) (telescope \(a_k=a_{k+2}-a_{k+1}\)). True.
(B) \(\frac{0.1}{1-0.1-0.01}=\frac{10}{89}\). True.
(C) \(a_{n-1}+a_{n+1}=\frac{\alpha^{n-1}(1+\alpha^2)-\beta^{n-1}(1+\beta^2)}{\alpha-\beta}\). Since \(1+\alpha^2=\alpha(\alpha-\beta)\), this is \(\alpha^n+\beta^n\). Also \(b_1=1=\alpha+\beta\). True.
(D) \(\frac{0.1+0.02}{0.89}=\frac{12}{89}\ne\frac8{89}\). False.
Answer: (A), (B), (C).
solutions.focus_note: \(1+\alpha^2=\alpha(\alpha-\beta)\) uses \(\alpha^2=\alpha+1\) and \(\alpha\beta=-1\). A neat Fibonacci-to-Lucas bridge.

solutions.key_idea: Solve for \(c\) in terms of \(n\). Exponential growth leaves only finitely many \(n\) to check.
hints: So \(c=\dfrac{2n(n-1)}{2^n-1-2n}\). Check small \(n\): the denominator soon outgrows the numerator.
solutions.focus_note: When one side grows like \(2^n\) and the other like \(n^2\), only small \(n\) can work.

solutions.key_idea: Distance from the origin to the centre + radius \(\le r\). Reduce to an inequality in \(2^{n-199}\).
solutions.full_html:
\(\sqrt2(2-2^{2-n})+2^{1-n}\le\sqrt2(2-2^{-198})\iff2^{1-n}\le\sqrt2\left(2^{2-n}-2^{-198}\right)\).
Dividing by \(2^{1-n}\): \(1\le\sqrt2(2-2^{n-199})\iff2^{n-199}\le2-\frac1{\sqrt2}\approx1.29\iff n\le199\).
So 199 circles. Answer (B).
solutions.focus_note: Normalise by the smallest power of 2 in the inequality. The boundary case is then easy to read.

solutions.key_idea: Find how many circles fit. The non-intersecting subset is every other circle.
solutions.full_html:
\(r=2-\frac1{513}\). \(2-2^{1-n}\le2-\frac1{513}\iff2^{n-1}\le513\iff n\le10\). So \(k=10\).
\(C_n,C_{n+1}\): the centres are \(a_n\) apart, with radii \(a_n,a_{n+1}\), so they intersect. \(C_n,C_{n+2}\): the distance is \(a_n+a_{n+1}>a_n+a_{n+2}\), so they are disjoint.
The maximum non-intersecting set is alternate circles, so \(l=5\). \(3k+2l=40\). Answer (D).
solutions.focus_note: For 'no two intersect', check neighbours and next-neighbours. That usually decides the pattern.
