	Hence \(7\tan\theta=\boxed1\).

All lines in the family pass through \(C=(2,3)\). If \(H=(x,y)\) is the foot of the perpendicular from \(P=(1,2)\) to one of these lines, then \(PH\perp CH\). Hence \(H\) lies on the circle with diameter \(PC\): \[ \overrightarrow{PH}\cdot\overrightarrow{CH}=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (x-1)(x-2)+(y-2)(y-3)=0. \] Thus option (A) is correct.

Since \(f'(a)=f''(a)=0\) and \(f\) is a monic cubic, \(f(x)=(x-a)^3+b\). Then \(g'(x)=(a-x)f''(x)+6(x-a)=(x-a)\left(6-6(x-a)\right)\); \(g'(2)=0\) with \(2\ne a\) gives \(a=1\), hence \(f''(2)=6(2-1)=6\).

Use \(\sin t\cos t=\frac12\sin2t\) and the product identity \(\prod_{r=1}^{n}\sin\frac{r\pi}{2n}=\frac{\sqrt n}{2^{n-1}}\). The product inside the \(n\)th root is \(\sqrt n/2^{2n-1}\), so the limit is \(1/4\) and the least \(a+b\) is \(5\).

\(g(a)=0\) and \(g(b)=d^3-3d^3+3d^2\) with \(d=b-a\); \(g(b)=0\) gives \(d=\frac32\), so \(b=\frac52\). Then \(64\displaystyle\int_1^{5/2}\left((x-1)^3+\tfrac52\right)dx=64\left(\tfrac{81}{64}+\tfrac{15}{4}\right)=321\).

(A) \(\ln L=\lim\dfrac{\ln(\sin x/x)}{1-\cos x}=\dfrac{-x^2/6}{x^2/2}=-\frac13\), so \(1/k^2=9\): (A) \(\to\) (t). (B) The logarithm is \(\tan^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\cdot\ln\frac{n^2}{n-1}\sim\frac{\ln n}{\sqrt n}\to0\), so the limit is \(1\): (B) \(\to\) (q). (C) \(8(1-2\sin^2x\cos^2x)=5\) gives \(\sin^22x=\frac34\), which has \(8\) solutions in \((0,2\pi)\): (C) \(\to\) (s). Near \(x=4\), \(|x|=x\) and \(\sin(x-2)>0\). Therefore \(f(x)=3-\sin(x-2)\) locally, so \(f'(4)=-\cos2\); option D.
By differentiability, \(f(3+5/n)-f(3-2/n)=(7/n)f'(3)+o(1/n)\). Multiplication by \(n\) gives \(7\cdot18=126\).

Put \(x_n=\tan\theta_n\). Then \(\tan\theta_{n+1}=\tan(\theta_n/2)\), so \(\theta_n=\pi/(3\cdot2^{n-1})\). Since \(\tan t\sim t\), \(2^nx_n\to2\pi/3\).

Expanding, the numerator is \((1-b^2)x^2+\left(\frac{b^4}{12}-a\right)x^4+O(x^6)\) and the denominator is \(\left(\frac{a^2}{2}-2\right)x^2+\frac{a^4}{24}x^4+O(x^5)\). For \(L=\frac{25}{8}\) or \(-\frac{23}{8}\) with integers \(a,b\), the \(x^2\) terms must vanish: \(b^2=1\), \(a^2=4\). With \(b=\pm1\): \(L=\frac{25}{8}\Rightarrow a+b\in\{-1,-3\}\) and \(L=-\frac{23}{8}\Rightarrow a+b\in\{1,3\}\). Hence (B) and (D).

(A) \(1-\cos2x\sim2x^2\) and \(e^{x^2}-e^x+x=\frac{x^2}{2}+O(x^3)\), so the limit is \(4\): (A) \(\to\) (r). (B) \(\frac1x\ln\frac{3+x}{3-x}\to\frac23\), so \(p+q=5\): (B) \(\to\) (s). At \(0\), \(f'(0)=\lim_{x\to0}x\sin(1/x)=0\), so \(f\) is differentiable. The ratio \(f/g=\sin(1/x)\) has no limit, while \(f'g'=4x^2\sin(1/x)-2x\cos(1/x)\to0\). The ratio \(f'/g'\) has no limit. Hence A, B and D are correct.

The two limits defining the auxiliary functions simplify to \(f(x)=\tan^{-1}(2x^2)\) and \(g(x)=-x^2\). Thus the numerator is \(e^{2x^2}-e^{\tan^{-1}(2x^2)}\). Using \(\tan^{-1}(2x^2)=2x^2-\frac83x^6+O(x^{10})\) gives the limit \(8/3\).

For every polynomial \(P\), the factor \(e^{-1/x^4}\) tends to zero faster than any power of \(1/x\) grows. Hence \(f(x)\to0=f(0)\) and \(\lim_{x\to0}f(x)/x=0\), so \(f\) is continuous and differentiable at \(0\) with \(f'(0)=0\). Thus B and D.

On \([-4,4]\), \(\lfloor3x+14\rfloor\) jumps wherever \(3x\) is an integer. In the open interval this gives \(3x\in\{-11,\dots,11\}\), i.e. \(23\) points; at the right end \(x=4\) the function also jumps (left limit \(25\), value \(26\)), while at \(x=-4\) it is constant on the right. The term \(|4x^2-1|(2x-1)(x+2)\) has a cusp at \(x=-\frac12\) only (at \(x=\frac12\) the factor \((2x-1)\) cancels the cusp), and \(-\frac12\) is not a jump point of the floor term. \(\sin\frac{\pi x}{2}\) is smooth. Total: \(23+1+1=25\).
Direct integration gives \(g(k)=\lim_{n\to\infty}n^k\frac{(1/n)^k}{k}=1/k\). Therefore \(\lfloor1/g(9)\rfloor=9\).
Apply Rolle's theorem to \(e^{x^2/2}f(x)\), \(e^{-x^2/2}f(x)\), \(e^{50x}f(x)\), and \(e^{(\ln50)x}f(x)\), respectively. Each auxiliary function vanishes at both endpoints, giving A–D.

Let \(c=\cos x\), so \(dc=-\sin x\,dx\) and \(\tan x\sqrt{\sec x}=\dfrac{\sin x}{c^{3/2}}\). Since \(\cos x+\sin^2x=1+c-c^2\),
	\[
	\int=-\int\frac{\left(1+c^2\right)dc}{c^{3/2}\sqrt{1+c-c^2}}=-\int\frac{\left(1+\frac{1}{c^2}\right)dc}{\sqrt{\frac1c-c+1}}.
	\]
	With \(w=\frac1c-c+1\), \(dw=-\left(\frac1{c^2}+1\right)dc\), so the integral is \(2\sqrt w\), i.e. \(2\sqrt{\sec x-\cos x+1}\). Hence \(f(x)=\sec x-\cos x+k\); \(f\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)=2-\frac12+k=\frac32\) gives \(k=0\). Then \(f\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\sqrt2-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\) and \(\left[f\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right]=\boxed0\).

(A) The integrand is \(\operatorname{cosec}^2x-\dfrac{1}{1+x^2}\), so the integral is \(-\cot x+\cot^{-1}x\) (up to a constant): \(A=1\), \(B=-1\): (p, q).
(B) With \(u=x+\sqrt{x^2+2}\), \(x=\dfrac{u^2-2}{2u}\), \(dx=\dfrac{u^2+2}{2u^2}du\): \(\displaystyle\int\sqrt u\cdot\frac{u^2+2}{2u^2}du=\frac13u^{3/2}-\frac{2}{u^{1/2}}\): \(A=1\), \(B=2\): (p, r).
(C) Differentiating the right side reproduces \(\dfrac{\sqrt{2-x-x^2}}{x}\) exactly when \(A=1\), \(B=2\): (p, r).
(D) With \(u=\tan^2x\): \(\displaystyle\int\frac{du}{1+u^2}=\tan^{-1}\left(\tan^2x\right)=-\cot^{-1}\left(\tan^2x\right)+\text{const}\): \(B=-1\), (q).

Integrate by parts with \(u=\sin^{n-1}x\) and \(dv=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos^mx}dx\), so \(v=\dfrac{1}{(m-1)\cos^{m-1}x}\) and \(du=(n-1)\sin^{n-2}x\cos x\,dx\):
	\[
	I_{n,-m}=\frac{\sin^{n-1}x}{(m-1)\cos^{m-1}x}-\frac{n-1}{m-1}\int\frac{\sin^{n-2}x}{\cos^{m-2}x}\,dx=\frac{\sin^{n-1}x}{(m-1)\cos^{m-1}x}-\frac{n-1}{m-1}I_{n-2,2-m}.
	\]
	Hence \(I_{n,-m}+\dfrac{n-1}{m-1}I_{n-2,\,2-m}=\dfrac{1}{m-1}\cdot\dfrac{\sin^{n-1}x}{\cos^{m-1}x}\).

Put \(y=\tan\theta\): the integral becomes
	\[
	\int\frac{\cos^6\theta}{\sin^2\theta}d\theta=\int\left(\frac{1}{\sin^2\theta}-3+3\sin^2\theta-\sin^4\theta\right)d\theta
	\]
	\[

	So \(P=-1\), \(Q=-\frac{15}{8}\), \(R=-\frac12\), \(S=2\), \(T=-\frac1{32}\) and \(P-\frac83Q-2R+S-32T=-1+5+1+2+1=\boxed8\).

Put \(\dfrac{x}{1+x}=z\): \(\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\frac{x^{m-1}}{(1+x)^{m+n}}dx=\int_0^1z^{m-1}(1-z)^{n-1}dz=\beta(m,n)\). Similarly the other integral is \(\beta(n,m)=\beta(m,n)\), so \(k=\boxed1\).

The denominator is \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), so the integrand is \(\dfrac4\pi\sin^{-1}\sqrt x-1\). With \(s=\sin^{-1}\sqrt x\),
	\[
	\int\sin^{-1}\sqrt x\,dx=xs-\frac12\int\sqrt{\frac{x}{1-x}}\,dx=-\frac12(1-2x)s+\frac12\sqrt{x}\sqrt{1-x}.
	\]
	Multiplying by \(\frac4\pi\): \(\frac2\pi\left[-s(1-2x)+\sqrt x\sqrt{1-x}\right]-x\), so \(A=\boxed2\).

Put \(\sin^2\theta=x\), \(2\sin\theta\cos\theta\,d\theta=dx\):
	\[
	\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^{2m}\theta\sin^{2n}\theta\,d\theta=\frac12\int_0^1(1-x)^{m-\frac12}x^{n-\frac12}dx=\frac12\beta\left(m+\frac12,\ n+\frac12\right).
	\]
	So \(u=v=w=2\) and \(u+v+w=\boxed6\).

Divide inside: the integrand equals \(\dfrac{\left(1-\frac1{x^2}\right)dx}{\left(x+\frac1x\right)\sqrt{\left(x+\frac1x\right)^2-1}}\) (for \(x>0\)). With \(u=x+\frac1x\) this is \(\displaystyle\int\frac{du}{u\sqrt{u^2-1}}=\sec^{-1}|u|\), so \(f(x)=x+\frac1x\).
	\(f\) has a local maximum \(-2\) at \(x=-1\) and a local minimum \(2\) at \(x=1\); its range is \((-\infty,-2]\cup[2,\infty)\) (C false); \(f\) increases for \(x>1\), so \(f(\pi)>f(e)\) (D false).

The numerator is \((1+x)\left(x^4+2x^2+1\right)=(1+x)\left(1+x^2\right)^2\) and the denominator factorises as \((1+x)^2\left(1+x^2\right)^2\). So the integrand is \(\dfrac{1}{1+x}\) and, with \(g(1)=\ln2\), \(g(x)=\ln(1+x)\).
	It increases for \(x>-1\) (A); \(g(99)-g(3)=\ln25\approx3.22\), so \([g(99)-g(3)]=3\) (B); it is not periodic (C false), and \(g(6)<g(7)\) (D false).

(A) With \(t^3=\tan x\), \(dx=\dfrac{3t^2\,dt}{1+t^6}\), so the integral is \(\displaystyle\int\frac{3t^3\,dt}{1+t^6}=\frac32\int\frac{u\,du}{1+u^3}\) (\(u=t^2\)). Partial fractions \(\dfrac{u}{1+u^3}=-\dfrac{1}{3(u+1)}+\dfrac{u+1}{3\left(u^2-u+1\right)}\) give \(\frac14\ln\dfrac{u^2-u+1}{(u+1)^2}+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\tan^{-1}\dfrac{2u-1}{\sqrt3}\): \(A=\frac14\), \(B=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\), (p, s).
(B) With \(c=\cos x\): \(\displaystyle\int\frac{-\left(2-c^2\right)dc}{2c^2-1}=\frac c2-\frac34\int\frac{dc}{c^2-\frac12}\), giving \(A=\frac12\), \(B=\frac{3}{4\sqrt2}\): (r, t).
(C) \(\dfrac{1}{\left(x^2+1\right)\left(x^2+4\right)}=\dfrac13\left(\dfrac{1}{x^2+1}-\dfrac{1}{x^2+4}\right)\): \(A=\frac13\), \(B=-\frac16\), (q).
(D) Divide numerator and denominator by \(x^2\) and put \(u=x+\frac1x\): the integral becomes \(\displaystyle-\int\frac{du}{u\sqrt{u^2-2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\sin^{-1}\frac{\sqrt2}{u}+\text{const}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\sin^{-1}\frac{\sqrt2x}{x^2+1}\). So \(A\sqrt2=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\), \(A=\frac12\): (r).

With \(s=\sin x+\cos x\):
	\[

	\]
	So the integrand is \(\dfrac{(s-1)^2}{4}=\dfrac{2+\sin2x-2s}{4}=\dfrac12+\dfrac{\sin2x}{4}-\dfrac{\sin x+\cos x}{2}\), and
	\[
	\int=\frac x2-\frac{\cos2x}{8}+\frac{\cos x-\sin x}{2}=\frac x2+\frac{\sqrt2\cos\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)}{2}+\frac{\cos2x}{-8}+d.
	\]
	Thus \(a=2\), \(b=2\), \(c=-8\) and \(|a+b+c|=\boxed4\).

\[
	\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{e^x}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\right)=e^x\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}-\frac{x}{\left(1+x^2\right)^{3/2}}\right)=e^x\frac{x^2-x+1}{\left(1+x^2\right)^{3/2}}.
	\]
	So \(f(x)=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\) (and \(f(0)=1\)): even, bounded, range \((0,1]\), with a single maximum at \(x=0\).

Differentiating,
	\[
	f'(x)=\frac{n\left(x^2+1\right)^n}{x^{n+1}}-\frac{4(n-1)\left(x^2+1\right)^{n-2}}{x^{n-1}}=\frac{d}{dx}\left[\frac{\left(x^2+1\right)^{n-1}\left(x^2-1\right)}{x^n}\right],
	\]
	and \(f(1)=0\) gives
	\[
	f(x)=\frac{\left(x^2+1\right)^{n-1}\left(x^2-1\right)}{x^n}.
	\]
	For every \(n\ge2\): \(f(-1)=0\) (IV); \(x^{n+1}f'(x)\to n\) (III); \(x^nf(x)\to-1\) (I); \(\dfrac{f(x)}{x^n}\to1\) as \(x\to\infty\) (II). So P–IV, Q–III, R–I, S–II, and only C–P–IV is correct.

(A) \(\sin3x+3\sin x=2\sin x\left(1+2\cos^2x\right)\); with \(\cos x=t\), \(dx=-\frac{dt}{\sin x}\), the integral becomes \(\displaystyle\int\frac{-dt}{\left(1-t^2\right)\left(1+2t^2\right)}\): A–Q–IV.
(B) \(\dfrac{2\sin x+\sin2x}{6\sin x-\sin2x}=\dfrac{1+\cos x}{3-\cos x}\); with \(\tan\frac x2=t\) this is \(\dfrac{1}{1+2t^2}\) and \(dx=\dfrac{2dt}{1+t^2}\): B–S–V.
(C) \(\dfrac{4\sin x}{\sin4x}=\dfrac{1}{\cos x\cos2x}\); with \(\sin x=t\), \(dx=\frac{dt}{\cos x}\), giving \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dt}{\left(1-t^2\right)\left(1-2t^2\right)}\): C–P–III.
(D) \(\sin^2x-\cos2x=2\sin^2x-\cos^2x\), so the integrand is \(\dfrac{1}{2\tan^2x-1}\); with \(\tan x=t\): \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dt}{\left(2t^2-1\right)\left(1+t^2\right)}\): D–R–I.
Of the options, only B–S–V is correct.

With \(t=\sin x\), the integrand is \(\dfrac{1-\frac6t}{t^2-t+3}=\dfrac{t-6}{t\left(t^2-t+3\right)}=-\dfrac2t+\dfrac{2t-1}{t^2-t+3}\). So \(g=\ln\dfrac{\sin^2x-\sin x+3}{\sin^2x}\) and \(\lim\limits_{t\to\pi/2}g(t)=\ln3\approx\boxed{1.10}\).

Write the numerator as \(\left(e^x+\cos x+1\right)-\left(e^x+\sin x+x\right)\). Then the integrand is \(\dfrac{\left(e^x+\sin x+x\right)'}{e^x+\sin x+x}-1\), so \(f(x)=e^x+\sin x+x\) (which has \(f(0)=1\), \(f'(0)=3\)) and \(g(x)=-x\).
	\(f+g=e^x+\sin x\) is not even; \(f-g=e^x+\sin x+2x\) has derivative \(e^x+\cos x+2>0\), so it is increasing (B, not C); \(h(x)=e^x-f-g=-\sin x\), whose maximum is \(1\) (D).
Differentiating the right side and multiplying by \(x^3-1\) gives \(f(x)=x^2-x-3\), so \(f(5)=\boxed{17}\).

Integrate \(I_n=\displaystyle\int1\cdot\frac{dx}{\left(x^2+a^2\right)^n}\) by parts:
	\[
	I_n=\frac{x}{\left(x^2+a^2\right)^n}+2n\int\frac{x^2}{\left(x^2+a^2\right)^{n+1}}dx=\frac{x}{\left(x^2+a^2\right)^n}+2n\left(I_n-a^2I_{n+1}\right).
	\]
	Hence \(2na^2I_{n+1}=\dfrac{x}{\left(x^2+a^2\right)^n}+(2n-1)I_n\), i.e. \(I_{n+1}+\dfrac{1-2n}{2n}\cdot\dfrac{1}{a^2}I_n=\dfrac{1}{2na^2}\cdot\dfrac{x}{\left(x^2+a^2\right)^n}\).

\(x(x+3)(x+1)(x+2)+1=\left(x^2+3x\right)\left(x^2+3x+2\right)+1=\left(x^2+3x+1\right)^2\), and \(2x+3\) is the derivative of \(x^2+3x+1\). So the integral is \(c-\dfrac{1}{x^2+3x+1}\): \(f(x)=x^2+3x+1\) (with \(f(0)=1\)) and \(f(1)=\boxed5\).

Let \(u=e^x-1-x\). The denominator is \(1+u^2-\cos^2x=u^2+\sin^2x\) and the numerator is \(u'\sin x-u\cos x\). Hence the integrand is \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{u}{\sin x}\right)\): \(f=\tan^{-1}\) and \(g(x)=\dfrac{e^x-1-x}{\sin x}\to0\). Then \(\dfrac{\tan^{-1}x}{x}\to1\) and \(\dfrac{g(x)}{x}=\dfrac{e^x-1-x}{x\sin x}\to\dfrac12\), so \(\dfrac mn=\dfrac32\) and \(m+n=\boxed5\).
A superset of a linearly dependent set remains dependent, so B is true. Every subset of a linearly independent set is independent, so C is true. A and D are false in general.
Using the vector triple-product identity on the first three terms gives \(-2[\vec b,\vec c,\vec d]\vec a=-48\vec a\). The equation therefore requires \(k=48\), so \(k/8=6\).

Perpendicularity gives \(\tan^2x-2\tan^2y-1=0\). Rearranging and using the tangent-to-double-angle identity yields \(\cos2x=-\sin^2y\). Therefore \(\vec p\cdot\vec q=\cos^2x-\sin^2x+\sin^2y=\cos2x+\sin^2y=0\), so option D is correct.

For three planes sharing a common line, the compatibility condition forces \(a(\vec n_2\times\vec n_3)+b(\vec n_3\times\vec n_1)+c(\vec n_1\times\vec n_2)=\vec0\), so A. A non-zero scalar triple product means the normals are linearly independent, giving a unique intersection point (C); the displayed vector formula in D is Cramer's rule for that point. Hence A, C and D.

Since \(\vec a,\vec b,\vec c\) are non-coplanar, compare their coefficients. For \((p,q)=(1,1)\), \(\vec r_1=\vec r_2=\vec a+\vec b+\vec c\), so the two specified vectors coincide. The other offered pairs fail coefficient proportionality. Thus D.

Dot \((\vec a\cdot\vec x)\vec b=\vec c+\vec x\) with \(\vec a\) to get \((\vec a\cdot\vec x)(\vec a\cdot\vec b-1)=\vec a\cdot\vec c\). Substituting \((\vec a\cdot\vec x)=\dfrac{\vec a\cdot\vec c}{\vec a\cdot\vec b-1}\) back into the original equation gives option A.

The vector \(\hat i-2\hat j+\hat k\) is perpendicular to \(\hat i+\hat j+\hat k\) and lies in the plane spanned by the two given vectors. Its magnitude is \(\sqrt6\). Both it and its negative are unit vectors satisfying the conditions. Hence A and C.

Write \(\vec V=x\hat i+y\hat j+z\hat k\). Comparing coordinates in \(2\vec V+\vec V\times(\hat i+2\hat j)=2\hat i+\hat k\) gives \((x,y,z)=(7/9,1/9,-2/9)\). Hence \(|\vec V|^2=2/3\), so \((3|\vec V|)^2=6\) and \(m=6\).

With \(\vec a=(3,0,-3)\), \(\vec b=(2,2,2)\) and \(\vec c=(0,1,2)\), coefficient comparison gives \(\vec c=-\frac13\vec a+\frac12\vec b\). The coefficients sum to \(1/6<1\), but the coefficient of \(\vec a\) is negative; hence \(C\) is outside the triangle but inside \(\angle OAB\). Option C.

The angle and dot product give \(|\vec b|=1\) and \(|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=3\). From \(\vec r+2\vec a-10\vec b=\lambda(\vec a\times\vec b)\) and the given condition, \(8\lambda|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=4\sqrt3\), so \(\lambda=\sqrt3/6\). Therefore \(1/(3\lambda^2)=4\).

Match each plane separately. (A) has normal \((1,-1,2)\) and passes through \((3,6,2)\), so \(\vec r\cdot(\hat i-\hat j+2\hat k)=1\); thus \(A\to S\). (B) has normal proportional to \((1,-3,-2)\) and its constant is \(3\), so \(B\to P\). (C) has normal \((1,-1,-1)\) and passes through \((2,0,0)\), giving \(\vec r\cdot(\hat i-\hat j-\hat k)=2\); thus \(C\to Q\). (D) gives the plane \(x-y-z=0\), so \(D\to R\).

Since \(\vec c=\lambda(\vec a\times\vec b)\) and \([\vec a,\vec b,\vec c]=1\), we obtain \(\lambda|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=1\). Together with \(|\vec c|^2=1/3\) this gives \(\sin^2\theta=1/2\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\vec a\) and \(\vec b\). Taking \(\theta\) acute, \(\theta=\pi/4\) and \(k=4\).

The unit vector along the bisector must be chosen consistently with the given angle-bisector direction. The bisector condition gives \((x,y,z)=\left(-\frac23,-\frac{11}{15},\frac{2}{15}\right)\). Hence \(x-15y+5z=-\frac23+11+\frac23=11\).

If \(a_1=a\) and the common difference is \(d\), the determinant magnitude for the cyclic triple is \(9(a+d)d^2=54\). Hence \((a+d)d^2=6\). Since \(a,d\) are positive integers, \(d=1\) and \(a=5\), giving \(a_6=10\).
Here \(\vec c=\vec a+2\vec b\). Both coefficients are positive, placing \(C\) inside the angle \(AOB\), while their sum is \(3>1\), placing it outside triangle \(OAB\). Option B.

Determine the line from the two plane equations in each case. (A) gives \(x=-y=z\), so \(A\to R\). (B) fixes \(x=2\) and \(y=3\) while \(z\) is free, so \(B\to S\). (C) gives \(x=2\) and \(y+z=3\), which is line P; therefore \(C\to P\). (D) gives \(x=2\) and \(y+z=1\), which is line Q; therefore \(D\to Q\).

Let \(D(x)=[\vec f(x),\vec g(x),\vec h(x)]\). The determinant has the antisymmetry \(D(\pi-x)=-D(x)\); pairing the integrand at \(x\) and \(\pi-x\) makes the integral over \([0,\pi]\) equal to zero. The apparent singularity in \(\tan x\) at \(x=\pi/2\) is removable in the scalar-triple-product expression.

From \(\vec a+2\vec b+3\vec c=\vec0\), we get \(\vec b\times\vec c=\frac13(\vec a\times\vec b)\) and \(\vec c\times\vec a=\frac23(\vec a\times\vec b)\). Thus the required sum is \(2(\vec a\times\vec b)=6(\vec b\times\vec c)=3(\vec c\times\vec a)\). Hence A, B and C.

Since \(\vec b\cdot\vec c=-1\) and \(|\vec c|^2=6\), the projection of \(\vec b\) on \(\vec c\) is \(\dfrac{\vec b\cdot\vec c}{|\vec c|^2}\vec c=-\vec c/6\), giving B. Also \(\vec a=\vec b\times\vec c\), so \(\vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)=|\vec a|^2\ne0\); the vectors are linearly independent, giving C. A and D are false.

solutions.key_idea: Differentiate the claimed form: $\left(\frac{g\sqrt Q}{k}\right)'$ must equal the integrand; match with $g$ quadratic.
solutions.focus_note: When the form of the answer is given, differentiate it instead of integrating. Matching degrees tells you $g$ is quadratic.

solutions.key_idea: AM–GM on the four positive terms ($2$ written as $1+1$) gives a lower bound equal to the subtracted term; equality fixes each $\sin$.
hints: $16\sin^4x+2\sin^4y+4\sin^4z+2\ \ge\ 4\sqrt[4]{16\cdot2\cdot4\cdot2}\,|\sin x\sin y\sin z|=16|\sin x\sin y\sin z|$.
So the equation needs equality in AM–GM and $\sin x\sin y\sin z>0$.
solutions.full_html:
By AM–GM, $$16\sin^4x+2\sin^4y+4\sin^4z+2\ \ge\ 16\,|\sin x\sin y\sin z|\ \ge\ 16\sin x\sin y\sin z.$$The equation says the left side equals $16\sin x\sin y\sin z$, so both inequalities are equalities:$$16\sin^4x=2\sin^4y=4\sin^4z=2,\qquad \sin x\sin y\sin z>0.$$So $\sin^4x=\frac18$, $\sin^2y=1$, $\sin^4z=\frac12$.
In $[0,2\pi]$: $\sin x=\pm8^{-1/4}$ has 2 solutions for each sign; $\sin y=\pm1$ has 1 for each sign; $\sin z=\pm2^{-1/4}$ has 2 for each sign.
Sign patterns of $(\sin x,\sin y,\sin z)$ with a positive product: $(+,+,+),(+,-,-),(-,+,-),(-,-,+)$. Each gives $2\cdot1\cdot2=4$ triples.
Total $=4\times4=16$. Answer: (C)
solutions.focus_note: The usual slip is to drop the sign condition and count all 32 sign choices. The product of the sines must be positive, because the right side is $16\sin x\sin y\sin z$, not $16|\sin x\sin y\sin z|$.

solutions.key_idea: Normal at $t$ meets again at $-t-\frac2t$; $90^\circ$ at the vertex gives $t^2=2$.
solutions.full_html:
For chord $t_1t_2$ to subtend $90^\circ$ at the vertex, $t_1t_2=-4$; with $t_2=-t-\frac2t$: $t^2=2$.
With $t=\sqrt2$: $P(2a,2\sqrt2a)$, $Q(-2a,0)$, $R(8a,-4\sqrt2a)$.
$PQ=\sqrt{16+8}\,a=2\sqrt6\,a$ (A true). $PR=\sqrt{36+72}\,a=6\sqrt3\,a$ (B true).
Area $=\frac12|PQ|\,|PR|$ (tangent ⊥ normal) $=\frac12\cdot2\sqrt6\cdot6\sqrt3\,a^2=18\sqrt2\,a^2$ (C true).
Answer: (A), (B), (C)
solutions.focus_note: Keep the parameter facts ready: normal at $t$ meets again at $-t-\frac2t$; a chord subtends $90^\circ$ at the vertex iff $t_1t_2=-4$.

solutions.key_idea: $(k^2+5k+7)(k+2)!=(k+4)(k+4)!-(k+3)(k+3)!$-type difference; the sum telescopes to $(n+3)(n+3)!$.
solutions.focus_note: With factorials, always try writing the term as $F(k+1)-F(k)$ with $F(k)=(k+2)(k+2)!$ or similar. The added $3\cdot3!$ is the hint that the sum starts with a $-3\cdot3!$.

solutions.key_idea: Each row separately: H.P. identity, double geometric sum, a limit, and the period of the given sequence.
solutions.full_html:
(A) For the H.M., $\frac{H+p}{H-p}+\frac{H+q}{H-q}=2$, so the value is $3\times2=6$, so (P).
(B) The double sum factors: $\left(\sum\frac1{2^n}\right)\left(\sum\frac k{2^k}\right)=1\cdot2=2$, so (S).
(C) $x\sin(\sin x)-\sin^2x=x^6\left(\frac1{10}-\frac2{45}\right)+\cdots=\frac{x^6}{18}+\cdots$, so $L=\frac1{18}$ and $72L=4$, so (R).
(D) $f$ is $x-2n$ on $[2n,2n+1)$ and $\frac12$ on $[2n+1,2n+2)$: the pattern repeats every $2$, so (S).
A–P, B–S, C–R, D–S. Answer: (B)
solutions.focus_note: For (C), expand to order $x^6$ carefully: the $x^2$ and $x^4$ terms cancel, and that is the whole point.

solutions.key_idea: Complete the square: $\int_0^1\left(g-2x^2\right)^2dx=0$, so $g(x)=2x^2$.
solutions.full_html:
$\int_0^1(g-2x^2)^2dx=\int_0^14x^4dx-\int_0^1g(4x^2-g)dx=\frac45-\frac45=0$, and $g$ is continuous, so $g(x)=2x^2$.
Mean of $g(2^{-k})$, $k=1..10$: $$\frac1{10}\sum_{k=1}^{10}\frac2{4^k}=\frac15\cdot\frac{\frac14\left(1-4^{-10}\right)}{3/4}=\frac1{15}\left(1-\frac1{2^{20}}\right).$$$m=15$, $n=20$, $m+n=35$. Answer: 35
solutions.focus_note: An integral condition with a single value and a "square" hidden in it is a completing-the-square trick: the integrand must be zero.

solutions.key_idea: Sketch $h(x)=\frac{e^{-x}}{1+x}$: decreasing on $(-1,\infty)$; on $x<-1$ it has a maximum $-e^2$ at $x=-2$.
hints: On $(-1,\infty)$, $f$ falls from $+\infty$ to $0$. On $(-\infty,-1)$ it rises to $-e^2$ at $x=-2$, then falls to $-\infty$.
solutions.full_html:
$f'(x)=-\frac{e^{-x}}{1+x}-\frac{e^{-x}}{(1+x)^2}=-\frac{e^{-x}(x+2)}{(1+x)^2}$.
On $(-1,\infty)$: $f'<0$; $f\to+\infty$ as $x\to-1^+$ and $f\to0^+$ as $x\to\infty$. Range $(0,\infty)$, each value taken once.
On $(-\infty,-1)$: $f<0$; $f\to-\infty$ at both ends; maximum at $x=-2$: $f(-2)=\frac{e^2}{-1}=-e^2$. Range $(-\infty,-e^2]$, each value below $-e^2$ taken twice.
So: $\lambda>0$: exactly one root, so (C) is true. $\lambda<-e^2$: two roots, so (B) is true. $-e^2<\lambda\le0$: no root; since $-e>-e^2$, (D) is true.
Answer: (B), (C), (D)

wrong_options.A: For $\lambda>0$ only the branch on $(-1,\infty)$ is positive, and it is strictly decreasing there, so there is exactly one root, not two.

solutions.focus_note: Root-counting = graph-sketching. Always split at points where the function is undefined, and compare the given numbers ($-e$ vs $-e^2$) carefully.
solutions.note_html: For $x<-1$ the local maximum is $-e^2$ at $x=-2$.

solutions.key_idea: Write the numerator of $11I+2J$ as $A\cdot(\text{denominator})+B\cdot(\text{derivative of denominator})+C$.
hints: With $D=3\sin x+4\cos x+25$, $D'=3\cos x-4\sin x$: solve $2\sin x+11\cos x+50=\alpha D+\beta D'$.
solutions.full_html:
$11I+2J=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{2\sin x+11\cos x+50}{D}dx$ with $D=3\sin x+4\cos x+25$.
Match $2\sin x+11\cos x+50=\alpha D+\beta D'$: $3\alpha-4\beta=2$, $4\alpha+3\beta=11$, $25\alpha=50$, giving $\alpha=2$, $\beta=1$ (and the constant term matches exactly).
$$11I+2J=\int_0^{\pi/2}\left(2+\frac{D'}D\right)dx=\pi+\Big[\ln D\Big]_0^{\pi/2}=\pi+\ln\frac{28}{29}.$$So $a=1,b=1,c=28,d=29$ and $a+b+c+d-55=4$. Answer: 4
solutions.focus_note: Numerator $=\alpha(\text{denominator})+\beta(\text{its derivative})$ is the standard move for $\frac{p\sin x+q\cos x+r}{a\sin x+b\cos x+c}$. The question combines $I$ and $J$ so that the leftover constant is exactly $0$.

solutions.key_idea: Differentiate each candidate answer, or use trig/hyperbolic substitutions for each integral.
solutions.full_html:
(I) $\frac{a^2+x^2}{2a^2(a^2-x^2)^2}=\frac1{(a^2-x^2)^2}-\frac1{2a^2(a^2-x^2)}$ ✓, so (P).
(II) $x=a\sec\theta$: $\int\frac{a\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta}{a^2\sec^2\theta\cdot a\tan\theta}=\frac1{a^2}\sin\theta=\frac{\sqrt{x^2-a^2}}{a^2x}$, so (Q).
(III) $x=a\sin\theta$: $\int\cot^2\theta\,d\theta=-\cot\theta-\theta=-\frac{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}x-\sin^{-1}\frac xa$, which is (R) up to a constant ($\cos^{-1}=\frac\pi2-\sin^{-1}$), so (R).
(IV) $x=a\sec\theta$: $a\int\tan^2\theta\,d\theta=a(\tan\theta-\theta)=\sqrt{x^2-a^2}-a\sec^{-1}\frac xa$, so (S).
Answer: (B)
solutions.focus_note: In matching questions with antiderivatives, differentiating the options is often faster than integrating. Answers can differ by a constant, like $\cos^{-1}$ vs $-\sin^{-1}$.

solutions.key_idea: Plane through the line: $P_1+\lambda P_2=0$; perpendicularity to the third plane fixes $\lambda$.
solutions.full_html:
$(2+\lambda,3+\lambda,-1-2\lambda)\cdot(3,-1,-2)=5+6\lambda=0$, so $\lambda=-\frac56$.
Multiplying by $6$: $(12-5)x+(18-5)y+(-6+10)z+(6-15)=0$, i.e. $7x+13y+4z-9=0$. This matches $lx+13y+mz+n=0$ with $l=7$, $m=4$, $n=-9$.
$$\frac{l-n}m=\frac{16}4=4.$$ Answer: 4
solutions.focus_note: Scale the plane so its $y$-coefficient is exactly $13$ before reading off $l,m,n$; the sign of $n$ is where most slips happen.

solutions.key_idea: $S'P=7$ gives $SP=3$ and $P$; $Q$ is the reflection of $S$ in the tangent at $P$, lying on $S'P$ produced with $S'Q=2a$.
hints: The tangent bisects the angle between $SP$ and $S'P$ externally, so the reflection of $S$ in it lies on line $S'P$.
solutions.full_html:
$S'P=5+\frac45x=7$, so $P=\left(\frac52,\frac{3\sqrt3}2\right)$.
The tangent at $P$ is the external bisector of $\angle SPS'$, so the image of $S$ in the tangent lies on $S'P$ produced; that point is $Q$, with $PQ=PS=10-7=3$ and $S'Q=10$.
(A) $PQ=3$: true. (D) $S'Q=10$ always, so $Q$ moves on the circle centre $S'$, radius 10: true.
(B) Tangent: $\frac{x}{10}+\frac{\sqrt3y}{6}=1$; distance of $S(4,0)$ from it is $\frac{3\sqrt3}{\sqrt7}$, so $SQ=\frac{6\sqrt3}{\sqrt7}$, not $\frac{3\sqrt3}{\sqrt7}$: not true.
(C) Slope $=-\frac{b^2x}{a^2y}=-\frac{\sqrt3}5$, not $+\frac{\sqrt3}5$: not true.
Answer: (B), (C) (the statements that are NOT true)

wrong_options.A: $PQ=PS=2a-S'P=3$, so (A) is true, and a "NOT true" question must not include it.
wrong_options.D: $S'Q=2a=10$ for every $P$, so the locus really is that circle: (D) is true.

solutions.focus_note: Read "NOT true" twice and mark the false statements. The reflection property of the ellipse turns this into a one-line question about $S'Q=2a$.
solutions.note_html: $P=\left(\frac52,\frac{3\sqrt3}2\right)$; $Q$ is the image of $S$ in the tangent, so $SQ=\frac{6\sqrt3}{\sqrt7}$ and the slope is $-\frac{\sqrt3}5$.

solutions.key_idea: Find the plane, then reflect $A$ in it; the shortest path meets the plane on line $A'B$.
hints: Image of $A$: $A'=(2,0,-2)$. The minimising $P$ is where $A'B$ meets the plane.
solutions.focus_note: Same side → reflect one point (shortest path); opposite sides → join directly. Check sides first.

solutions.key_idea: The asymptotes are $(x-1)(y-2)=0$, so $H$ and $H'$ are $(x-1)(y-2)=\pm k$; $(3,0)$ fixes the conjugate.
hints: Shift $X=x-1$, $Y=y-2$. For $XY=c$, $a^2=2|c|$, $ae=a\sqrt2$, and the transverse axis is $Y=X$ ($c>0$) or $Y=-X$ ($c<0$).
solutions.full_html:
A hyperbola and its conjugate have the same asymptotes: $H:(x-1)(y-2)=c$, $H':(x-1)(y-2)=-c$. $H'$ passes through $(3,0)$: $-c=-4$, so $c=4$.
Both are rectangular, so $e=\sqrt2$: (A) is true.
With $X=x-1,Y=y-2$: $H$ is $XY=4$, transverse axis $Y=X$, i.e. $x-y+1=0$: (D) is true.
For $XY=4$: $a^2=8$, $ae=4$; foci of $H$ at $(X,Y)=\pm(2\sqrt2,2\sqrt2)$, i.e. $(1\pm2\sqrt2,\ 2\pm2\sqrt2)$. Foci of $H'$: $(1\pm2\sqrt2,\ 2\mp2\sqrt2)$.
Answer: (A), (D)

wrong_options.B: $\left(2+\frac1{\sqrt2},2+\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)$ lies on $y=x$, but the transverse axis of $H'$ is $Y=-X$; the foci of $H'$ are $(1\pm2\sqrt2,\ 2\mp2\sqrt2)$.
wrong_options.C: The foci of $H$ are $(1+2\sqrt2,\,2+2\sqrt2)$ and $(1-2\sqrt2,\,2-2\sqrt2)$; $(\sqrt2,-\sqrt2)$ is not one of them.

solutions.focus_note: For $xy=c^2$-type hyperbolas, shift to the centre first. The transverse axis is the asymptote-bisector on the side where the curve lies.

solutions.key_idea: Solve separately for $y\ge0$ and $y<0$: $f=e^x-1$ for $x\ge0$, $1-e^{-x}$ for $x<0$.
solutions.full_html:
Since $y'=|y|+1>0$, $f$ is increasing with $f(0)=0$.
$x\ge0$: $y'=y+1$, $y=e^x-1$. $x<0$: $y'=1-y$, $y=1-e^{-x}$.
On $[-1,1]$ the range is $[1-e,\ e-1]\approx[-1.72,\,1.72]$, containing the integers $-1,0,1$. Answer: 3
solutions.focus_note: With $|y|$ in a differential equation, first find the sign of $y$ on each side, then solve two linear equations.

solutions.key_idea: Graph $f$ (increasing through the origin) against $\sin2x$; intersections only near the origin.
hints: $f(-x)=-f(x)$ (from the two formulas), and $\sin2x$ is odd too, so roots come in $\pm$ pairs with $0$ a root.
For $x>0$: $e^x-1=\sin2x$ has exactly one positive root (about $0.68$), since $e^x-1$ starts below $\sin2x$ (slope $1<2$) and soon exceeds $1$.
solutions.full_html:
Both $f$ and $\sin2x$ are odd, so the roots are $0$ and pairs $\pm\alpha$.
For $x>0$: near $0$, $\sin2x>e^x-1$ (slopes $2$ vs $1$); $e^x-1$ reaches $1$ at $x=\ln2<\frac\pi2$ and keeps growing, while $\sin 2x\le1$. Exactly one crossing, at $\alpha\approx0.68\in(0,1)$.
Roots: $-\alpha,0,\alpha$. $[-\alpha]+[0]+[\alpha]=-1+0+0=-1$, absolute value $1$. Answer: 1
solutions.focus_note: Greatest integer of a negative non-integer goes down: $[-0.68]=-1$. Use oddness to halve the work.

solutions.key_idea: The second region is the unit disc centred at $(2,1)$; remove the part inside the square $|x-1|+|y-1|<1$.
hints: $|x-1|+|y-1|=1$ is a square with vertices $(2,1),(1,2),(0,1),(1,0)$; $(2,1)$ is the centre of the disc.
solutions.full_html:
The second condition is the disc $(x-2)^2+(y-1)^2\le1$ (centre $(2,1)$, radius $1$).
$|x-1|+|y-1|\ge1$ is the outside of the square with vertices $(2,1),(1,2),(0,1),(1,0)$. The sides through $(2,1)$, $x+y=3$ and $x-y=1$, are perpendicular, and each has length $\sqrt2>1$. So the part of the disc inside the square is exactly a quarter-disc.
$$\lambda=\pi-\frac\pi4=\frac{3\pi}4,\qquad\frac{8\lambda}\pi=6.$$ Answer: 6
solutions.focus_note: Draw both curves first. A rotated square $|x-a|+|y-b|=k$ has right-angled corners, so a disc centred at a corner loses exactly a quarter (if the radius is smaller than the side).
solutions.note_html: Disc $(x-2)^2+(y-1)^2\le1$ minus the quarter-disc inside the square's corner at $(2,1)$: $\lambda=\tfrac{3\pi}4$.

solutions.key_idea: Volume of the parallelepiped on cross products is $[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]^2$ times the coefficients; compute the box product.
hints: $[\vec b\times\vec c\ \ \vec c\times\vec a\ \ \vec a\times\vec b]=[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]^2$, so $V=\frac16\cdot24[\vec a\vec b\vec c]^2$.
With $\vec u=\vec a-2\hat i$: $\vec u+\vec b+\vec c=\vec0$ (sums of $\sin,\cos$ over angles $2\pi/3$ apart vanish). So $[\vec a\vec b\vec c]=[2\hat i\ \vec b\ \vec c]$.
solutions.full_html:
Volume. $V=\frac16\left[2\vec b\times\vec c\ \ 3\vec c\times\vec a\ \ 4\vec a\times\vec b\right]=\frac{24}6[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]^2=4[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]^2$.
The box product. $\vec u=(\sin\theta,\cos\theta,\sin2\theta)$, $\vec b$, $\vec c$ are the same vector at angles $\theta,\theta\pm\frac{2\pi}3$, so $\vec u+\vec b+\vec c=\vec0$ and $[\vec u\,\vec b\,\vec c]=0$. Hence, writing $\alpha=\theta+\frac{2\pi}3$, $\beta=\theta-\frac{2\pi}3$:$$[\vec a\vec b\vec c]=2(\cos\alpha\sin2\beta-\sin2\alpha\cos\beta)=4\cos\alpha\cos\beta(\sin\beta-\sin\alpha).$$$\sin\beta-\sin\alpha=-\sqrt3\cos\theta$ and $\cos\alpha\cos\beta=\frac12\left(\cos2\theta-\frac12\right)$, so $[\vec a\vec b\vec c]=-2\sqrt3\cos\theta\left(\cos2\theta-\frac12\right)$.
Maximise. With $t=\cos^2\theta\in(0,1)$: $V=48t\left(2t-\frac32\right)^2=12\,t(4t-3)^2$.
$\frac{d}{dt}\big[t(4t-3)^2\big]=(4t-3)(12t-3)=0$ at $t=\frac14$, where $t(4t-3)^2=1$. (At $t\to1$ the value also tends to $1$, but that end is not reached in the open interval.)
So $V_{\max}=12$ (at $\theta=\frac\pi3$). Answer: 12
solutions.focus_note: Two facts to keep ready: $[\vec b\times\vec c\ \vec c\times\vec a\ \vec a\times\vec b]=[\vec a\vec b\vec c]^2$, and the "three angles $2\pi/3$ apart sum to zero" trick. The slip is forgetting the factor $\frac16$ for a tetrahedron.
solutions.note_html: Volume $=\frac{24}6[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]^2$; maximised numerically: $12$.

solutions.key_idea: Reflect the vertex in the angle bisector to get a point on the opposite side; combine with the median's midpoint condition.
hints: Neither line passes through $A(3,-1)$, so the bisector is from $B$ and the median from $C$ (or the other way round, which gives the same triangle).
Mirror image of $A$ in $x-4y+10=0$ is $A'(1,7)$; $B=(4t-10,t)$ and the midpoint of $AB$ is on the median.
solutions.full_html:
Mirror image. $A'=(3,-1)-\frac{2(3+4+10)}{17}(1,-4)=(1,7)$; it lies on line $BC$.
Vertex $B$. $B=(4t-10,t)$. Midpoint of $AB$: $\left(\frac{4t-7}2,\frac{t-1}2\right)$ on $6x+10y=59$: $12t-21+5t-5=59$, so $t=5$ and $B=(10,5)$.
Side $BC$ (through $B$ and $A'$): $2x+9y-65=0$.
Vertex $C$: $2x+9y=65$ and $6x+10y=59$ give $C=\left(-\frac72,8\right)$.
Sides: $AB: 6x-7y-25=0$; $AC: 18x+13y-41=0$; $BC: 2x+9y-65=0$.
Answer: (B), (C), (D)

wrong_options.A: $6x+7y-13=0$ is not a side: it doesn't pass through $B(10,5)$ or $C\left(-\frac72,8\right)$, and not through $A$ either ($18-7-13\ne0$).

solutions.focus_note: The two standard tools: the mirror image of a vertex in an angle bisector lies on the opposite side, and a median passes through the midpoint. Decide first which vertex each line comes from.

solutions.key_idea: Find $Q,R$ from $t_1t_2=6$, $t_1+t_2=5$; a circle tangent at $Q$ through $S$ has its centre on the normal at $Q$.
hints: For $Q(t^2,2t)$, a circle tangent at $Q$ through $S(1,0)$: the centre is on the normal, equidistant from $Q$ and $S$.
solutions.focus_note: Tangency at a point = centre on the normal at that point. Keep the parameter form $(t^2,2t)$ and the normal $y=-tx+2t+t^3$ ready.

solutions.key_idea: Each row: weighted AM–GM, calculus on $x<0$, a beta-type maximum, and a cubic's range.
hints: (P): split $49a$ into three equal parts, $3b$ into two: $49a+3b+c\ge6\sqrt[6]{\left(\frac{49a}3\right)^3\left(\frac{3b}2\right)^2c}$.
(S): $7x+5y\ge12\sqrt[12]{x^7y^5}$; the condition holds for all $x,y$ exactly when $a\ge1$.
solutions.full_html:
(P) $49a+3b+c\ge6\left(\frac{49^3\cdot9}{27\cdot4}a^3b^2c\right)^{1/6}=6\left(\frac{49^3\cdot9\cdot12}{108}\right)^{1/6}=6\cdot7^{1}=42$, so (5).
(Q) For $x<0$: $\left|2x^3-\frac3{x^2}\right|=|x|^3+|x|^3+\frac1{x^2}+\frac1{x^2}+\frac1{x^2}\ge5$, equality at $|x|=1$, so (2).
(R) $x^5(8-x^3)$: with $t=x^3$, maximise $t^{5/3}(8-t)$: at $t=5$, value $5^{5/3}\cdot3$; divided by $25^{1/3}=5^{2/3}$ gives $15$, so (4).
(S) $7x+5y\ge12(x^7y^5)^{1/12}=12a^{1/12}$; this is $\ge12$ for all such $x,y$ iff $a\ge1$. Minimum $a=1$, so (1).
P–5, Q–2, R–4, S–1. Answer: (D)
solutions.focus_note: Weighted AM–GM: split each term into as many equal parts as its power in the constraint. Check equality is reachable.

solutions.key_idea: $P_n=\frac23P_{n-1}+\frac13P_{n-2}$ (score 1 with probability $\frac46$, score 2 with $\frac26$); then $P_n-P_{n-1}=-\frac13(P_{n-1}-P_{n-2})$.
hints: A perfect square on a die (1 or 4) has probability $\frac13$ and scores 2; otherwise ($\frac23$) the score is 1.
To reach exactly $n$, the last step came from $n-1$ (scoring 1) or $n-2$ (scoring 2).
solutions.focus_note: The squares on a die are $1$ and $4$ (two faces). Watch the order $P_8-P_9$ in the denominator: it flips the sign.

solutions.key_idea: The window $[x,x^2+x+1]$ contains 1 iff $x\le1\le x^2+x+1$; otherwise the minimum is at the nearer end.
hints: For $-1<x<0$ the interval lies left of $1$, so the minimum is $f(x^2+x+1)$; for $x>1$ it is $f(x)$.
solutions.full_html:
$$g(x)=\begin{cases}2,&x\le-1\\ 2-x-x^2,&-11\end{cases}$$All pieces agree at $-1,0,1$, so $g$ is continuous: (A) is true.
Slopes: at $-1$: $0$ vs $1$; at $0$: $-1$ vs $0$; at $1$: $0$ vs $1$. So $g$ is not differentiable at $-1,0,1$: (B) and (C) are true.
Answer: (A), (B), (C)

wrong_options.D: At $x=1$ both sides give $2$, so $g$ is continuous there (it just has a corner).

solutions.focus_note: For "min over a moving interval", first find when the interval contains the minimum point of $f$; outside that, use the nearer endpoint.

solutions.key_idea: Integrate by parts twice to move from $f''$ back to $\int e^{-2x}f$, using the boundary values.
solutions.full_html:
$\left[e^{-2x}f'\right]_0^{\ln2}=\frac14\cdot4-3=-2$. $\left[e^{-2x}f\right]_0^{\ln2}=\frac14\cdot6=\frac32$.
$$\int_0^{\ln2}e^{-2x}f''dx=-2+2\left(\frac32+2\cdot3\right)=-2+15=13.$$ Answer: 13
solutions.focus_note: $e^{-2\ln2}=\frac14$. Keep the signs: each parts step gives $+2\int$ because $\frac{d}{dx}e^{-2x}=-2e^{-2x}$.

solutions.key_idea: $4n^2(1-\cos\frac xn)\to2x^2$ and $\frac{n^2}2\ln\cos\frac{2x}n\to-x^2$; expand to order $x^6$.
solutions.full_html:
$1-\cos\frac xn\approx\frac{x^2}{2n^2}$, so $f(x)=\tan^{-1}(2x^2)$. $\ln\cos\frac{2x}n\approx-\frac{2x^2}{n^2}$, so $g(x)=-x^2$ and $e^{-2g}=e^{2x^2}$.
With $u=2x^2$: $\tan^{-1}u=u-\frac{u^3}3+\cdots$, so $$e^u-e^{\tan^{-1}u}=e^u\left(1-e^{-u^3/3+\cdots}\right)=\frac{u^3}3+\cdots=\frac{8x^6}3+\cdots$$So the limit is $\frac83$. Answer: (A)
solutions.focus_note: Factor out $e^u$ before expanding; then only the difference of the exponents matters. The slip is getting $g$ wrong by a factor of $4$ (the angle is $\frac{2x}n$).

solutions.key_idea: Posterior of each coin after two heads ($\propto p^2$), then predictive probability $\sum p^3/\sum p^2$.
solutions.full_html: $$P(\text{3rd H}\mid\text{HH})=\frac{P(\text{HHH})}{P(\text{HH})}=\frac{\frac1{27}+\frac8{27}+1}{\frac19+\frac49+1}=\frac{36/27}{14/9}=\frac67.$$So $a=6$, $b=7$ and $a^2+b^2=85$. Answer: 85
solutions.focus_note: The three tosses are not independent once you don't know which coin was picked. Don't multiply $P(\text{H})$ three times; condition on the coin.

solutions.key_idea: Tetrahedron volume $=\frac16[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]$ with $[\,]^2=\det$ of the Gram matrix.
solutions.full_html: $[\vec a\vec b\vec c]^2=\begin{vmatrix}1&c&c\\c&1&c\\c&c&1\end{vmatrix}=1-3c^2+2c^3$ with $c=\frac{\sqrt3}2$:$$1-\frac94+\frac{3\sqrt3}4=\frac{3\sqrt3-5}4.$$Volume of the tetrahedron $=\frac16\sqrt{\frac{3\sqrt3-5}4}=\frac{\sqrt{3\sqrt3-5}}{12}$. Answer: (A)
solutions.focus_note: The Gram determinant $[\vec a\vec b\vec c]^2=\det(\vec u_i\cdot\vec u_j)$ handles every "equal angles" box-product question. Remember $\frac16$ for a tetrahedron, $1$ for a parallelepiped.

solutions.key_idea: The distance between the parallel lines is $\frac{\text{plane gap}}{\sin\theta}$ where $\theta$ is the angle between the third plane and the parallel planes.
solutions.full_html:
Both lines lie in the third plane. In that plane they are parallel, and their separation is the gap between the two parallel planes divided by $\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the third plane and the parallel planes.
Gap $=\frac{7}{2\sqrt3}$; $\cos\theta=\frac{-2}{\sqrt{90}}$, $\sin^2\theta=\frac{86}{90}$.
$$d^2=\frac{49/12}{86/90}=\frac{735}{172},\qquad d\approx2.07.$$$[d]=2$. Answer: 2
solutions.focus_note: Draw a cross-section perpendicular to the lines: you get two parallel lines (the planes) cut by a slanted line (the third plane). Divide by $\sin\theta$, not multiply.
The derivative of an inverse is $1/f'$ evaluated at the preimage. Find the preimages first.

solutions.key_idea: Put $t=x^2+1$: $\frac{x^4}{t}=t-2+\frac1t$, so the base is $t+\frac1t$; expand and read off the polynomial part's constant.
hints: With $u=x^2+1$: $\left(u+\frac1u\right)^{10}=\sum\binom{10}k u^{10-2k}$; the polynomial part is $\sum_{k\le5}\binom{10}k u^{10-2k}$.
solutions.full_html: $2+\frac{x^4}{x^2+1}=u+\frac1u$ with $u=x^2+1$. So $$\left(u+\frac1u\right)^{10}=\sum_{k=0}^{10}\binom{10}ku^{10-2k}.$$Terms with $10-2k\ge0$ ($k\le5$) are polynomials in $x$; the rest are the $\frac{B_j}{(x^2+1)^j}$ part. The constant term of $u^m=(x^2+1)^m$ is $1$, so$$A_0=\sum_{k=0}^5\binom{10}k=1+10+45+120+210+252=638.$$ Answer: 638
solutions.focus_note: The substitution $u=x^2+1$ makes the split into polynomial and fractional parts obvious. Include $k=5$ ($u^0=1$) in the polynomial part.

solutions.key_idea: Start from $\binom{20}2$; subtract pairs among the 5 parallel lines and merge the $\binom52$ intersections at $A$ into one.
hints: The two families $\{L_4,L_8,\dots,L_{20}\}$ and $\{L_1,L_5,\dots,L_{17}\}$ have no line in common.
Five parallel lines lose $\binom52$ points; five concurrent lines give $1$ point instead of $\binom52$.
solutions.full_html:
With all 20 lines in general position we would get $\binom{20}2=190$ points.
• The 5 parallel lines never meet each other: lose $\binom52=10$.
• The 5 lines through $A$ meet in a single point instead of $10$ different points: lose $10-1=9$.
Every other pair can still be made to meet at a new point, so the maximum is $$190-10-9=171.$$ Answer: 171
solutions.focus_note: Check that the two special families don't overlap (they don't: indices $\equiv0$ and $\equiv1\pmod4$). For the concurrent family, subtract $\binom52-1$, not $\binom52$.

solutions.key_idea: From $(E+M)^T=17(E-M)^T$: $M=\frac89E$; then $(EM)^T=20I$ gives $E^2$.
solutions.full_html:
$(E+M)^T=17(E-M)^T\Rightarrow E+M=17(E-M)\Rightarrow M=\frac89E$.
$(EM)^T=M^TE^T=\frac89(E^2)^T=20I$, so $E^2=\frac{45}2I$.
$$E^2+M^2=\left(1+\frac{64}{81}\right)\frac{45}2I=\frac{145}{81}\cdot\frac{45}2I=\frac{725}{18}I.$$$a+b=725+18=743$. Answer: 743
solutions.focus_note: Take transposes off both sides first; the rest is scalar algebra because $M$ is a multiple of $E$.

solutions.key_idea: Put $h=fe^{-x}$: $h(xy)=h(x)+h(y)$, so $h=k\ln x$ and $f=e^x\ln x$ (from $f'(1)=e$).
solutions.full_html:
Dividing by $e^{xy}$: $h(xy)=h(x)+h(y)$ with $h(x)=f(x)e^{-x}$. Differentiable solutions: $h(x)=k\ln x$. Then $h(1)=0$, so $f(1)=0$, and $h'(1)=e^{-1}\big(f'(1)-f(1)\big)=1=k$. So $$f(x)=e^x\ln x.$$(A) The limit is the derivative of $e^x(\ln x-1)$ at $x=e$: $e^e(1-1)+e^e\cdot\frac1e=e^{e-1}$. True.
(C) On $[1,e]$, $e^x\ln x(D) $f'(x)=e^x\left(\ln x+\frac1x\right)$, and $\ln x+\frac1x\ge1>0$ (minimum at $x=1$). Strictly increasing. True.
Answer: (A), (C), (D)

wrong_options.B: $f(x)=xe^x$ means $\ln x=x$, which has no solution ($\ln x<x$ for all $x>0$). So there are $0$ solutions, not $2$.

solutions.focus_note: Functional equations with exponential factors: look for the substitution that turns them into Cauchy's $h(xy)=h(x)+h(y)$.
solutions.note_html: $h=fe^{-x}$ satisfies $h(xy)=h(x)+h(y)$, so $f=e^x\ln x$. (B): $\ln x=x$ has no root.

solutions.key_idea: $\angle C$ is twice the angle between side $CB$ and the bisector; get $\tan\frac C2$ from the slopes, then double it.
hints: Slope of $CB$ is $\frac{13}{6}$; the internal bisector at $C$ has slope $3$.
solutions.full_html:
Angle $\phi$ between $CB$ (slope $\frac{13}6$) and the bisector (slope $3$): $\tan\phi=\frac{3-\frac{13}6}{1+3\cdot\frac{13}6}=\frac{5/6}{45/6}=\frac19$.
$$\tan C=\tan2\phi=\frac{2/9}{1-1/81}=\frac{2/9}{80/81}=\frac9{40}.$$$p+q=49$. Answer: 49
solutions.focus_note: Use the internal bisector (not the external) for half of $\angle C$, and the double-angle formula.

solutions.key_idea: Arrange the 6 consonants first, then place the 4 vowels in gaps that leave at least two consonants between them; divide for repeated letters.
hints: DARJEELING: vowels A, E, E, I (4); consonants D, R, J, L, N, G (6).
Vowel positions $p_1<p_2<p_3<p_4$ in $1..10$ with gaps $\ge3$: substitute $q_i=p_i-2(i-1)$.
solutions.full_html:
With $q_i=p_i-2(i-1)$, we need $1\le q_1Arrange vowels: $\frac{4!}{2!}=12$ (two E's). Consonants: $6!=720$. $N=12\cdot720=8640$.
Digit sum of $8640$ is $18$, and of $18$ is $9$. Answer: 9
solutions.focus_note: The gap substitution turns "at least $k$ between" into a plain choice. Don't forget the repeated E.

solutions.key_idea: Compare degrees: $f$ is linear, $f=2x+b$; matching coefficients gives $b=1$, $p=5$.
hints: If $\deg f=n$, then $\deg f(f(f(x)))=n^3$. The identity can only hold if $n^3\le n$, so $n=1$.
solutions.full_html:
If $\deg f=n\ge2$, then $f(f(f(x)))$ has degree $n^3>n$ and nothing can cancel it, so $f$ is linear: $f=2x+b$.
$f(f(f(x)))=8x+7b$, so $8x+7b+(1-p)(2x+b)=3$ for all $x$:
$x$: $8+2(1-p)=0$, so $p=5$. Constant: $7b-4b=3$, so $b=1$. Thus $f(x)=2x+1$.
$f(f(x))=4x+3$, so $\frac{d}{dx}f(f(x))=4$ (at any $x$, including $x=5$).
$f^{-1}(x)=\frac{x-1}2$, so $2f^{-1}(x)+1=x$ and $\int_{-5}^5x\,dx=0$.
Total $=4+0=4$. Answer: (C)
solutions.focus_note: Degree comparison is the first move for any polynomial functional equation. Then the integral is of an odd function over a symmetric interval, so it vanishes.

solutions.key_idea: All roots are positive (signs) with product $\frac32$ and $\sum\frac1{x_i}$-type sum; weighted AM–GM equality fixes the roots.
hints: Signs alternate and $a,b,c>0$, so no root is negative (and $0$ is not a root): all four roots are positive. Their product is $\frac64=\frac32$.
solutions.full_html:
Replacing $x$ by $-x$ gives $4x^4+ax^3+bx^2+cx+6$, all coefficients positive, so there is no negative root. Hence $x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4>0$ and $$x_1x_2x_3x_4=\frac64=\frac32.$$By AM–GM, $$\frac1{x_1}+\frac2{x_2}+\frac3{x_3}+\frac4{x_4}\ \ge\ 4\sqrt[4]{\frac{1\cdot2\cdot3\cdot4}{x_1x_2x_3x_4}}=4\sqrt[4]{\frac{24}{3/2}}=4\sqrt[4]{16}=8.$$The sum is given to be $8$, so equality holds: each term equals $2$. So $x_1=\frac12,\ x_2=1,\ x_3=\frac32,\ x_4=2$ (distinct, in increasing order, and $4(x-\frac12)(x-1)(x-\frac32)(x-2)$ does have positive $a,b,c$).
$$\frac{x_4}{x_1}=\frac{2}{1/2}=4.$$ Answer: (C)
solutions.focus_note: Whenever a symmetric-looking condition gives one exact number, test whether it is the AM–GM (or Cauchy) bound. Don't forget to justify that all the roots are positive before using AM–GM.
solutions.note_html: All roots positive, product $\frac32$; AM–GM equality: roots $\frac12,1,\frac32,2$.

solutions.key_idea: Find $P,Q$ from the two curves; tangents meet the $x$-axis at $R$ and $S$; compute the quadrilateral area.
hints: Ellipse tangent at $P$ meets the axis at $x=\frac{a^2}{x_1}=6$; parabola tangent at $P$ meets it at $x=-x_1=-\frac32$.
solutions.full_html:
$P=\left(\frac32,\sqrt3\right)$, $Q=\left(\frac32,-\sqrt3\right)$. $R=(6,0)$ (ellipse tangents), $S=\left(-\frac32,0\right)$ (parabola tangents).
The diagonals $RS$ (length $\frac{15}2$) and $PQ$ (length $2\sqrt3$) are perpendicular: $$A=\frac12\cdot\frac{15}2\cdot2\sqrt3=\frac{15\sqrt3}2.$$$\frac2{5\sqrt3}A=3$. Answer: 3
solutions.focus_note: Tangent intercepts on the axis: $\frac{a^2}{x_1}$ for an ellipse, $-x_1$ for $y^2=4ax$. Area of a quadrilateral with perpendicular diagonals is half their product.

solutions.key_idea: Put $s=\sqrt x+\frac1{2\sqrt x}$: $x^{3/2}+\frac1{8x^{3/2}}=s^3-\frac32s$ and $x+\frac1{4x}=s^2-1$; minimise the cubic in $s\ge\sqrt2$.
solutions.full_html: With $u=\sqrt x$, $v=\frac1{2\sqrt x}$, $uv=\frac12$: $u^3+v^3=s^3-3uv\,s=s^3-\frac32s$ and $u^2+v^2=s^2-1$. So $$f=s^3-\frac32s-\frac{17}4(s^2-1),\qquad s\ge\sqrt2.$$$\frac{df}{ds}=\frac12(6s^2-17s-3)=\frac12(s-3)(6s+1)$: negative on $[\sqrt2,3)$, positive after. Minimum at $s=3$: $$m=27-\frac92-34=-\frac{23}2.$$$100+2m=77$. Answer: 77
solutions.focus_note: Symmetric expressions in $t$ and $\frac{c}{t}$: substitute their sum. Check that the critical point ($s=3$) is in the allowed range $s\ge\sqrt2$.

solutions.key_idea: $a+b\omega^2+c\omega$ is the conjugate of $z=a+b\omega+c\omega^2$; $z^{2026}=\bar z$ forces $|z|=1$, and $|z|^2$ is the required expression.
solutions.full_html:
Let $z=a+b\omega+c\omega^2$. Then $\bar z=a+b\omega^2+c\omega$, and the equation says $z^{2026}=\bar z$.
$|z|^2=z\bar z=a^2+b^2+c^2-ab-bc-ca=\frac12\left[(a-b)^2+(b-c)^2+(c-a)^2\right]>0$.
Taking moduli: $|z|^{2026}=|z|$ with $|z|\ne0$, so $|z|=1$. The required value is $|z|^2=1$. Answer: 1
solutions.focus_note: Recognise $a^2+b^2+c^2-ab-bc-ca$ as $|a+b\omega+c\omega^2|^2$; it appears often.

solutions.key_idea: Use parametric points $(\frac l4t^2,\frac l2t)$ and compute each projection/length.
hints: (A): the perpendicular to $OP$ at $P$ meets the axis at $x=at^2+4a$.
(B), (D): write the midpoint, eliminate $t$. (C): a tangency condition (discriminant $=0$).
solutions.full_html:
Take $y^2=4ax$ with $4a=l$, $P(at^2,2at)$.
(A) Slope of $OP$ is $\frac2t$; the perpendicular at $P$: $y-2at=-\frac t2(x-at^2)$ meets $y=0$ at $x=at^2+4a$. Projection of $PQ$ on the axis $=4a=l$, so (R).
(B) $G=(2a+at^2,0)$; midpoint of $PG$: $(at^2+a,\ at)$. So $y^2=a(x-a)$, latus rectum $a=\frac l4$, so (P).
(C) The touching parabola opens the other way: $(y-k)^2=-l(x-h)$. Put $x=\frac{y^2}l$: $2y^2-2ky+k^2-lh=0$; tangency $\Rightarrow4k^2-8(k^2-lh)=0\Rightarrow k^2=2lh$. Latus rectum $2l$, so (S).
(D) Midpoint of $SP$: $\left(\frac{at^2+a}2,\ at\right)$, so $y^2=2a\left(x-\frac a2\right)$, latus rectum $2a=\frac l2$, so (Q).
A–R, B–P, C–S, D–Q. Answer: (C)
solutions.focus_note: In matching lists, settle the easiest rows first ((A), (D) here) and eliminate options. Then only one row needs full work.

solutions.key_idea: Units digits of squares repeat with period 10; compute mean and variance over a period (2025 = 202 periods + 5).
solutions.focus_note: Simplify the expression before computing the mean and variance separately; here you never need $p$ or $q$ on their own.

solutions.key_idea: $P$ must match values 0, 1 and slopes 0 at both ends: $P=3x^2-2x^3$.
hints: Four conditions: value and slope must match at $x=0$ and $x=1$.
solutions.full_html:
Differentiability needs $P(0)=0$, $P'(0)=0$, $P(1)=1$, $P'(1)=0$. With $P=ax^2+bx^3$: $a+b=1$, $2a+3b=0$, so $a=3$, $b=-2$.
$$A=\int_0^1(3x^2-2x^3)dx=1-\frac12=\frac12,\qquad6A=3.$$ Answer: 3
solutions.alt_html: $P(x)+P(1-x)=1$ (check it), so the area under $P$ on $[0,1]$ is half the unit square: $A=\frac12$.
solutions.focus_note: Count the conditions to know the least degree (four conditions, but two kill the constant and linear terms). Symmetry $P(x)+P(1-x)=1$ also gives $A=\frac12$ at once.

solutions.key_idea: Each row separately: positivity conditions, domain of $\ln(\cos^{-1}x)$, simplification at allowed $x$, etc.
solutions.full_html:
(P) Solving: $y=\frac{2K^2-K}3$, $x=\frac{4K-2K^2}3$. $x,y>0\iff\frac12(2).
(Q) $\ln(\cos^{-1}x)$ needs $\cos^{-1}x>0$, i.e. $-1\le x<1$: integers $-1,0$. Two, so (3).
(R) Only $x=1$ is allowed. There $\sin^{-1}1=\operatorname{cosec}^{-1}1$, $\cos^{-1}1=\sec^{-1}1$, $\tan^{-1}1=\cot^{-1}1$, so the value is $1$, so (2).
(S) $f\circ f=\text{id}$ for a Möbius map $\frac{x+a}{x+b}$ ($a\ne b$) needs trace $1+b=0$: $b=-1$. Then $a\ne-1$, so $a+b=a-1$ can be anything except $-2$. All of $0,1,2,3,4$ are possible, so (1),(2),(3),(4),(5).
Answer: (B)
solutions.focus_note: Read every row's domain first. (R) looks like heavy algebra but collapses once you see only $x=1$ is allowed.
solutions.note_html: R: only $x=1$ is allowed, value 1. S: $b=-1$, $a+b=a-1$ (any value except $-2$).

solutions.key_idea: Tangents from $(-2,0)$ to the circle: find the points of contact and keep the one with positive coordinates.
hints: Point of contact $(a,b)$: on the circle and $(a-4)(a+2)+(b-8)b=0$.
Subtracting the circle equation gives a line; the positive solution is $(6,4)$.
solutions.full_html:
For $M=(a,b)$: $(a-4)^2+(b-8)^2=20$ and $(a-4)(a+2)+(b-8)(b-0)=0$ (radius ⊥ tangent).
Expanding, the two equations are $a^2+b^2-8a-16b+60=0$ and $a^2+b^2-2a-8b-8=0$; subtracting gives $3a+4b=34$. With the circle: $(a,b)=(6,4)$ or $\left(-\frac25,\frac{44}5\right)$. Positive coordinates: $(6,4)$.
$\frac{12a}b=\frac{72}4=18$. Answer: 18
solutions.focus_note: The chord of contact from $(x_1,y_1)$ is $T=0$; using it directly gives $3a+4b=34$ too.
solutions.note_html: Points of contact from $(-2,0)$: $(6,4)$ and $(-\tfrac25,\tfrac{44}5)$; positive coordinates give $(6,4)$.

solutions.key_idea: Symmetry about $x=-1$ gives $f'(-1)=0$, so both squares vanish: $f(1)=5$, $f(-1)=1$.
solutions.full_html:
The vertex is at $x=-1$, so $f'(-1)=0$, and the sum of squares is $0$: $f(1)=5$, $f(-1)=1$. With $f=a(x+1)^2+c$: $c=1$, $4a+1=5$, so $f=(x+1)^2+1$ and $f\ge1$.
(P) $\sin^{-1}f$ is defined only when $f=1$: $\left[\frac\pi2\right]=1$, so (2).
(Q) $f>0$, so $[1+1]=2$, so (3).
(R) $\frac1f\in(0,1]$, so $\tan^{-1}\frac1f\in\left(0,\frac\pi4\right]$ and its integer part is $0$, so (1).
(S) $2^{-f}\in\left(0,\frac12\right]$, so $\cot^{-1}2^{-f}\in\left[\cot^{-1}\frac12,\frac\pi2\right)\approx[1.11,1.57)$: integer part $1$, so (2).
Answer: (A)
solutions.focus_note: Spot the hidden "sum of squares $=0$". After that each row is just a range question.

solutions.key_idea: Sum-to-product: $2\cos(x^2+\frac x2)\sin\frac x2=\sin x$ reduces to $\cos(x^2+\frac x2)=\cos\frac x2$.
hints: $\sin x=2\sin\frac x2\cos\frac x2$ and $\sin\frac x2\ne0$ on $[2,3]$.
solutions.full_html:
Cancel $2\sin\frac x2\ne0$: $\cos\left(x^2+\frac x2\right)=\cos\frac x2$, so $x^2+\frac x2=2k\pi\pm\frac x2$.
Case $x^2=2k\pi$: in $[2,3]$, $x^2\in[4,9]$, so $k=1$: $x=\sqrt{2\pi}\approx2.51$.
Case $x^2+x=2k\pi$: $x^2+x\in[6,12]$, so $k=1$: $x=\frac{-1+\sqrt{1+8\pi}}2\approx2.06$.
Two solutions. Answer: 2
solutions.focus_note: Before cancelling, check that the factor ($\sin\frac x2$) can't vanish on the interval.
solutions.note_html: Equivalent to $\cos(x^2+\tfrac x2)=\cos\tfrac x2$: $x^2=2\pi$ or $x^2+x=2\pi$ in $[2,3]$.

solutions.key_idea: $x\to\frac4x$ swaps the two terms: $\int_1^2\frac{e^{4/x}}x=\int_2^4\frac{e^x}x$, so $I=\int_1^4\frac{e^x}xdx$.
hints: So $I=\int_1^4\frac{e^x}x\,dx$; the same trick shows $\int_1^4\frac{e^{4/x}}x\,dx=\int_1^4\frac{e^x}x\,dx$ too.
solutions.full_html:
With $x=\frac4t$, $\frac{dx}x=-\frac{dt}t$: $\int_1^2\frac{e^{4/x}}x\,dx=\int_2^4\frac{e^t}t\,dt$. Hence $$I=\int_1^4\frac{e^x}x\,dx.$$(A) On $[1,4]$ the same substitution gives $\int_1^4\frac{e^{4/x}}x\,dx=\int_1^4\frac{e^x}x\,dx=I$, so $\int_1^4\frac{e^x+e^{4/x}}x\,dx=2I$. True.
(C) $I=\int_1^4\frac{e^x}x\,dx>\int_1^2\frac{e^x}{x}dx+\int_2^4\frac{e^x}4dx>\frac{e^4-e^2}4>e^2-e$ (indeed $I\approx17.7$). True.
Answer: (A), (C)

wrong_options.B: The combined integral over $[1,4]$ equals $2I$, not $4I$.

solutions.focus_note: The substitution $x\to\frac{k}{x}$ swaps the limits $1\leftrightarrow k$ and keeps $\frac{dx}x$ (up to sign). Use a quick estimate rather than computing the integral.

solutions.key_idea: $\sin x\sec3x=\frac12(\tan3x-\tan x)$; telescope.
solutions.full_html:
$\tan3x-\tan x=\frac{\sin2x}{\cos3x\cos x}=\frac{2\sin x}{\cos3x}$, so $\sin x\sec3x=\frac12(\tan3x-\tan x)$.
Summing over $x=\theta,3\theta,\dots,3^9\theta$: $$\frac12\left(\tan3^{10}\theta-\tan\theta\right).$$With $\theta=\frac\pi{3^5}$: $3^{10}\theta=3^5\pi$, so $\tan3^{10}\theta=0$. The sum is $-\frac12\tan\frac\pi{3^5}$. Answer: (A)
solutions.focus_note: Telescoping trig sums need the right identity; $\tan A-\tan B=\frac{\sin(A-B)}{\cos A\cos B}$ is the usual one. Don't miss that $3^{10}\theta$ is a multiple of $\pi$.

solutions.key_idea: Treat $x$ as a function of $y$: $\frac{dx}{dy}+\frac x{1+y^2}=\frac{\tan^{-1}y}{1+y^2}$, linear.
hints: Integrating factor $e^{\tan^{-1}y}$; with $u=\tan^{-1}y$ the solution is $x=u-1+Ce^{-u}$.
solutions.focus_note: When $dy$ carries the messy factor, solve for $x$ in terms of $y$.

solutions.key_idea: Write the normals at $\theta$ and $\phi=\frac\pi2-\theta$ and solve; the ordinate simplifies to a constant.
solutions.full_html:
Normal at $P$: $3x\cos\theta+2y\cot\theta=13$. Normal at $Q$ (with $\phi=\frac\pi2-\theta$): $3x\sin\theta+2y\tan\theta=13$.
Multiply the first by $\sin\theta$, the second by $\cos\theta$ and subtract:$$2y\left(\cot\theta\sin\theta-\tan\theta\cos\theta\right)=13(\sin\theta-\cos\theta)\ \Rightarrow\ 2y(\cos\theta-\sin\theta)=13(\sin\theta-\cos\theta).$$Since $P\ne Q$, $\cos\theta\ne\sin\theta$, so $y=-\frac{13}2$ and $|y|=\frac{13}2$. Answer: (C)
solutions.focus_note: The number $13=a^2+b^2$ in the normal of $\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ is worth memorising. Cancelling $(\sin\theta-\cos\theta)$ needs $P\ne Q$, which the question gives.

solutions.key_idea: Inclusion–exclusion: the alternating sum counts something like choosing 10 from 10 pairs with one from each pair: $2^{10}$.
solutions.full_html:
$\binom{20-2k}{10}$ is the coefficient of $x^{10}$ in $(1+x)^{20-2k}$ (and is $0$ for $k>5$). So $S$ is the coefficient of $x^{10}$ in$$\sum_{k=0}^{10}(-1)^k\binom{10}k\big((1+x)^2\big)^{10-k}=\big((1+x)^2-1\big)^{10}=x^{10}(2+x)^{10}.$$Coefficient of $x^{10}$: $2^{10}=1024$.
$1024$ is a four-digit number, so (C) is true. (A): $2^{10}$ has $11$ divisors. (B): digit sum $7$. Answer: (C)
solutions.focus_note: Alternating sums of products of binomials are almost always "coefficient of $x^r$ in a product". Write each factor as a coefficient first.

solutions.key_idea: Recover $\sum x$ and $\sum x^2$ from mean 30, SD 5, remove 12 and 10, recompute.
solutions.focus_note: Work with sums, not with the mean and SD directly. The new mean ($31$) is a whole number, which keeps the arithmetic clean.

solutions.key_idea: Let $a=\frac xy,b=\frac yz,c=\frac zx$ with $abc=1$: the product is $\frac{(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)}{30}$ and $(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)=(a+b+c)(ab+bc+ca)-1$.
solutions.full_html:
Let $a=\frac xy$, $b=\frac yz$, $c=\frac zx$, so $abc=1$, $a+b+c=13-3\sqrt2$ and $ab+bc+ca=\frac xz+\frac yx+\frac zy=13+3\sqrt2$.
The required value is $\frac{a+b}2\cdot\frac{b+c}3\cdot\frac{c+a}5$, and $$(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)=(13-3\sqrt2)(13+3\sqrt2)-1=169-18-1=150.$$So the value is $\frac{150}{30}=5$. Answer: 5
solutions.focus_note: Spot that the second sum is $ab+bc+ca$ (each term is a product of two of $a,b,c$). The identity $(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)=e_1e_2-e_3$ is worth memorising.

solutions.key_idea: Factor $r^4+r^2+1=(r^2+r+1)(r^2-r+1)$ and split the numerator; each part telescopes.
solutions.full_html:
Numerator $=(r^4+r^2+1)+r(r^2+r)$, so the term is $\frac1{r^2+r}+\frac{r}{r^4+r^2+1}$.
$\sum\frac1{r(r+1)}=1$. And $r^4+r^2+1=(r^2-r+1)(r^2+r+1)$ gives $\sum\frac{r}{r^4+r^2+1}=\frac12\sum\left(\frac1{r^2-r+1}-\frac1{r^2+r+1}\right)=\frac12$.
Total $=1.5$. Answer: 1.5
solutions.focus_note: Factor $r^4+r^2+1=(r^2+1)^2-r^2$; it shows up in many telescoping sums.

solutions.key_idea: The normal at $P$ fixes $a,b$; $SM'$ and $S'M$ meet at the midpoint of $P$ and the normal's axis-point-type construction (here on the normal).
hints: Normal at $(x_1,y_1)$: $\frac{a^2x}{x_1}-\frac{b^2y}{y_1}=a^2-b^2$. Compare with $5x-3y=8\sqrt2$ and use that $P$ is on the ellipse: $a=5$, $b=3$.
$SM\parallel S'M'$ (both perpendicular to the tangent), so $SMM'S'$ is a trapezium. Where do its diagonals meet?
solutions.full_html:
Step 1 (the ellipse). The normal at $P$ is $\frac{\sqrt2a^2}{5}x-\frac{\sqrt2b^2}{3}y=a^2-b^2$. Comparing with $5x-3y=8\sqrt2$: $\frac{a^2/5}{b^2/3}=\frac53$, so $a^2:b^2=25:9$. Putting $P$ in the ellipse: $\frac{25}{2a^2}+\frac9{2b^2}=1$ gives $a^2=25$, $b^2=9$, so $c=4$, $S(4,0)$, $S'(-4,0)$.
Step 2 (where the diagonals meet). Let $X=SM'\cap S'M$. In the trapezium $SMM'S'$:
• The focal radii $SP$, $S'P$ make equal angles with the tangent, so $SM:S'M'=SP:S'P=MP:PM'$. The foot of $X$ on the tangent divides $MM'$ in the ratio $SM:S'M'$, so it is $P$ itself: $X$ lies on the normal at $P$.
• The height of $X$ above the tangent is $\frac{SM\cdot S'M'}{SM+S'M'}=\frac{b^2}{2p}$, where $p$ is the perpendicular from the centre to the tangent (because $SM\cdot S'M'=b^2$ and $SM+S'M'=2p$).
• The normal meets the axis at $G$ with $PG=\frac{b^2}{p}$.
So $X$ is the midpoint of $PG$.
Step 3. $G$: put $y=0$ in $5x-3y=8\sqrt2$, so $G=\left(\frac{8\sqrt2}5,0\right)$. Then $$X=\left(\frac12\left(\frac5{\sqrt2}+\frac{8\sqrt2}5\right),\ \frac3{2\sqrt2}\right)=\left(\frac{41}{10\sqrt2},\ \frac3{2\sqrt2}\right).$$ Answer: (C)
solutions.alt_html: Direct coordinates. Tangent at $P$: $3x+5y=15\sqrt2$. Feet of perpendiculars: $M=S-\frac{12-15\sqrt2}{34}(3,5)$, $M'=S'-\frac{-12-15\sqrt2}{34}(3,5)$. Solving the lines $SM'$ and $S'M$ gives $(2.899\ldots,\,1.0607\ldots)=\left(\frac{41}{10\sqrt2},\frac3{2\sqrt2}\right)$.
solutions.focus_note: Remember the three standard tangent facts: $SM\cdot S'M'=b^2$, the feet $M,M'$ lie on the auxiliary circle, and (normal length to the axis)$\times p=b^2$. If a coordinate attempt gets messy, look for these.

solutions.key_idea: Bayes over the four transfer points: luggage lost at a given point means correct transfers before it.
solutions.full_html:
Lost at Dubai means correct at Delhi and Chennai, wrong at Dubai: $\frac{19}{20}\cdot\frac{9}{10}\cdot\frac15=\frac{171}{1000}$.
Reaches Muscat: $\frac{19}{20}\cdot\frac9{10}\cdot\frac45\cdot\frac9{10}=\frac{6156}{10000}$, so lost: $\frac{3844}{10000}$.
$$P(\text{Dubai}\mid\text{lost})=\frac{1710/10000}{3844/10000}=\frac{1710}{3844}=\frac{855}{1922}.$$ Answer: (B)
solutions.focus_note: Once the bag is on the wrong plane it is lost, whatever happens later, so "lost at Dubai" needs correct transfers before Dubai only (not after).

solutions.key_idea: The centres lie on the normal at $(1,2)$, at distance 5 on either side; test which circle contains the origin.
hints: The normal to $4x+3y=10$ at $(1,2)$ has direction $(4,3)$, a vector of length $5$.
Centres: $(1,2)\pm(4,3)$, i.e. $(5,5)$ and $(-3,-1)$. Which circle has the origin inside?
solutions.full_html: The circles touch at $(1,2)$, so both centres lie on the normal there, at distance $5$: $$C=(1,2)\pm(4,3)=(5,5)\ \text{or}\ (-3,-1).$$Origin inside means $OC<5$: $|(5,5)|=5\sqrt2>5$, $|(-3,-1)|=\sqrt{10}<5$. So the centre is $(-3,-1)$ and the circle is $$(x+3)^2+(y+1)^2=25\iff x^2+y^2+6x+2y-15=0.$$ Answer: (B)
solutions.focus_note: Check "origin inside" with $S(0,0)<0$: for (B), $S(0,0)=-15<0$. Option (A) is the other circle, which leaves the origin outside.

solutions.key_idea: Solve the recurrence $P_n=\frac23P_{n-1}+\frac13P_{n-2}$ with $P_0=1$, $P_1=\frac23$; the limit is $\frac1{1+\frac13}$.
solutions.full_html:
$P_n-P_{n-1}=\left(-\frac13\right)^{n-1}(P_1-P_0)=\left(-\frac13\right)^n$.
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}P_n=1+\frac{-1/3}{1+1/3}=1-\frac14=\frac34.$$ Answer: 0.75
solutions.alt_html: Long-run argument: the mean step length is $\frac43$, so the fraction of integers landed on is $\frac34$.
solutions.focus_note: Elegant check: in the long run the average step is $\frac23\cdot1+\frac13\cdot2=\frac43$, so a given score is hit with probability $\frac{1}{4/3}=\frac34$.

solutions.key_idea: Local extrema of $g_1$ are where $\prod(x-i)^i$ changes sign (odd $i$); for $g_2$ and $g_3$ check sign changes of the derivative.
hints: $g_1'=\prod(x-i)^i$ changes sign only at odd $i$: $1,3,\dots,19$ (ten points, alternately max and min).
solutions.full_html:
$g_1$: $g_1'(x)=\prod_{i=1}^{19}(x-i)^i$. For $0$g_2$: $g_2'=4900(x-1)^{48}(x-2)$: no sign change at $1$, a minimum at $2$. $\alpha_2=1$, $\beta_2=0$.
$g_3$: near $x=1$, $g_3\le0$ with $g_3(1)=0$: a maximum. Near $3$, $g_3\ge0$: a minimum. No extremum at $2$ (odd power). $g_3'/g_3=0$ is a quadratic with one root in $(1,2)$ (a minimum, $g_3<0$ there) and one in $(2,3)$ (a maximum, $g_3>0$). So $\alpha_3=\beta_3=2$.
$$\lambda=25+0+4=29,\qquad\lambda-20=9.$$ Answer: (D)
solutions.focus_note: At a zero of even multiplicity a function touches the axis, which is an extremum, even though the derivative there does not "change sign" in the usual way.

solutions.key_idea: $A$ must be upper triangular unipotent: $A=I+xE+yE^2$ with $E$ the shift; expand $A^{2025}$ binomially.
solutions.full_html:
Write $\begin{bmatrix}2&2&0\\0&2&2\\0&0&2\end{bmatrix}=2I+2E$, where $E$ has 1s just above the diagonal and $E^3=O$. The polynomial $t^{2025}+t$ is strictly increasing, so $A$ is a polynomial in $E$ as well: $A=I+xE+yE^2$. Then$$A^{2025}+A=2I+2026x\,E+\left(2026y+\tbinom{2025}2x^2\right)E^2.$$So $x=\frac1{1013}$ and $y=-\frac{2025\cdot2024}{2\cdot2026}x^2=-\frac{2025\cdot1012}{2\cdot1013^3}$.
(A) $A^{2025}=2I+2E-A$ has diagonal $2-1=1$: trace $3$. True.
(B) $A$ is unitriangular, so $|A|=1$ and $|A^{2026}|=1$. True.
(D) $a_{13}=y=-\frac{2025\cdot1012}{2\cdot1013^3}$. True.
Answer: (A), (B), (D)
solutions.focus_note: Nilpotent matrices make huge powers easy: the binomial expansion stops after $E^2$. Read the entries of $I+xE+yE^2$ carefully: $a_{12}=a_{23}=x$ and $a_{13}=y$.

solutions.key_idea: Use $\sum rC_r=n2^{n-1}$ and $\sum r^2C_r=n(n+1)2^{n-2}$.
solutions.full_html:
$$\sum(r^2-3r+1)C_r=n(n-1)2^{n-2}-2n\cdot2^{n-1}+2^n=2^{n-2}(n^2-5n+4).$$So $f(x)=x^2-5x+4$ with roots $1$ and $4$.
(A) $3\alpha+4\beta=19$ or $16$: true. (B) $\alpha\beta(\alpha+\beta)=4\cdot5=20$: true. (D) $2,5$ are roots of $x^2-7x+10$: true.
Answer: (A), (B), (D)

wrong_options.C: $f(x+1)=0$ means $x+1\in\{1,4\}$, so the roots are $0$ and $3$, not $1$ and $3$.

solutions.focus_note: Write $r^2$ as $r(r-1)+r$ so that standard binomial sums apply.

solutions.key_idea: Expand the triple products: $\vec a=\vec y-\vec z$, $\vec b=\vec z-\vec x$; then $(\vec a+\vec b)\times\vec c=\vec x+\vec y$.
hints: $\vec x\times(\vec y\times\vec z)=(\vec x\cdot\vec z)\vec y-(\vec x\cdot\vec y)\vec z=\vec y-\vec z$.
$\vec a+\vec b=\vec y-\vec x$, and $(\vec y-\vec x)\times(\vec x\times\vec y)=\vec x+\vec y$.
solutions.full_html:
With $|\vec x|^2=2$ and all mutual dot products $=\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt2\cos60^\circ=1$:
$\vec a=\vec y-\vec z$, $\vec b=\vec z-\vec x$, so $\vec a+\vec b=\vec y-\vec x$.
$(\vec y-\vec x)\times(\vec x\times\vec y)=\big[(\vec y\cdot\vec y)\vec x-(\vec y\cdot\vec x)\vec y\big]-\big[(\vec x\cdot\vec y)\vec x-(\vec x\cdot\vec x)\vec y\big]=\vec x+\vec y$.
Let $\vec w=(\vec a+\vec b)\times\vec c=\vec x+\vec y$. Then:
(A) $\frac12[\vec w-(\vec a+\vec b)]=\frac12[(\vec x+\vec y)-(\vec y-\vec x)]=\vec x$. True.
(B) $\frac12[(\vec a+\vec b)+\vec w]=\vec y$. True.
(C) $\frac12[(\vec b-\vec a)+\vec w]=\frac12[(2\vec z-\vec x-\vec y)+\vec x+\vec y]=\vec z$. True.
Answer: (A), (B), (C)

wrong_options.D: $\vec w=\vec x+\vec y$, which is not $\vec x+\vec y+\vec z$ (it misses $\vec z\ne\vec0$).

solutions.focus_note: Expand every triple product with "BAC–CAB" first; with equal dot products the expressions collapse.
solutions.note_html: $\vec a=\vec y-\vec z$, $\vec b=\vec z-\vec x$, $(\vec a+\vec b)\times\vec c=\vec x+\vec y$.

solutions.key_idea: Binomial with $n=50$, $p=\frac1{100}$: compute each case.
solutions.full_html:
(A) At least once $=1-\left(\frac{99}{100}\right)^{50}$, so (R).
(B) Exactly once $=\frac12\left(\frac{99}{100}\right)^{49}$, so (P).
(C) At least twice $=1-\left(\frac{99}{100}\right)^{49}\left(\frac{99}{100}+\frac12\right)=1-\frac{149}{100}\left(\frac{99}{100}\right)^{49}$, so (S).
(D) At most twice $=\frac{99^{48}}{100^{50}}\left(99^2+50\cdot99+1225\right)=\frac{15976\cdot99^{48}}{100^{50}}$, so (Q).
Answer: (D)
solutions.focus_note: Factor out the common power $\left(\frac{99}{100}\right)^{48}$ or $^{49}$ to match the listed forms quickly.

solutions.key_idea: $2^{n+1}+\frac1{2^n}=\frac{1+2^n\cdot2^{n+1}}{2^{n+1}-2^n}$, so each term is $\tan^{-1}2^{n+1}-\tan^{-1}2^n$; telescope.
solutions.focus_note: Inverse-trig series almost always telescope via $\tan^{-1}\frac{a-b}{1+ab}$. Write the general term with $n$ first, then spot $a$ and $b$.

solutions.key_idea: Intersect the internal bisectors for $I$ and the external ones for $I_A$; $B$, $C$, $I$, $I_A$ are concyclic with diameter $II_A$.
hints: $I$ = meet of the internal bisectors: $x+y=1$, $3x-y=-9$ give $I(-2,3)$.
$I_A$ = meet of the external bisectors: $x-y=-4$, $x+3y=-12$ give $I_A(-6,-2)$.
solutions.full_html: $\angle IBI_A=\angle ICI_A=90^\circ$ (internal ⊥ external bisectors), so $B$, $C$ lie on the circle with diameter $II_A$. Its centre is the circumcentre of $\triangle IBC$: $$\left(\frac{-2-6}2,\frac{3-2}2\right)=\left(-4,\frac12\right).$$$2b-a=1+4=5$. Answer: 5
solutions.focus_note: Internal and external bisectors at a vertex are perpendicular, so $I$, $I_A$, $B$, $C$ are concyclic. That fact is the whole question.

solutions.key_idea: With $a=e^{ix}$ etc., the two conditions say $a+b+c=2abc$; then $ab+bc+ca=abc\,\overline{(a+b+c)}$.
hints: $\cos x+\cos y+\cos z=2\cos(x+y+z)$ and the same for $\sin$ combine to $a+b+c=2abc$.
solutions.full_html:
Multiply the sine condition by $i$ and add it to the cosine condition: $a+b+c=2e^{i(x+y+z)}=2abc$, where $a=e^{ix}$ etc. ($|a|=|b|=|c|=1$).
Now $$ab+bc+ca=abc\left(\bar a+\bar b+\bar c\right)=abc\cdot\overline{2abc}=2|abc|^2=2.$$The real part of $ab+bc+ca$ is $\cos(x+y)+\cos(y+z)+\cos(z+x)$, so the value is $2$. Answer: (C)
solutions.focus_note: Whenever $\cos$ and $\sin$ sums appear in the same ratio, combine them into one complex equation. On the unit circle, $\frac1a=\bar a$ does the rest.

solutions.key_idea: Factor $A^{2024}(A+2I)(A+2\beta I)$; since $A$ is invertible, one factor must be singular.
solutions.full_html:
$$A^{2026}+2(\beta+1)A^{2025}+4\beta A^{2024}=A^{2024}\big(A^2+2(\beta+1)A+4\beta I\big)=A^{2024}(A+2I)(A+2\beta I).$$$\det A=-2\beta(-3+3)-0+1(3-4)=-1\ne0$, so we need $\det(A+2I)=0$ or $\det(A+2\beta I)=0$.
With $p(\lambda)=\lambda^3+(2\beta+2)\lambda^2+(4\beta-4)\lambda+1$:
• $p(-2)=-8+8\beta+8-8\beta+8+1=9\ne0$, so $A+2I$ is never singular.
• $p(-2\beta)=-8\beta^3+8\beta^3+8\beta^2-8\beta^2+8\beta+1=8\beta+1$. Zero when $\beta=-\frac18$.
Then $20\beta=-2.5$, $[-2.5]=-3$, and $|[20\beta]|=3$. Answer: 3
solutions.focus_note: The greatest integer of a negative number goes down: $[-2.5]=-3$, not $-2$. Also factor the matrix polynomial before computing anything: you never need $A^{2024}$.
solutions.note_html: $\det A=-1$, so we need $(A+2I)(A+2\beta I)$ singular; $-2$ is never an eigenvalue, so $\beta=-\tfrac18$. $[20\beta]=[-2.5]=-3$. The paper prints the bracket as a double bracket; the key 3 only fits $|[20\beta]|$ (not $[|20\beta|]=2$), so it is typeset that way here.

solutions.key_idea: Write $3\cos B\cos C=\frac32(\cos(B-C)-\cos A)$; then $2\sin A-\frac32\cos A\le\frac52$, so equality forces $B=C$.
solutions.full_html:
$$2\sin A+3\cos B\cos C=\left(2\sin A-\tfrac32\cos A\right)+\tfrac32\cos(B-C)\le\tfrac52+\tfrac32=4.$$Equality needs $B=C$ and $(\sin A,\cos A)\parallel\left(2,-\frac32\right)$: $\sin A=\frac45$, $\cos A=-\frac35$.
So (A) and (D) are true. The triangle is isosceles with $a=8$ and $\tan\frac A2=\frac{\sin A}{1+\cos A}=2$, so the altitude from $A$ is $\frac a2\cot\frac A2=2$ and the area is $8$.
Answer: (A), (D)

wrong_options.C: The altitude to $BC$ is $2$, so the area is $\frac12\cdot8\cdot2=8$, not $1$.

solutions.focus_note: An "$=$ maximum" condition in a triangle is a disguised equality case. Find the upper bound, then read off the equality conditions.
solutions.note_html: $2\sin A-\tfrac32\cos A+\tfrac32\cos(B-C)\le\tfrac52+\tfrac32=4$; equality forces $B=C$, $\sin A=\tfrac45$, $\cos A=-\tfrac35$. Then the altitude is 2 and the area is 8.

solutions.key_idea: Note $\frac{\cos x-\sin x}{(\cos x+\sin x)^3}=\frac{d}{dx}\left(-\frac1{2(\cos x+\sin x)^2}\right)$; integrate by parts twice.
hints: $\frac{d}{dx}\frac1{(\cos x+\sin x)^2}=\frac{-2(\cos x-\sin x)}{(\cos x+\sin x)^3}$, and $(\cos x+\sin x)^2=1+\sin2x$.
solutions.full_html:
Let $I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{x^2(\cos x-\sin x)}{(\cos x+\sin x)^3}dx=-\frac12\int_0^{\pi/2}x^2\,d\!\left(\frac1{1+\sin2x}\right)$.
By parts: $$I=-\frac12\left[\frac{x^2}{1+\sin2x}\right]_0^{\pi/2}+\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{x}{1+\sin2x}dx=-\frac{\pi^2}8+J.$$With $x\to\frac\pi2-x$ (note $\sin2x$ is unchanged): $2J=\frac\pi2\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{dx}{1+\sin2x}$.
Since $1+\sin2x=2\cos^2\left(x-\frac\pi4\right)$: $$\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{dx}{1+\sin2x}=\frac12\Big[\tan\left(x-\tfrac\pi4\right)\Big]_0^{\pi/2}=\frac12(1+1)=1.$$So $J=\frac\pi4$ and $I=\frac\pi4-\frac{\pi^2}8$. Then $8I=2\pi-\pi^2=\pi(2-\pi)$, so $k=2$. Answer: (B)
solutions.focus_note: Spot the derivative hiding in the integrand before trying substitutions. The slip here is a sign in the parts step or forgetting the boundary term $-\frac{\pi^2}8$.

solutions.key_idea: Use $\bar z_k=\frac1{z_k}$: (B) $|z_1z_2+\ldots|=|z_1z_2z_3|\,|\bar z_1+\bar z_2+\bar z_3|$; (C) the expression equals its conjugate; (D) a right isosceles triangle.
hints: For (D): the condition makes the triangle right-angled at $z_3$.
solutions.full_html:
(B) $|z_1z_2+z_2z_3+z_3z_1|=|z_1z_2z_3|\cdot|\bar z_1+\bar z_2+\bar z_3|=|z_1+z_2+z_3|$. True.
(C) Let $w=\frac{(z_1+z_2)(z_2+z_3)(z_3+z_1)}{z_1z_2z_3}$. Using $\bar z_k=\frac1{z_k}$: $$\bar w=\frac{\left(\frac1{z_1}+\frac1{z_2}\right)\left(\frac1{z_2}+\frac1{z_3}\right)\left(\frac1{z_3}+\frac1{z_1}\right)}{\frac1{z_1z_2z_3}}=\frac{(z_1+z_2)(z_2+z_3)(z_3+z_1)}{z_1^2z_2^2z_3^2}\cdot z_1z_2z_3=w.$$ So $w$ is real. True.
